" TENTH SOCIETY SIFTATE ": A Social Brochure. --By ALEXANDER WADDELL. Excerpts from some of the many Press opinions : "The writer urges the necessity and the pleasure of spiritual intercourse with GOD."—Liverpool Mercury, April 15, 1891.

" Mr. Waddell writes in a pleasant and earnest style, sifting the experiences he has had in various parts of the country with a view to presenting something to the reader which is well worth considering.' —Warrington Examiner, June 27th, 1891. _

"The papers are written from a remarkable knowledge of Scripture, and recommend themselves by their quiet earnest- ness of style."---Scotsman, March 23rd, 1891. - "With this key to the character of the work, the pages which follow prove interesting reading, and reveal the author as a close and appreciative observer of nature, and one who sees sermons in stones, books in the running brooks, and good in everything"—Preston Herald, April 4th, 1891. - "A deep religious tone pervades the book, and as the writer has evidently travelled far and near, his anecdotes and description of places are both telling and interesting."— The Isle of Wight Times, May 7th, 1891. " ' The Tenth Society Siftate' deserves, and should have, a wide circulation."—Northasnptors Herald, May 2nd, 1891. "There is the ring of sound common sense in all the writer says. He sets up before young men a high ideal of life. * * * It is bright and interesting and in many parts, especially the first chapter, it is humorous."— Christian Union, April 18,1891. Extract from letter received by the author from his friend, the Rev. J. Lewellyn Roberts, M.A., vicar of Spratton, and Hon. Canon of Peterborough, March 22nd, 1891.—" There is something so chattyand cheerful, so kindly and friendly, that one takes up the book and lays it down again, and dips in here and dips in there, and finds that one has learned a good deal, or received many a happy suggestion, all by way of a pleasant talk." "It is .sot often that an unprofessional autbor writes with such tact and skill, with such ease and grace, and yet with such masterly force as the author of the Tenth Society Siftate. The treatise has in it all the traits of that originality and piquancy that makes a social brochure popular and fasein- ating."—The Christian Union (2nd Notice), June 29th, 1891.

IT is the diamond miner who is the roost uccess- fill discoverer of strata-gems. AN engagement is a very fragile thing. It, cannot be dropped without breaking it. So= gentlemen who wind their watches at night are apt to wind them up tight. THERE are several ways to pay bills, but the Majority of the big ones are paid with reluctance. HE—" I never laugh at an inferior." She-7 "It would be imposeible for you to do such a thing." FIRST LITTLE GIRL—" IS your doll a French doll 7" Secand Little Girl—" I den:t, know; she can't talk." LAWYER (explaining to client)—" Well, now, my dear sir, to tell you the truth ' Client (bouncing up and out)—" You are no lawyer." "I AM surpr:sed at Charley's squandering so much money on a phonograph." "Well, I'm not. He always did like to hear himself talk." A NEGRO offering to lift a yoneg lady over a gutter, she insisted that she was too heavy. " Lor, missus," said he, 'Use used to lifting barrels of sugar." POETESS—" I have here a little poem—the only one I ever wrote, and—" Editor (grandly)—" Keep It, dear madam, keep it. I would not deprive you of it for the world." Mus. Cultso—"Johnny, put on your shoes and go to llars. Jones and borrow some coffee." Johnny— " Why can't I go barefooted ? " Mrs. Cumse— "Because I don't want you to go on% bootless errand." STRANGER (in the Cond-room)—" What time have you got, please?" Prisoner (at counsei4 table)—"l can tell you better after the trial." ON a certain Scotch Earl—a notoriously dull man —demanding the Order of the "Thistle," Lord Melbourne exclaimed, "Give the Thistle to— Why, damn it, he'd eat it " PERDITO—" What a cheerful way you must have of refusing a man. You seem to send them sway supremely happy." Beatrice—" I tell them that the report that I am a great heiress is a mistake." ONE of the pretty young women at the 'Arlon masquerade represented La Grippe. Some of the young men present would have given something nice to have been seized by La Grippe—and held for life. PONBONBY—" We were sitting at dinner, and I was telling a story, when the roof fell in without the slightest warning." Dolliver—" No warning? Didn't they know you were going to tell one of your funny stories?" MISS THIRTY-EIGHT (coyly)—" What a pity it Seems, Mr. Somerset, that a man like you should be' a bachelor." Mr. Somerset—" Yes, Miss Thirty- eight, it does seem a pity, but I can't help it, you ' know. I was born so." ONE NIGHT, during a heated discussion in the House of Commons in which Horn Tooke bore a principal part, his chief antagonist said, "PH take the sense of the House." "And I'll take the non- sense and I'll beat you," retorted Toceie. LITTLE SISTER—" Ma wants you Sammy. Where've you been ' Sammy—" Fishin'." Little Sister—" Did you catch anything ? " Sammy (sadly)—"Nothin"t all." Little Sister (re- assuringly)—" Oh, but you will when you get home." YABEILEY—" These novelists make me tired. The idea of a • whithering glance!' As if anyone could be withered by a mere look." Wickwire—" You are young yet, Yabsley. You never stepped on your wife's train at a ball." HUBBY—" I do wish that baby next door would keep quiet. It's yelling is a terrible nuisance." Wiley—" Why, John, that's not the Smith's baby, It's ours in the back room." Hubby—"l.B that so The dear little darling." "WELL, John," said a gentleman to his servant, "I must say that it doesn't tak-: me half the time 1.0 dress that it does you." "No doubt, sir; no doubt; but then, sir, we are not alike, sir; for I've no valet to help me, sir." "COME here, waiter," said an Irishman who was drinking laser beer at a restaurant the other day, "now just tell the proprietor," he went on, when the garcon had answered his call, "that if this beer Isn't better to-morrow than this is which you've just brought me I will never enter this place again alter to-night.' THE PATERNAL Vinw.—Daughter—"l'a, Mr. Slim and I were discussing which was the prefer- able, 'he will go,' or 'he shall go.' What do you say ?" Pa (looking at his watch)—" As it is 11.30 o'clock, I should say he must go' was the correct expression." MOTHER—" John, you went to church as n,:ual to-day ?" Son—" Ye, mother." Mother—" What was the text ?" Son—" Well, er—you see I didn't get there in time to hear the text." Mother— " What was the gist of the sermon ?" Son—" I can't tell You see, mother, I came out just before he got to the gist." ACCORDING to the Boston Post, a Boston sign bears the artless inscription, "Cigars and cigarettes sold on the Sabbath for medicinal purposes only." This is by no means bad, but we still think that the blue riboon belongs to the proprietot of a Western skating rink Who advertised a sacred dog fignt for Sunday. • HUSBAND—" This gymnasium exercise is a great thing for one, I can tell you; Why, I sent an hour and a half- on the rowing macnine this afternoon, and didn't feel a bit tired." Wife (next morning) —"I wish you'd help with the washing machine work." Husband—" Do you want sue to break my back, Sarah? Go and get sonic tramp to do it." "HAVE the groceries come in yet, John? It is only five minutes before dinner, and the pantry's empty!" "No, ma'am, but they're on the way— the self-raising flour, the three-quarters cooked oatmeal, and the canned vegetables, Jimpson's XXX. ready prepared coffee, Erin's patent mashed potatoes, the twenty-second tea, the self-eating Limburger and all." QUICK, the comedian, once played for his benefit Richard 111. His intention was to have acted with becoming seriousness, but the public, anticipating a burlesque, would be satisfied with nothing else. When he came to the famous line, "A horse! a horse I my kingdom for a house I" he convulsed the house by adding quietly, "And if you can't get a horse bring a jackass." "AB, well," said Mrs. Naggleton, after a long dispute with Mr. N., and she thought the time had come for making a small concession; " Ah, well, I suppose I, too, have my faults I" "Indeed you have!" replied her husband emphatically. "What!" screamed Mrs. N., once more uplifting the battle- flag. "I should just like you, then, to tell me. what they are." A PARTY had gone one week day into a church to get a child baptised. While awaiting the arrival of the clergyman, the sexton created no little con- sternation by chucking the infant under the chin and addressing the person whom he took to be the author of its being—" You ahoul4 consider yourself lucky, sir. in havin4 a child that so closely resem- bles you." The person addressed was the god- father.

"GOOD MORNING, John," said the minister to a young friend whom he met on the street the first warm day of the season, " hosc does jour father stand the helt 7 " The young nian made no reply, but went his way with a clouded brow. And when the good pastor learned that the young man's father had died only a week before, he understood why his cordial greeting was met so coldly. "AT last my dearest," cried 'ln impassioned lover to the object of his affections: "At last we are alone in this room, far from the guests who crowd the drawing-room, and I can tell thetellyefuaihrobweinmgutchhuls love you!" "Impossible I" cried addressed, "don't you know that my mamma has just taken her seat at the piano? In another moment she will begin to sing, and then everyone will be taking refuge in here." SALESMAN—" Those confounded dress goods don't go cif worth a cent. They've been in stock now for over a year, and we haven't sold more 'n fifty yards, all told. Proprietor—" What did they nest as?" "Thirty-five cents. and I've been offer- ing them for a quarter." "Wily not try them on the bargain-counter I" "I suppose we might try It." "All right. And, Mr. Tatling, mark them at 79 cents. We must get rid of them in some way." —BoBton Transcript. "I SAY, Jenkins, can you tell a young chicken from an old one ? " "Of course I can." "Well, how?" "By the teeth." "Chickens don't have teeth." "No, but I have."

div.head: " CAPITAL "
div.p: " CAPITAL "

MastgT Henry Dickens, a grandson of the great novelist,was one of the prize winners at the Annual summer term distribution at the Ronian Catholic Beaumont College, at Windsor. Mister Dickens, also distinguished himself at the entertainment by reciting a selection from "Oliver Twist" in the German translation of Herr E. Seidt.

Taffy has held • his Eisteddfod this week at Swansea. The festival seems to be gaining strength and popularity every year, which is perhaps, in consequence of the new demands of Welsh nation- alism. Wales wants a capital and a msasure of Home Rule, but more than that, it wants the Church disestablished and the land laws reformed.

The very latest thing that ingenious woman has invented is that of wearing new hoots for other peo- ple. In a small and pettifogging way this has been practised in many households without fee or re- ward by long-suffering younger sisters, but the first to pet it .on a business ,footing —the word is used advisedly—is, of course, a smart qankee dam • sel.

Signor Foli has resolved to spend next summer in the Antipodes, and will sail in March to undertake a series of forty concerts in Australia. Madame Patey is expected in London from Australia during the second week of September, but Sir Charles and Lady Hallo will not return till about three weeks later. M. Paderewski, the pianist,. will also spend next summer in Australia.

A horse show, in connection with which was a jumping competition, was held a week or two ago at Calwell Court, Herefordshire. lam told that the rector of the parish gave instructions that none of the school-children were to attend the show,on the express ground that such an exhibition would carry them on the road to hell. If this is the result of exhibiting a prize horse, I would respectfully ask this rector what is likely to be the effeet in the parish of exhibiting himself as a prize donkey?

Miss Olive Schreiner, the South African novelist, is at present residing at Cape Town, where she mingles very freely in society and is frequently to be met at Government House. Miss Schreiner is quite a young lady, rather below the medium in height, with girlish form, dark lustrous eyes, and a profusion of brown hair. Unlike most writers, she is brilliant in conversation and will discuss without reserve the leading topics of the time. She is greatly interested in public matters, and is often present at the debates in the Cape Parliament.

The priest of Argenteuil, continuing the "Holy Coat" controversy, states that during the French Revolution the Coat of Argenteuil was not properly looked after, and a piece of it was lost, probably stolen. "It seems," says the priest, "that on the Treves. coat there is a piece of stuff which corres- ponds exactly with that of ours. This piece is of camel hair, woven by hand, and has the same ed- dish lustre as ours." The Bishop of Versailles is ap- pealing on the subject of the authenticity of the re- lics to the Pope hit.self against the decision of the Congregation of Rites.

During a recent visit of the Prince of Wales to Doncaster his Royal Highness and a friend went out for a stroll near Wentworth House, and came across a miner accompanied by a brace of bull pups. Wishing to appear sociable the Prince's friend asked how much he had paid for them. "Two quid" was the laconic reply. H.R.H. looked them over criti- cally, and remarked, "Don't you think two pigs would have been a better investment for you, my good man ?" "Happen so," replied the collier, "but, mister, what a blooming fool a chap would look going a rattin' wid two pigs."

Riverside resorts are very popular just now with artistes, actors, and literary Londoners whose work will not let them go further afield. Madame An- toinette Sterling has taken up her abode for the rest of the summer and autumn at Caversham, a charm- ing spot near Reading. Mrs. Jopling Rowe, the well- known artiste, has fixed on the beautiful Goring as her summer quarters. Jerome Jerome, the dramatic critic and "Idle Fellow," has moved from Clifton Hampden to lovely Pangbourne, and young actors and actresses may be seen lazily punting or sculling or camping out on sunny mornings.

The Prince of Wales has reached Homburg. He remains there for nearly a month. He will be glad of a rest after an unusually fatiguing season; but he has quite recovered his spirits, which were somewhat depressed-after the worries of the bac- carat trial and the tax upon his energies while he was following the too active young Raiser about Windsor and London. The Prince will take his cure, like other visitors to Homburg; will then pay 4ome visits; and will have afterwards to proceed to Denmark, where possibly he will stay to witness the betrothal of the Czarewitch to his cousin, the Princess Marie of Greece.

It has been ascertained by a careful observer that a swarm of flies cannot travel at any greater pace than eleven miles an hour. So much the better for the cyclist who has only to put on a spurt to get at any time clear away from this intolerable pest of the highways in warm weather. For the unfortun- ate outside passenger by drag or chaise there is no, help unless it is that patent fly veil which enabled the American editor to look forward to the time when whole congregations would be able in August to listen to a sermon in comfort while the flies in church," united as one fly." were "taking it out of the preacher in the pulpit."

Mr. Bradlaugh carried his plan of "thorough" to the reading of his books. His books now on sale have, in many cases, pencil marks or notes on the margins. He read pencil or pen in hand, and cor- rected as he went along. In Mr. Giffen's "Growth of Capital," for instance, he has corrected an error in subtraction, which Mr. Giffen and his proof- and also corrects Mr. or e iaf fdeenrn had gallowedgiving a tor epf ea rs es n, ce to one of his own books. Mr. Giffen says, "See Essays in Finance,' page 176." Mr. Bradlaughhas taken the trouble to alter to "page 165." Buying some of the books which he has thumbed well is like getting a revised edition of the works.

For the world of labour the Brussels !Congress is far and away the most important of the autumn caucuses. Every year that passes brings it home more clearly to the workers that if their condition is to be permanently improved, the advance must proceed by simultaneous and equal steps in every State. That English workers have at last thoroughly grasped this fact is shown by the strength of the contingent which England sends to the Brussels Congress. The influence of the English party may no doubt be seen in the decisive vote by which the Anarchists were on Sunday excluded—a vote which looks well for the prospects of a moder- ate and practical temper in the proceedings of the next few days.

A new danger has arisen for cyclists. Two wheel- men were charged recently with furious riding whereby a horse was caused to shy and occasion grievous damage to the occupants (two police offi- cers) of the vehicle it was drawing. Evidence was given that the speed of the cyclists, judging from the movements of their legs from directly in front, about sixty yards off, was sixteen miles an hour. As the men were riding low-geared safeties, this estimate must be taken for what it is worth. The shying of the horse, however, war, not ascribed to the speed of the riders, but to the white trousers worn by one of them. In face of this testimony, what could the Stevenage Petty Sessions Bench do hut fine the hardy wheelmen 30s. each, including costs? It appears, therefore. that if a cyclist dare to don white trousers, or to ride with one so appa- relled, his doom is sealed if a horse chooses to shy It 18 not so much a matter of brakes as of "breeks."

A good story (says the "Daily Telegraph ") comes from a well-known London club which has attached to it chambers for the use of members wanting temporary accommodation. Recently the Bishop of Nottingham telegraphed from the country for a bedroom, and on arriving in the town he drove at once to the chambers. "What name, sir ?" asked the porter., in answer to the suffragan's inquiry whether his apartments had been prepared, " The Bishop of Nottingham," replied Dr. Trollope. "There's no such .name," said the official, after a search through his book. "Look again," urged the astonished prelate. "No sir, nothing booked to you," was the answer; "But there is a room put down for Edward Nottingham, Esq..' This recalls two well-known cases of confusion arising from episcopal signatures. The late Archbishop of York once, putting up at a certain hotel, excited the, suspicions of the head waiter there by writing his name in the visitors' book. "'Shy," exclaimed Robert, "he is a regular impostor. . He isn't the Archbishop. Look here ! He signs himself 'W. Ebor ':" Again, there was the worthy trades-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATFRDAY, AUGUST 22, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATFRDAY, AUGUST 22, 1891.

man who wrote, in reply to a letter, "L am in re- ceipt of your esteemed order, but regrOt I cannot serve you without payment or a referende; as I am unacquainted with the name of your firm.—l am, "To Messrs. Sodor and Man."
ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.

Home for the homeless, for the protection, assistance and support of respectable aged or infirm women; Home of the Good Shepherd, for the care, maintenance and instruction of friendless, neglected or destitute children, irrespective of age, sect, creed or condition; St. Vincent's industrial school, for destitute children from Oneida and adjacent counties; St. Elizabeth hospital and home, whose object is to afford medical end surgical aid to the sick and destitute of both sexes, without regard to age, colour or creed ; Utica orphan asylum, for boys and girls ; Utica dispensary, where physicians are in daily attendance for free treatment of the sick poor. Every church and organisation in the city has its special charitable work, and the necessities of the worthy poor never fail to find here a prompt and speedy relief. The state hospital for the insane, in which there are nearly eight hundred inmates,:is a charitable institution located there, but as it is maintained by the state, Utica only claims for it that good judgment was used in the selection of its site.
A DARING IMPOSTOR:
THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT.
Br ALFRED R. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER I. AT LONG BRANCH.
"By Jove! Reybold, you are the most fortunate fellow in the world to know that girl; every young man at the Branch is crazy for an introduction, and even I—"

"And even you, Jack, can be crazy without it. Because I have the honour and good luck to know Miss Irene Lefferts and I stand well with her father why should I make myself a medium to put every other fellow, good, bad, and indifferent, in the same box?"

Mott Reybold switched his boot with a dainty cane, and gazed from his companion Jack Hyde, to the retreating figure of a queenly-looking girl, who with a number of girls of her own age and station of life, was on the way to the bathing-houses that line the shore along the cliff, or sea-bank at Long Branch.

These two young men, though more flashy in their attire than is customary with men of good breeding, yet had in their bearing more refinement than is often found among the betting men at race tracks, which their appearance at once suggested. After watching the bevy of laughing maidens till they were out of sight, Jack Hyde, the younger, lighter and more sprightly of the two men, ...id, with a manner that showed he did not consider an answer necessary to confirm his belief: "1 understand the fair lady's father is one of the richest men in the city." "Yes," drawled Mott Reybold, "he 'll do." "Owns great iron works, and all that ?" " Yes ; there's no danger of his going to ttte poorhouse." "And this young lady is hi 3 only heir?"
"Oh, no; there 's another." - " Indeed I I never heard of that. Boy or girl?" "Boy. I should say he 's a man. Come, Jack, don't tell me that you do not know Flashy II rank."

"What !—the faro king 7" cried Jack Hyde. "The faro king, the racing prince, the betting lord, and all that, as he is known to us; and the. disgraced outcast, as he is known to his own family and a few of their friends," said Mott Reybold switching his boots with his cane again, and sighing, as if to convey to his companion the impression that this was to him a very painful sub. ject indeed. "But what has Flashy Frank to do with Mr. Lefferts 9"
"Nothing, now." "But, did he ever have 7" "Yes." "In what way 7" "Oh, simply as his son. But, come, let us talk about something pleasanter."

"Your failure at the last Monmouth race, for instance," laughed Jack Hyde, as he lit a cigar, took his companion's arm, and started to walk along the shore, where, on the one hand, they could see the bathers sporting among the breakers and children playing in the sand, while on the other, carriages of every pattern and colour that wealth and varied taste could furnish rolled by with their fashionable occupants. That these two young men were well known to many of the occupants of carriages was evident from the frequency with which they raised their hats and the military regularity with which they bowed.

But their acquaintances were evidently not con- fined to this class, for they exchanged salutations with other men whose attire, dyed moustaches, and vulgar display of jewellery marked them to every one as members of what is known as "the sporting world." After walking a few hundred yards past the bathing houses, to which Irene Lefferts and her friend had gone, Mott Reybold and Jack Hyde came to a sudden stand, or rather the latter was forced to stand by the example of his companion, which was enforced by a strong grip on his arm. " Hello, Reybold 1 What's up ? Have you caught sight of your tailor or some other neglected creditor 1"

"Don't be a fool," was the emphatic rejoinder. "But look do you see that man standing over there on the bank, with his side face to us 7" "As my eyes are good, and the fellow is rather conspicuous, I will confess that I do see him," said Jack Hyde, with that airiness of manner that ap- peared to be his distinguishing characteristic. The man in question was a little above the medium height, slender, smootlf-taced, and certainly etill under thirty years of age, though there was an ex- pression in the dark eyes and a set to the lips that indicated great anxiety, if not physical suffering. The stranger's dress was old-fashioned, thread- bare, and even shabby, yet there was a certain something about it that told of a refinement that was present and a prosperity that was past. "That is rather a noted man," said Reybold. "Pray, what is he noted for 7" asked Jack Hyde. "In the first plac2, he must have left the peni- tentiary very lately, for I thought him there still." "If being in the penitentiary makes a man noted, why there are thousands of noted—" "Try to be serious, Jack. That fellow's name is, or was, Allen Lee; but criminals do not stick to one name. Four years ago he was the confidential Clerk of one of our most prominent bankers—" "Ah, say no more," interrupted Jack Hyde. "He took to gambling in stocks, playing at faro, or betting on horses; or, perhaps, he did all these things, which you and I think so wicked, and added thereto a gentleman's love for fine wines and good livitg. His income was inadequate; he failed in his speculations; stole money from his employer, or forged his name, intending to make it all right when he got flush. Never got flush. Discovery, disgrace, trial, conviction, penitentiary. Ah, it is the old story, and it is very common that I can't very well see how you can call the man 'noted.'" "If for nothing else, that he committed a forgery for a large amount without any apparent reason.. It was shown on the trial that his habits were excellent; that he cared for his mother and invalid father and educated his sister; and his efforts in his own defence—for he denied the charges—howed that he . was a man of wonderful acquirements and ability. The trial created a great sensation, so that I think I am justified in saying he ,is noted." I might add that our friend, Flashy Frank, was in some way mixed up with it. Hello! What's that 7"

This sudden turn in Mott Reybold's speech was caused by a chorus of shrill cries that came from the direction of the shore. As if that cry were a signal for which he was intenpy watching, the "noted" man sprang for- ward and leaped down the bank.
Mott Reybi-ad and Jack llyde turned pale and the former gasped: "There's some one drowning among the breakers!"

If tliis really were the ease, neither of the young men showed any disposition to go to the rescue. But the shrieking crowd from the roadway swept them over to the bank in an instant, and they looked in the direction from which the cries came.

Swarms of trembling, dripping bathers had fled from the surf to the shore. Crowds of white-faced people had run down to the sand, where they stood wringing their hands and shouting for " Help ! " Every face was turned to the line of breakers, beyond which the head of a helpless swimmer could be seen, while now and then a white arm was raised appealingly for aid. "Where's the life-boat 7 " "Where are the swimmers paid to watch the shore " " Who is she ?"
"Is there no man to go to the rescue 7"

As this last question was shouted by ;ome one In the crowd, a young man, who had been divesting himself of hat, boat and shoes as he ran down to the shore, dashed through the throng and plunged into the breakers booming along the shore. The brave act loosened the tongues of the spell- bound people, and they greeted, with a cheer of approval, the deed of which they welt themselves Incapable. The lady who had been swept beyond the line of breakers by the undertow must have seen the man coming to her rescue, for she raised both arms and held them towards him for an instant: then, over- come by the last effort, .she sank out of sight. " Hurry 1 Hurry 1" cried the now frantic crowd on shore. '
But with the roar of the surf thundering in his ears, and his eyes fixed on the sinking figure, the daring swimmer did not hear them, nor could he have put forth a mightier effort had he done so.
"He has gone down, too I" cried the people, as the brave fellow disappeared from sight over the place where had vanished the person to whose rescue he had gone. "He dived I"
"lie dove !" "lie's sunk !" "Both are zone 1'

Over the breakers curling at their teet the people bent in their eagerness to catch a glimpse of some one or something rising above the expanse of Un- dulating calm beyond the line of surf. " Hurrah I There they arc!" . __

Twenty yards beyond the place where he had dis- appeared the swimmer came up, and as he turned his face to the shore another face could be seen resting on his shoulder. At this sight women ell sobbing with joy on each other's necks, and men who were strangers shook hands with each other like old friends offer- ing congratulations. But the swimmer needed their help instead of their plaudits. Alone, he could have made the shore with an effort; but, burdened as he was, and with the tide and undertow against him, it was impossible for him to do more than keep afloat. "Where is the boat 9" "Where are the men with the life-lines 9"

The men who sent up these shouts knew what was wanted, but they were unable to help, for there is a world of difference between knowing what should be done and doing it. But the life-boat men have heard the alarm. From the direction of the iron pier—it seemed miles away to the eager people—the life-boat shot down, urged by four powerful rowers, while a bronzed sailor, with a coil of rope in his hands, stood up in the bow and watched the two white faces as they drifted out to sea. A few minutes, that seemed like hours, and the life-boat shot in between the people on shore and the people out amid the waves. "Hurrah! they are up with them!" "They've got the girl on board ! " "The man Where's the man ? " "He's gone down I "

"Save him! Save him 1" shouted the people to the men in the boat, as if their wild cries could urge them to more coolness and greater effort. They were right. The instant the precious burden had been taken from his arms by the men in the life-boat the brave fellow sank as if be had been deprived of the one thing that supported him during this most trying ordeal. On the instant the man in the bow of the boat was seen to leap through the air, and, a silvery spray shot up over the place where he disappeared. At such times seconds seem like minutes to those watching but unable to help. The coolest on shore was beginning to feel that ueither the sailor nor the man to whose rescue Re had gone would ever appear again, when the men in the boat could be seen bending over and lifting a body from the water._
Than the sailor was helped in, and took his place in the stern of the boat.
A great gasp of relief went up from the people on shore, and every one seemed, on the instant, to understand what _should be done next.
Doctors suddeglY appeared by the half dozen, and men ran off to get stretchers to carry the lady and her rescuer to their homes.

By this time it had become generally known that the lady was Miss Irene Lefferts, but the man who had gone to help her was known to only one in the crowd, and Mott ybold kept his knowledge to himself.
But the time had comp for him to manifest interest.

He knew that Mr. Lefferts was in New York, and his housekeeper at their beautiful cottage, a short distance away; so, as a friend of the family, he took upon himself the care of Irene as soon as the life-boat shot up on the sands. The young lady, though much exhausted, was perfectly conscious and self-possessed as she was lifted from the boat amid the plaudits of the crowd.

"Let me carry you to the carriage. A doctor will accompany us to the house," said liott Reybold, as he supported Irene. "I can make my way home," she said, "but care for that brave man." And she pointed to the boat. "I fear he has given his life for mine."
CHAPTER IL ALLEN LEE.

Surrounded by swarms of friends, Irene Lefferts was conducted to her home, and every than who had seen her rescue tried to look as if he vvere the one who had accomplished it. The world is full of cool, heroic men, when the need for them is past, but when wanted it is a rare thing to find the right man in the right ph, (:e. But, after all, there is a great well of sympathy and a fine apppreciation of a brave achievement in the average human heart. Allen Lee was not forgotten when the safety of Irene Lefferts was assured.
Brave fellow 1" "What's his name?" "Where does he live?" "Will he 1e V'

These questions were asked by the crowd without any thought that an answer would be given, as the four sailors placed Allen Lee on a stretcher, and, followed by a doctor, hastened to the life-saving station near by. One countryman, who had been a witness of the young man's act, looked dawn on the white face on the stretcher and gave expression to his feelings after this fashion:
"If that young feller lives, an' he chances to be from Jarsey, I'd like powerful much to vote for him for_gov'nor, no matter which party put him up."

The doctor, :who followed the- stiet-cher-bearers to the life-saving station, found there all the appli- ances invented by medical science for the resuscita- tion of those apparently drowned. • The doors of the place were closed against the crowd, but they sell hung about the place, for death—inevitable to all, and with which the most favoured must be familiar—stirs as nothing else can the morbid curiosity of the masses. Familiar with such things, the life-boatmen proved to be most valuable assistants to the doctor. " Ah, he's built like a blooded racer; no spare flesh on him, and every muscle fine as polished steel," said one of the men, as the body was stripped and placed on a cot prepared under the doctor's directions.

" His clothes don't look as if he was over-well to- do, but, judging by his hands, I should say he was not in the labouring line," said another, as he began rubbing an arm, while the doctor was pressing on the breast to induce artificial respira- tion.
After a half hour's constant effort the breast began slowly to rise and fall of its own accord, and the nervous twitching of the eyelids told that con- sciousness was returning. _ _

Brandy was forced between the blue lips, and then hot blankets were wrapped about him, though the sun was very warm outside. While one of the men was telling the crowd that still lingered without, that the young man was out of danger, the poor fellow—as if roused by the cheering—opened his eyes and asked:

"Is the lady saved f" "Yes, thanks to you, my brave friend, she is alive and well. You will be all right in a few hours. In the meantime, if you give me your name, I will telegraph your safety to your friends, and gratify your thousands of admirers by telling them who you are," said the doctor, as he took out a memorandum book and made ready to write. "Friends, admirers ?" repeated the young man; and he rubbed his eyes, as if the act might clear his brain and enable him the better to under- stand. _ _

"Yes," said the doctor, "every one who witnessed your act to-day and the millions who will read of it to-morrow must be your admirers; and a gallant fellow like you cannot be without friends. Come let me begin with your name." And the doctor bent over and moistened the tip of his pencil between his lips. After a pause that was becoming painful, the young man whispered: "Just *rite 'Allen Gilbert.' That's all. I 'll be well directly. Find my hat, coat and shoes. I threw them off as I ran down—"
Exhausted by the effort, his head fell back and he closed his eyes again, as if to sleep. "Let him rest and have quiet for an hour or two, and he will be himself again," said the doctor.

The men of the life-boat went out with him, and one of' them started off to find the articles of cloth- ing thrown off by Allen " Gilbert " as he made his way to the rescue. Shabby enough articles they were, and the only thing found in the pockets of the coat was a slip on which was written "Try 128, Pine-place, Brook- lyn." The sailor who had found the clothing held them on his arm, and was talking with the doctor, when they were joined by Mott Reybold. "Have I the honour of addressing Doctor Put- nam 7 Ah, yes; thought I could not be mistaken. My name is Reybold," said the new-comer, as he held out his hand.

In answer to Mott Reybold's inquiries, the doctor said that the young man who had rescued Miss Lefferts was out of danger; his name was Allen Gil- bert, and he modestly requested not to be made an object of attention. ".31r, Lariats heard from some MM. I don't know."

div.head: BY "TOWNSMAN." X.-A TYPICAL AMERICAN CITY.
div.p: BY "TOWNSMAN." X.-A TYPICAL AMERICAN CITY.
A FINE THOROUGHFARE-BEAUTIFUL HOUSES- BUSINESS HOUSES-THE PEOPLE-PUBLIC BUILD- INGS - SQUARES AND PARKS-FIRE ENGINE
STATIONS-A CITY OF CHARITY.

Nearly three hundred miles north-west of New York City, and in the very centre of New York State, lies the city of Utica, which may be taken as a typical American city. Utica is beautifully situ- ated in the middle of the Mohawk valley, and is surrounded by an extensive amphitheatre of hills. Viewed from the southern heights, the valley greatly reminded me of Derwentwater, but the Mohawk differs in two features—the panorama is much vaster than that presented by the English lake, and the valley consists of farming land in- stead of water. For all that, the prospect is very charming, bathed as it is in most brilliant sunshine, and every object in the landscape visible for miles in the clear atmosphere. So impressed was I with the lovely outlook, that I could not help thinking of the former possessors of the soil, who wandered at will over the enchanting valley, and who, poor fellows, have now been deprived of a most in- teresting inheritance. To the fierce Mohawk Indians has succeeded a peaceful, industrious population, with all the characteristics of the American people. They live in a city of great area, with well laid-out streets, well provided with trees. Indeed, so numerous are the trees that the city, seen from the hills, seems to be completely buried in them. The only objects visible above the great tree tops are the church spires and the factory chimneys. If you enter the city by tt e West-Shore Rail-road, you are" let down" at a very barn-like depot, and at once enter upon Genesee-st.,

div.head: FINEST THOROUGHFA.RE IN THE CITY.
div.p: THE FINEST THOROUGHFA.RE IN THE CITY.

It stretches on the straight from the river that flows at the foot of the city, to New Hartford, a very pleasant village, four miles south of Utica. Taken altogether, Genesee-st. is a gem. It is worth braving the dangers of an Atlantic voyage to feast your eyes upon one of the finest, neatest, and most picturesque streets that I have yet beheld. I have seen the leading thoroughfares in London, Paris, Dublin, and Chicago, but still this richly-kept road in a small city of 40,000 inhabitants takes my eye. We have certainly nothing like' it in England. There are, it is true, a few bits of Southport that are a little similar, but there is nothing that will bear comparison. For the two miles that Genesee- st. runs into the city, it is wide enough to admit half-a-dozen buggies abreast, and on each siiie of it are footpaths almost as wide as an English street. Part of this space, however, is occupied with noble elms that line the thoroughfare to the business portion of the city, and that form shady avenues across the paths, and almost across the street itself. Between the road and the path, too, are grass plots that extend the length of the trees, and impart an additional attraction to the way. But the great charm of the street lies in its houses.

div.head: BEAUTIFUL STRUCTURES
div.p: BEAUTIFUL STRUCTURES

of wood, or brick, or stone, of every conceivable style of architecture,from a box-like building to a Moorish house, front the road, and give to it a colour that charms the beholder. The houses are faced by beautiful lawns that skirt the footpath without any protection, and impart to their surroundings an air of freedom that is totally lacking in English cities. Indeed, the majority of the houses are such as in England would Ipe built in the middle of a park, or surrounded with an Bft. wall—to keep the passers-by from even obtaining a glimpse of the building. But though American houses and grounds are thus open to the road, no advantage is taken of this fact, and not a blade of grass is disturbed by pedestrians. The houses are occu- pied by the leading and wealthiest families of the city, and I was informed that amongst the residents were some half-dozen millionaires. This half-dozen included two or three widow ladies, and the number of widows who live along the street is remarkable. The street is undulating in character, and is covered for half its length with asphalt. This portion is the favourite prac- tice ground for the city cyclists, and I have seen as fine exhibitions of cycle riding here as can be seen in many circuses. Among the cyclists was a fair proportion of lady riders, and the cycle, as a means of recreation, seems to be in greater favour with yotvig American ladies than with their eousines in England. The as- phalt ends about Oneida-square, an open space where several streets converge. The most conspicuous object in the square is a tall electric lizhtincr erection, which is soon to give place to a monument to the memory of the soldiers who fell in the war. A couple of drinking foun- tains also occupy positions on the square, but their use- fulness was impaired for want of water. A little dis- tance from this point the street slopes down to

div.head: TTIE BUSINESS HOUSES OF THE CITY
div.p: TTIE BUSINESS HOUSES OF THE CITY

Many of the shops are of recent erection, and are of very good proportions. They are mostly built in blocks after the natimial fashion and the upperrooms are let off for offices. This portion of Genesee-st. affords a com- plete contrast to the southern part. The sylvan quietude of the depot end is replaced with the activity of American city life. The street is crowdcd with an eager, bustling throng, and the roar of business is heightened with the constant passing of electric trams, and the flitting to and fro of private buggies and tradesmen's carts. Over- head the street is, as usual with all American cities, a network of wires, and the telephone is installed iu all business houses, and most private residences of any pre- tension.

div.head: PEOPLE AND PUBLIC BUILDINGS.
div.p: THE PEOPLE AND PUBLIC BUILDINGS.

The inhabitants of the city are of every nationality, and shade of colour, but there is a large German colony. They are employed in cotton and woollen mills, garden implement works, and house furnace foundaries. There are also boot manufactories, and extensive lumber works where 'all the latest improvements in wood working machinery are in full swing. The city boasts of several handsome public buildings. It has a splendid Post Office —twice the size of the Warrington Chief Office—three sides of which are open to the public, who are permitted to see through the numerous windows what is going on inside. It has a large justice hall with a court room, such as befits a city of 40,000 inhabitants, and such as is badly wanted in Warrington. It has a nice little public library, some extensive public schcols, an imposing Y.M.C.A. building and several handsome churches. Be- sides Genesee-street, the city has numerous fine avenues, and in addition to these, there are two or three

div.head: SQUARPS AND SMALL PARKS.
div.p: SQUARPS AND SMALL PARKS.

The largest of these-hi—C—ba-ne;11;:e, a plot about at large as the Warrington Recreation ground at Bank Park. Unlike the Recreation ground, however, with its asylum-like enclosure, Chancellor-square is without fence of any sort,and 15 intersected by paths in every direction. In the middle is a large fountain, with an allegorical figure, which plays throughout the day. Park seats are placed in all the paths, and great advantage is taken of this sylvan retreat. At the dinner hour and after work in the evening,the square paths are crowded with people making for their homes, who are thus enabled to enjoy the sight of a little greenery to cheer them on their way. As I sat and watched the factory lasses crossing the square, I could not help thinking of the dog-in-the- manger policy pursued with respect to Bank Park,where the authorities think they are conferring a favour upon us by admitting us at gates quarter of a mile out ot our way. When will our powers-that-be repose more confi- dence in the people?
FIRE ENGINE STATIONS.

The city possesses six fire stations, which are situated in different parts of the city, and wkich are communi- cated with by means of some eighty alarm boxes at various places. These alarms are so arranged that when given people all over the city can tell the immediate neighbourhood of the fire. I visited one of the stations in Park Avenue, and found it a brick building specially erected for the purpose. The engine Szc. occupied the main floor, and behind these were the stables in which were the four horses required. Above were the men's quarters, and very neat, clean and comfortable were the beds for the six men engaged, at the station. Fire engine appli- ances have been brought to perfection by the Americans, and I had an opportunity of witnessing a rehearsal. Though I repeatedly saw the fire engines rushing along the streets of Chicago and Montreal, I never saw them in action. Still, the practice showed what they are capable of. At seven o'clock in the evening, the men were standing about when the great gong sounded with apractise alarm from the chief station. Immediately the gates of the station vjTele thrown open by electricity, theer estable a sed doors were IY opened, and the horses w frwomthselmstialallrsi. With flashing eyes and rel dilating nostrils the horses rushed to their places at the engine, the harness mechancially dropped upon them, and they were ready to stFt• The turn-out was smartly performed, and was done in a few seconds. To-test one of the horses, a chair was purposely placed in its way, but eager as the animal was to take its position, it did so without even touching the obstacle. In six minutes from an alarm being given, the brigade could be orga- nised, and in attendance across the city.

THE CITY OF CHARITY is the name complimentarily given to Utica. N.Y. for it is preeminently the city of charitable institutions. Their number exceeds that of any other city of 100,000 or less in the United States. In Utica, there are forty associa- tions devoted to charity,nearly one for every 1,000 popu- lation, and the amount of money expended annually for charitable purposes exceeds that of many cities of four times the population. Among the leading institutions that have been long iR successful operation are the fol- lowing: Faston hospital and home for aged men, a home for men of advanced age, whose need of shelter and care is due to misfortune, and not to intemperance and vice. The hospital is free of access to physicians of all schools.

div.head: ROARING TRADE IN FITS.
div.p: A ROARING TRADE IN FITS.

There is a young man named Fretwell in Shef- field who has for some time been doing what may be called a roaring trade in fits. The Sheffield folk are reputed to be rough in speech and manner, but they are kindly folk for all that, and the sight of a fellow-creature in suffering moves them to give ac- cording to their means. Accordingly, when Fret- well was found lying on the ground 'Sin a fit" the other day, the Sheffield good Samaritans lifted him up, and having brought him to with brandy and other restoratives and learned that he was on his way to Barnsley, where his mother was lying dead, their first inquiry was "What money he had got?" Fivepence-half penny was the answer. "Of course," said one of the number, "we made a collection round and got 2s. Thd., and I gave him a hand down Wostenholm-road and led him to the car." Unfortunately for this afflicted person the good-hearted Sheffield man happened on the next morning to be in another part of the town, and there he saw the same Barnsley man lie down on the ground and go through the entire performance once more with like pecuniary results. Fretwell has been sent to prison for twenty-ono days ; but it is stated by the police that for six months the Sheffield Autolycus has been practising this ancient fraud, obtaining thereby "a great deal of money," not to speak of brandy, from the repeated doses of which he occasionally wound up the day in a drunken state. A doctor who examined him on one occasion reported that he " smelt strongly of Arink," but otherwise "there was nothing the matter with him."

div.head: UNCONSCIoUS HUMOUR IN THE WITNESS BOX.
div.p: UNCONSCIoUS HUMOUR IN THE WITNESS BOX.

(FROM THE "YANKEE ELADE.'') Some of the peculiarities of witnesses are comical in the extreme, their mistakes and retorts oft- times causing roars of laughter in court. One,wben asked whether her husband struck her with impunity, said, " Yes, sometimes, but gene- rally with his fist."

Another spoke of the existence of &family duel, evidently meaning "feud." A policeman, who is well known in South Lon- don, said, speaking of his use of the stave, "I am willing to be contradicted, your honour, but not al- together. The law must be dedicated ; give him justice tampered with mercy." A boy, who had perhaps heard of police trials be- fore the Commissioners, was examined as to his knowledge of the nature of an oath, and in ansm er to a question as to what was done with persons who swore falsely, said, "They makes policemen out of 'em."

A woman, who certainly appeared much older, told the magistrate in a French court that the was twenty-five years old. A young man, who was called as the next witness, acknowledged twenty- seven years. "Are you related to the previous witness ?" was the first question. "Yes, lam her son," was the reply. " Ah," muttered the magis- trate, "your mother must have married very young."

An English judge had an experience which is not frequently repeated in courts of law. The witness, in relating a conversation, would give the substance rather than the words, and the judge, Baron Martin, started to teach him the proper method of testifying. He said to the witness, "My man, tell me just what was said."

"Now, my good man, he did not say that he had been keening the pig; he said "I have been keeping the pig." "I assure you, my lord, there was no mention of your lordship at all. We are on different stories. There was no third person there; and if there had been anything said about your lordship's keeping a pig, I must have heard it."

THE ORIGIN OF CHESHIRE MERES.

Probably no English shire of the same size can boast the possession of so many good-sized natural sheets of water as the county of Chester. Shropshire has meres not a few; and East Anglia has its lake- land, the district of the Norfolk Broads ; but neither furnishes an exact parallel as regards natural fea- tures with the Cheshire plain, which is so thickly dotted with lakelets, great and small, that we naturally look about for some explanation of their presence. And here geology steps in with a ready answer; so we must be geological, but only for a moment. Every one knows of the great deposits of rock salt which underlie this part of the country; and most of us have seen pictures of deserted vil- lages or houses, whose tottering walls, thrown sadly out of the perpendicular, suggest the work of an earthquake. The disaster is of course due to sub- sidence, the settling down of the ground owing to the mining and burrowing operations which have gone on below. Now, suppose Nature, centuries ago, to have worked some of these salt beds in her own fashion by allowing the steady infiltration of water—as the saline deposits dissolved, the ground, subsiding, formed the hollows which the meres now occupy.. As an item lending support to this theory, we are told that in the depths of one of the deeper meres a kind of fish is occasionally met with which is only found elsewhere in the brackish water of estuaries. If PO, there is probably sufficient saline matter remaining in the bed of this particular pool to effect to some extent the composition of the water which comes into contact with it. The mere which wo know best is one of the largest of the group. It is a fine pool of over 100 acres, and withal so near to the great Lancashire hive, that half an hour's run even of the slowest of stopping trains, brings us within an easy walk of it. It is difficult to rea- lise that we are only a dozen miles or so from one of England's noisest and busiest industrial centres. The lake lies in a natural hollow, the ground almost everywhere rising from its margin. No obtrusive new built villas break the sweep of green- sward which stretches down from below the shelter- ing fringe of coppice to the ripple-marked water line. Hardly a house is in sight: but, overlooking the head of the lake, a church tower, built strong and square of the red sandstone of the district, just shows amongst elms and aspens. The village just beyond it is unseen : but entering it, we are struck by an air of neatness and quiet prosperity unusual even in a district all of whose villages are pretty. There is no public house in the hamlet, and one feels that a newspaper less than two days old would be out of place. We enter the churchyard through the old carved lych-gate. Inside the church itself is a chapel, whose marble monuments bespeak the resting place of members of an old and titled family. The mystery is explained: all around stretches the estate of one of the greatest land- owners of the country-side; and to this it is due that the lake lies below us in all its unspoilt beauty. If its surroundings were in the hands of smaller pro- prietors, the building speculator would be here in a week ; so let many-acred landlordism at the worst never want one argument to lean upon.—Chamberes Journal.

said Iteybold, "that the brave te' chauic, st, he sent me with this e• . tains some money, but it is only a 2.. . . . . _ _
of what he is wiiiing to do, if Mi.—Mr.-- what did you say his name wa, 7" "Allen Gilbert," said the doctor.

"Thanks. Yes, if Allen Gilbert will call on hit, Here is a card with Mr. Leffert's office aJdress 01 it. And, well, I shall pencil my name on the back, with a line saying I am ready to:co-operate with my friend, Mr. Lefferts, if I can be of any service." Mott Reybold wrote on the card, handed it to the doctor, and said, as he raiSed his hat and half turned to leave:
"I am glad to have met you again, Doctor Put- nam."

In response, the handsome young doctor merely bowed; but when Reybold had gone oat of hearing he said ; "If Mr. Lefferts knew that man as well as I do, he would rather see his daughter drowned than married to him."

" He's a gay boy, that Reybold," said the sailor. "I know a thing or two about him, and I will say that it's often been a wonder to me how sich fellers can get inter good comp'ny and made much of by ladies as is young, and rich and good-lookin'—" A rapping on the inside wall of the station near which they were standing put an end to their con- versation, and told them that Allen Gilbert was not only awake, but up. The clothing he had on in the water had been left hanging in the sun and nop was quite dry. The sailor took it in with the other things, and he and the doctor found the young man sitting on the edge of the cot, with a blanket about him. "I was in hopes you would take a good long sleep, Mr. Gilbert," said the doctor, as he felt Allen's pulse and added: "But your recuperative power is wonderful."
" Thanks : I feel like myself again. I will dress, and, get back to New York before it is dark," said Allen Gilbert.
He hurried into his clothes' ran his fingers through his short brown hair, and announced him- self ready to leave.

The doctor handed him the card and envelope left by Mott Reybold, and added, after he had given his own address: "I hope, 'Mr. Gilbert, you may never stand in need of my professional services; but if I can ever be of use to you in that, or in any other way, let me know and I shall be glad of the chance to show my regard." "And if Bob Davidson of the Branch—that's me, can ever help you to a trick' said the sailor, "why, holler out, and I'll come for you, as I did when I seed you go down long side o' that boat. . . .
Allen Gilbert—to Continue the name he had assumed—thanked the men for their professions of regard, and then with the manner of one anxious to be alone he shook hands with them and started out.
With his soft felt hat pulled over his eyes, he hurried by the groups who were still discussing his heroism, though they did not recognise him, and made his way to the station.
He found the train ready to start for New York, and leaped aboard, just as the signal was given to start.
He found the smoking car nearly empty, and tak- ing an end seat, he drew out the envelope left by Mott Reybold and tried to guess at the contents by feeling the outside. _ _

At 'length he tore it open, and brought to light five ten-dollar bills, all in that delicious state of crispness that gives such an ephemeral beauty to new Treasury notes. "Ah !" he muttered, "it's many and many a day since I saw so much money as that. This morning I would have given my right hand for half the amount. Well, the quarter that took me down on the boat was well spent, even if I did net find Frank Lefferts. Curse him? I might have killed him, if we had met. As it was, I saved his sister, and here is the reward. Well, well, lam the foot- ball of Fate,* and must consent to being kicked or tossed without resistance." As if fascinated he counted the money over and over again, and it was not till the train pulled into- the depot at Jersey City that he rolled up the bills. and carefully placed them in his pocket. From the cars he fairly ran to an eating-house, and at once ordered "a good meal of what was already cooked." Cold meat, bread, butter and coffee were set. before him, and these he devoured with the appetite of a man who had been starving for days. "That feller," said the keeper of the restaurant, as he gazed after his customer, "either hasn't had nothin' to eat for a week, or else he's laid in a supply for a week to come." On his way over the Annex Ferry, connecting. Jersey City with Brooklyn; the young man took from his pocket the memorandum before referred to, and read: "128, Pine Place, Brooklyn." "I'll try again; I may be more lucky this time," he said, as he put the address back. It was true that Allen Lee, or Allen Gilbert, had been the confidential clerk, some years before this, of one of the most prominent bankers in the city of New York. It was also true that he had been charged with forgery, tried, and sent to the peni- tentiary,,from which he had been released just ten days before this date. Prior to this forgery Allen had many friends; indeed, he was esteemed by all who knew him, and the general belief was that he would become not only a rich but a noble model man. This belief was strengthened by the fact that the young man's personal habits were not only above reproach, but because of his unswerving devotion to his father and mother, and his care for his lovely sister, who was some six years his junior. His father had been a wealthy and an honoured merchant, but in the panic of '73 that sent so Aany hard-earned fortunes crashing into the dust, Mr. Lee lost not only all his property, but also his health, and so became dependent on his son, who left college at the, age of nineteen to hasten to the support of his dear ones. But the evidence of guilt was so strong against Allen that his best friends were convinced of it; , and his persistent denial and stubborn defence only made them ttie more positive that they had been deceived beyond measure in their former estimates of his character.

To be sure, his father, mother, and sister Florence believed in his innocence, and stood by him to the last; but, in so doing, they sacrificed the esteem of old acquaintances, who, because of their natural love and fidelity, deemed them no better than the criminal Allen

For three years Allen had heard regularly from his family, but- though the letters were cheerful, he knew only too well that the pangs of bitter poverty had coin to intensify disgrace. . The year before leaving prison he did not hear from them at all, nor could the officials at Sing Sing, who took an interest in his troubles, get him any information as to the fate or whereabouts of those whose love alone made life endurable to the convict.
Allen had held a clerical position in the penitentiary, and, because of his skill and aood • conduct, he was pardoned out before the expiration of his full term.

So at length came a day when he laid aside the striped uniform of disgrace and resumed the old- fashioned, threadbare suit which he had on when he came to the prison. He had no money; but one of the officials whose association with criminals had not hardened his heart, gave him live dollars and led lalm to tne gale that opened out to the great, free world. "Here's my hand, Allen," said the official. "I've always been one of your friends, and now that you are a free man, I hope to hear you are winning your way.*
(To le continued.)
THE BEGINNINGMVidaYCLES.

It is generally understood that cycling machines are a purely modern invention, but this is not the case; as early as 1663 a Frenchman constructed a four-wheeled riding machine, propelled by treadles. In the year 1815 a foreigner constructed the first bicycle or " pedestrial hobby-horse," as it was called; of these there were more than one kind. We have seen a picture of one of these machines carry- ing three persons, a man in front propelling it; a lady was perched on a high seat in the middle, while a page-boy was ensconced in a sort of basket behind. Another engraving represents a lady alone on a sort of bi:.yele, the axle of which was bent in the form of the letter U, while the seat was placed on the upper end of one branch and a clumsy-look- ing treadle was the motive power. The bicycles used by the gentlemen had no treadles, and were set in motion by alternately striking the feet against the ground. Even with these rude machines a speed of eight or .10 miles an hour could be kept up for any krigth of time by a good rider. The craze, however, was of a short duration, and by 1820 the hobby-hones had almost ceased to exist. It was not iiiit il 1869 that Messrs. Nuchaud and Mayer turtle heir attention to the improvement of the old unnehines, and it is from that period that cycling really dates.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOIOD AND
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOIOD AND
FREE EDUCATION.

- A special meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday, for the purpose of consider- ing the assisted Education Act. Hr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present Rev. Father •(Narks' (vice-chairman), Rev. Dean Finegan, Dr. -01(eeffe, Dr. McDonnell, Major Wareing, Messrs. H. W. Deacon, C. E. Barlow, B. Brown, and G. Danby (clerk). Dean Finegan 'proposed that the Act be accepted.—The Chairman seconded, remarking that 103. was 10s., and he did not think they ought to refuse it. —The motion was carried.—The Chairman Said the question now was how were they to in- troduce the Act. If there were only Board schools • in the town it would be a very simple thing, and he would be in favour of making all the schools free, , but there were in the district a number of Denomi- national schools to whom he thought some con- sideration was due. Before the Elementary Educa- • tion Act was passed, the education of the town was under the control of the managers of Denomina- tional schools, and whatever the school Board had done during the past 15 years, there were still one half of the children educated in Denominational Schools. As far as the Church schools were concerned It would be a serious matter for them if the Board made "their scheols free. Mr. Garrett had informed him that e average amount of fees was its. per year. This large average was caused by the fact that in the Church Schools there were not so many infants; the scholars were mostly in the higher standards. This would mean s loss to the Church Schools of about £l2B a year, and the Vicar said he did not think he would be able to carry en the schools with such a loss. In addition there would be a further loss under the 14th Clause of about £2B. The only way in which they could carry on the Church Schools would be for som e of the parents who were saving about £2 a year by the reduction of fees to give a subscription of ss. or 10s. a year (Dean Finegan smiled). He (the Chairman) was of opinion that lithe Board made their schools free the denomina- tional schools would not be able to live, and it was' obvious that that was not a desirable thing as it would slogan a great burden on the rates. If Mr. Garrett had to close his schools, and the Board had fo purchase them it would entail a cost of about £lO,OOO. As a matter of economy it was to the interest of the ratepayers to keep the Church Schools going. The average fee in the Board schools was 124. 11d. a year and the adoption of the Act meant a lost of 2s. 11d, per scholar, which would amount to about £4lB on the three Beard schools. This was equal to about a penny rate, which produced £5OO. He (the chairman) was very much in favour of making all schools free if it had been a mere question of Board Schools. He could quite understand that it weuld be an immense boon to teachers if the schools were free, as the payment of fees involved a a good deal of detail work; but he could not go in for making them free because it would starve out the denominational schools, and he was not in favour of doing that.—(Major Wareing : hear, hear.)— Dean Finegan, as chairman of the School Management Committee, proposed that the Board should charge in fees a sum equal in amount to the deficiency between the 10s. grant and the average fee of 12s. 11d. The question of the amount of the fee could be fixed in Com- mittee.—The Chairman: Have you and Father Clarke some to any scheme for your own schools ?—Dean Fine- gan said they came willing to work with the Board, and if possible to adopt what the Board adopted. Father Chapman, of St. Patrick's schools, was willing to do the same. It would be an immense struggle for them to keep on their schools, if they were to make them free, and he hoped the Board would not do them an injustice by making the Board Schools iree.—Mr. Deacon seconded the motion, and said whatever the Board did they could not be responsible for any injustice to Denominational Schools, because the onus of making the schools free belonged to a higher authority. But he thought it would be wise under the circumstances to i charge n fees the difference between the 10s. grant and the fees they were now receiving from the scholars, be- cause to make the schools free would involve increased rates of a penny in the L and they would besides have to provide for a large number of children who now attended voluntary schools which would increase the rates still more. There was also another reason which ought to have weight with them. In some districts the education in voluntary schools was not up to the mark, and in such places it might be wise policy ,for the Board to make its schools free in order to starve out the voluntary schools; but in Widnes the voluntary schools from what he knew and what he read, gave an exceedingly good education, which was above the average of the United Kingdom and they frequently obtained the excellent merit grant.—Mr. Deacon pointed out that in future the Guardians would not pay the school fees of non-pauper children.—The Board had the Power to remit them but of course they could not remit them in the voluntary schools and unless there was some arrangements on this subject then there would be a hitch. Either the school managers would have to admit those children who could not pay without payment, or they would refuse them admittance, and then they would be forced into the Board Schpols. According to section Svc, of the New Act if there were not sufficient free seats in a school district then any number of ratepayers could . complain to the Education Department of that fact, and the Department would proceed to have the necessary ac- commodation provided. It seemed to him that it would be wise and necessary for the Board to provide free places foras many children as had had their fees paid during the past years, and pethaps Voluntary School managers would deem it advisable to provide free places in their schools also.—The Clerk said there were now in the Board School 203 children receiving free education, and in answer to a question he said that the average loss of 2s. 11d, per head included the fees received for non- pauper children from the Guardians.—The motion was passed and then the Board went into committee to con- sider details. Dean Finegan proposed, and Dr. O'Keeffe seconded that a fee of id. per head be charged in all de- partments of the Board Schools.—On the Board resum- ing this resolution was confirmed on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Father Clarke. THANKS TO GUARDIANS. Mr. A. F. Mann, clerk to the Prescot Union, wrote stating that in consequence of the passing of the Elementary Education Act, 1891, the Guardians would cease to pay the present school fees for either pauper or non pauper children on and after the 31st inst. They would be glad to learn what if any fees would be charged in the different standards of the Board schools, so that should the parents qf any children attending these schools be unable to pay such fees, arrangements might be made for dealing with these cases.—The Clerk was instructed to reply that it was not anticipated that any claim would arise for Payment of fees in the Board Schools. It was then pro- Posed by the Chairman and seconded by Father Clarke, that the best thanks ()Abe Board be given to the Guar- dians for deputing their authority to remit fees to the School Board for so many years thus saving cases of great hardship.—The resolution was carried, and Dean Finegan and Major Wareing were deputed to present it at the Best meeting of the Union.

PRESCOT RURAL DEANERY AND FREE EDTICATION.—A conference of the Rural Deanery of Prescot was held on Wednesday afterneon in the Town Hall, Prescot, and during the course of the proceedings the subjects of the management of schools and the free education act, and the equalisation of the marriage fees were discussed. The Rev. H. Mitchell, Rural Dean, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were the Rev. S. A. C. Sylvester (hon. sec,), Rev. F. Binney, Rev. W. Flaherty, Rev. J. M. Cotuteny, Rev. E. N. Hoare, Rev. H. S. Bolton, Rev. E. St. A. Duke, Rev. J. T. Owen, Rev. J. Wright Williams ; lay representatives—Major Willcocks, Messrs. J. C. Eccles, LE R. d'A Willis, Fletcher, Norton, J. R. Badger, F. Bowden, J. Hampton, J. Rudge, H. S. Welch, Sze. Apologies were received from a number of clergymen who were absent upon their holidays. The subjects were discussed at cnnsiderable length, and the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester suggested that the best way of meeting the Act and securing its advantages was a System of federation' of schools, and he proposed that that be adopted in this rural deanery. He wished man- agers would try and make parents feel that the responsi- bilities of educating their children were not entirely re- moved from their shoulders because they were receiving -what was called free education. The views put forward by Mr. Sylvester were adopted as the most feasible method of abtaining the advantages of the Act.—A dis- mission on the fees charged in different parishes for marriages took place, in which it appeared they varied from 4s. Bd. to 14s. 7d., and it was agreed that it was desirable to make them uniform with the registrar's fees, as recommended by the Conference in Liverpool last year.—The meeting then ended.
