DRUNKENNESS IN WARRINGTON.
SERMON BY THE REV. J. YONGE.

On Sunday evening at Wycliffe Church, the Rev. J. Yonge gave a discourse on" The public drunken- ness at Warrington, and the power and duty of the magistrates to suppress it." The text he spoke from was Isaiah lvii, v. 14: "Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way, take up the stumbling block out of the way of my people." He remarked that ithe book, in the divine inspiration of which they professed to believe, was against all "stumbling blocks in the way of the pe0p1,,." It spoke of a stumbling block as something which, when found, was always to be removed, and it distinctly declared that" no Man is to put a stumbling block in his brother's way." Having referred to various kinds of stumblii g blocks, he said he had to speak that night about a stumbling block as serious as any he had just alluded to. Yet, not only had it been allowed to be placed along every public high- way, and down many a bye-way, but even in many a back court, but the makers and owners of it were deemed most estimable citizens, worthy of all honour. Moreover they were protected in their deed by many a crafty law; and when law failed to help them and threatened to defeat them, then they were defended by astute officials who hinder or prevent the law from doing its work. Two remons had combined to lead him to his present utterance. One—what he believed to be, unless his eyes and ears deceived him, the in- creasing public drunkenness of this town. The other, that, since the last annual bre wster sessions a very important legal decision had been given on the licensing question. The House of Lords had finally declared, in its supreme court of legal ap- peal, that magistrates had unfettered discretionary power to refuse the renewal of licenses for the sale of drink, even as they all along had exercised the power of refusing the grant of new licenses. What were the facts of the case in Warrington? It was recorded in the Chief Constable's report to the licensing magistrates for last year, that in the borough there were 87 licensed victuallers, 48 beer- house keepers, and 70 shopkeepers—total 205. Es- timating the population roughly at 50,000 meant , a license of some sort, or, any way. a , means of obtaining drink, for every 240 per- sons. Now, according to census returns, it was found that more than one-half the population were females. A considerable proportion, therefore, of the 240 just named were women who should know how to do without intoxicants, and children who were never so well as Eaten trained up without them. Was it reason- ' able to sup se that the remainder of the 240 wanted a place, be it public-house, beerhouse, or grocer's license, specially provided for their convenience?. So much pro- vision was obviously unjustified by the needs of the population. On the ground, therefore, that the number of licenses was larger than was needed to accommodate the requirements of the population, and that so large a provision could only minister to what all must regard as unnecessary drinking of intoxicating liquors there was abundant reason why some steps should be taken to re- duce the number of 'licenses already existing, as well as whythe magistrates should absolutely refuse (as he be- lieved they were resolved to do) to grant any new ones. Mr. Yonge next referred to the work done in the last few years by the Warrington Temperance Federation, and he also quoted statistics which showed that in the 10 years from 1881 to 1890,7,132 persons were brought up before the bench for drunkenness and 6,085 convicted and punished. It was in the hope of helping to arouse and form a larger Christian public sentiment on the matter that he had ventured to call attention to it. They wanted to induce the magistrates to use their power, and do their duty. They could hardly, however, expect them to go very far in advance of public senti- ment. If the orderly, temperate, and Christian portion of the community were content with things as they were, if they had become so used to the sights and sounds of the manufacture of drunkards; if they were careless of the morals of their town and of the young people grow- ing up around, they could hardly expect the magistrates to be much better than themselves. The magistrates needed to be convinced of popular opinion, and then the same human nature which now bade them hold their hand would impel them to stretch it out. The magistrates needed enlightening and they needed stimulating. They needed enlightening as to the motives of temperance reformers. Many of them re- garded such moral enthusiasts as not only men who would "rob a poor man of his beer," but who would take away the livelihood of the publican. They were mistaken. Temperance reformers had no to the publican. Indeed, they wished him so well, that they could wish him earning more money at an honourable business, with the outlay of far less time and toil. Nor did they seek to "rob a poor man of his beer" from sheer wantonness. They wanted to keep men from get- ting drunk who could not keep themselves from that condition. They wanted to "take isp the stumbling block" which had thrown, and was throwing every day, many a man to his ruin. And the magistrates needed stimulating to the discharge of their duty, unfettered by private and selfish considerations. At present a subtle and powerful hindrance existed, which retarded magis- trates from doing what some of them, left to them- selves, would like to do. He accepted the entire responsibility for the remark he was about to make. In that borough alone, according to a Parliamentary return recently published, 62 licensed houses, what were called " tied " houses, belonged tc a wealthy firm, a limited brewery company, whose works were less than 100 miles from Warrington Bridge. To reduce the number of licenses in the borough meant to extinguish some of these, and that was a deed which called for considerable courage, and might probably entail upon men who were parties to it considerable personal and commercial penalty. That was the naked truth, and it might be useful that it should be put in plain terms by one, like himself, who was independent alike of bench and brewery. It would hardly be denied; nor did he refer to it for the purpose of any uncharitable comment upon the justices. But human nature had a good deal to do with human conduct. Magistrates were but men; and, although it would be a fine thing for them to have the courage of their convictions, and act altogether independently of personal considerations, yet too much must not be expected of "men of like passions with ourselves.", What was needed to stimulate those holders of high office in their com- munity was a clear unmistakeable evidence that the community required their action, would up hold their action, and would resent any injustice done to them through trying to do justice to the people. What, then, did they suggest that the magistrates should consider the desirability of doing? Briefly this : let them review their licenses of the borough, of all kinds; let them carefully inquire into the proportion of accommodation to necessity, into the adaptation of ex- isting buildings as places of reasonable public refresh- ment ; into the manner in which the houses were con- ducted, into the practices resorted to in them, and then let them deal summarily and peremptorily with any cases of glaring default, should there be such—refusing any longer continuance of licenses which had been forfeited by misuse. Further, let them notify others against which no delinquency was chargeable, but which were no longer necessary, that this is the last time of renewal. And so let them reduce the numbers, weeding out the bad, giving notice of withdrawal to the needless, and thereby rendering splendid moral service to the com- munity at large. REFERENCE BY THE REV. F. K. FREESTON.

On Sunday morning, in Cairo-st., Chapel, the Rev. Frank K. Freeston preached on "Fighting the Foe," and took for his text the words "Not peace but a sword." He contended that the highest Christian duty was not to be over anxious about your own soul, but to wage incessant warfare with the evils of the world. In- justice, intemperance, impurity, cruelty, cant and hy- pocrisy, gambling, betting and swearing—all these evils were gross and vast, were enemies of morality and foes to humanity, and they must be fought. But the direst foe of all was Intemperance. Against that foe before all others, all Christians should fight and all Churches combine, and he should not rest until every pulpit in Warrington at least had been invited to take part in a united Temperance Sunday on which intemperance should be condemned with no uncertain sound. In the meantime there was work at hand. An important meet- ing was to toe held to which he would call their most earnest attention. The purpose of the meeting was to afford a legitimate opportunity for the open expression of public opinion with regard to the large number of licensed houses in the town and the action of the Licens- ing Committee by whom these houses were controlled. That Committee was entrusted with a difficult and most responsible task. If they had to act for the welfare of the peoPle, they must know what the people desired. He rejoiced that there was sufficient public spirit in the town to have bestirred itself on this vital matter, and he felt confident that a large number of that congregation who had the real interest of the town at heart would attend the meeting on Thursday next.

THE LIMEHOUSE TRAGEDY.

A few (lays ago a woman was murdered in a public- house in London, and two witnesses deposed that it was the woman's husband who committed the crime. The police have found, however, that at the moment when the witnesses swore the man Was in Limehouse, he was actnally a prisoner in Cardiff Gaol.

EXECUTION OF THE HORSFORTH MURDERER.

On Tuesday morning the convict, Walter Lewis Turner, was executed at Leeds for the murder of the little girl Barbara Waterhouse, at Horsforth, near Leeds, on the 7th June last. Billington was the executioner. Turner passed a good night, and ate a hearty breakfast. On being pinoned the prisoner exhibited no signs of nervousness. The usual procession was formed to the scaffold, and' Turner walked on to it with a firm step. The straps were quickly adjusted, and Billington was putting on the white cap, when Turner said, "I don't want that cm." No notice was taken, however, of this remark, and the bolt being drawn, he was immediately launched into eternity. The execution was carried out without any hitch, all the arrangements working per- fectly. _

The facts of the case are well-known. The child dis- appeared from her home one Saturday night, and no- thing was seen of her until the Wednesday following, when her mutilated remains were found wrapped in a shawl near the Municipal Buildings atLeeds. The shawl was afterwards found to belong to Turner's mother, and this led to the arrest of the mother and son. They re- moved their furniture to Leeds, and later Mrs. Turner seemed worried and depressed, and a neighbour enquir- ing the cause, she made statements admitting that both she and her son took measures to conceal the crime. Mrs. Turner was advised to communicate with the police, and she did so. Turner was sentenced to death, and his mo- ther was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment. Since his sentence Turner had strongly maintained his innocence. His version of the affair was that he invited a chance acquaintance to the house, and that he found the body at the bottom of the stairs. He became alarmed, and endeavoured to hide it.

div.head: INTERNATIONAL SOCIALIST CONGRESS.
div.p: THE INTERNATIONAL SOCIALIST CONGRESS.

An International Socialist Labour Congress, organised by the Belgian labour party,was inaugurated on Sunday, at the Maison du Peuple, the headquarters of the labour party at Brussels. The proceedings were of a purply formal character. Every country in Europe, excepting Russia and Portugal, is represented. In all, 363 dele- gates have reported themselves, a considerable number being ladies. The sittings of the Congress will extend over the whole week. It is announced that the voting will b 3 taken by nationalities. Anarchists and other re- volutionary factious are excluded from the Congress. The business on the programme includes the following important subjects :—The legislative protection of la- bour, the laws concerning combination, strikes, and boy- cotting, the position and duty of the working-classes with respect to militarism, the attitude of the organised workmen of all countries with respect to the Jewish question, universal suffrage, the emancipation of labour, the eight hours question, and the Socialist org anisation and Socialist problems.

THE WELSH NATIONAL EISTEDDFOD.
ALARMING ACCIDENTS.

In brilliant weather the Welsh National Eisteddfod was opened at Swansea on Tuesday morning. Proceedings commenced with the Gorsedd of the Bards, after which, a procession was formed to the Eisteddfod pavilion which accommodates about 20,000 people. The Mayor delivered the opening address, dwelling an the antiquity of the Eisteddfod and the good results the institution has had on the literary and musical education of the Welsh for the last thousand years. Thepreceedings on Tuesday, which was presided over by Sir J. T. D. Llewelyn, were marred by an unusually heavy fall of rain, which did considerable injury to the roof of the pavilion. One of the posts sustaining the roof gave way, fatally injuring a woman. In Tuesday's competitions the Cardiff band won the £5O prize in the orchestral competition. the Swansea band being second. In the choral competition confined to Wales, the Morris- ton Choral Union Choir carried off the £5O prize, with a gold medal to the conductor, the Glantawe Union Choir being second. The usual concert took place in the even- ing,and was very numerously attended. About 20,000 people, on Wednesday, attended the National Eisteddfod at Swansea, over which Lord Windsor presided. At noon a scene of confusion took place owing to people in the galleries breaking down the barriers and , rushing into the first seats. The wildest excitement was the result, several ladies fainting. Mr. Ben Davies sang the Welsh national air, "Land of my fathers," the vast audience singing the chorus with fine effect. The Llan- nelly choir conducted by Mr. R. C. Jenkins, won the first prize of £2OO • and the Carnarvon choir, conducted by Mr. John .Williams, was awarded the second prize. Gounod's " Redemption" was perforraed in the evening, but Madame Patti was not present.

The Prince of Naples, on Saturday, visited Palmer's shipbuilding yard at Jarrow-on-Tyne, where some steamships are being built for an Italian line. A staging fell at the yard at a spot the Prince had passed only a few minutes before, and five men were injured. In the evening his Royal Highness sailed for Norway.

div.head: MURDER NEAR HULL.
div.p: THE MURDER NEAR HULL.

Very little progress has been made towards clearing up the mystery that surrounds the murder of Mary Jane Langley. the farmer's daughter, whose dead body was found in a ditch at Presten, near Hull, over a week ago. The Treasurer ordered the prosecution of John Rennard, who was arrested on suspicion, but the accused was dis- charged. He leceived a tremendous ovation outside the court. No importance is attached to the confessions of a man whose clothes bore blood stains and who asserted that he was the murderer of Miss Langley. The inquiry relative to the death of Mary Jane Lang- ley, who was found dead in a ditch at Preston, near Hull, was resumed on Wednesday,and the jury returned a verdict that the girl had been murdered by some per- son unknown. It has been decided to offer a reward for information that may lead to the arrest of the murderer.

div.head: FRENCH FLEET AT PORTSMOUTH.
div.p: THE FRENCH FLEET AT PORTSMOUTH.

The French fleet arrived off Portsmouth on Wednesday afternoon, and was conducted by H.M.S. Seagull from the Nab Light through the lines of the British Channel squadron to moorings in the Solent. On entering British waters Admiral Gervais' squadron fired a salute of twenty-one guns and ran up the British Standard at the main. The Duke of Connaught, as representing the land forces answered the salute. The French sailors manned ship as they entered the British lines, and shouted loud hurrahs, which were enthusiastically res- ponded to by the men of our own fleet. Further salutes were given on passing the Camperdown and the Anson in honour of the naval Commander-in-Chief and Admiral Seymour, and the spectacle, which was witnessed by the Queen from the terrace at Osborne, was alike brilliant and impressive. _

On Thursday morning the British commanders were received by Admiral Gervais on his flagship the Marengo, the Duke of Connaught cordially welcoming the French commander and his squadron to English waters. Immediately afterwards Admiral Gervais, with 17 of his senior officers, landed at Osborne Bay, and were con- veyed in royal carriages to the Queen's residence, the French warships giving the royal salute of 21 guns. The Queen, who was accompanied by the Duchess of Con- naught, Princesses Louisa and Beatrice, and her chief officers, received the guests in the drawing room, the French officers being personally introduced by M. Waddington. Her Majesty expressed great gratification at the presence of her visitors, whose stay she hoped would be enjoyable.
THE QUEEN'S PRIZE AT SHOEBURY- NESS.

At the Shoeburyness camp, on Wednesday, the result of the competition for the Queen's Prize was announced. The coveted trophy has gone to the sth detachment of the Ist Cheshire and Carnarven Artillery, who have scored 100 points with the 64-pounder and 40-pounder this week. It is a creditable victory, considering that the whole of the detachment are scarcely more than youths and form part of a battery from the Chester Dio- cesan Training College. None of the detachment had been up to Shoeburyness before. The score was made up of 40 points out of a possible 48 in the 40-pounder competition of Monday, 27 points in the 64-pounder competition of Monday, and 33 points in the 40-pounder competition of Tuesday. The Prince of Wales's Cup was won by the 18th detachment of the 2nd Middle- sex.

Yesterday at the Artillery Volunteers meeting at Shoeburyness, the fourth detachment 4th Durham were awarded the Harcourt Callenge Cup and badges for the i highest aggregate, 280 marks, n the 64-pounder, 40-pounder, and repository competitions combined. the Ist Gloucester team, under Colonel Ord, have won the silver cup in the fire discipline competition, and the 4th West York, under Captain Clifford, take the prize cup in the field artillery competition. The Duchess of Teck distributed the prizes.

div.head: EXECUTION AT CHELMSFORD.
div.p: EXECUTION AT CHELMSFORD.

Thomas Sadler, labourer, was executed on Tuesday morning at Springfield Prison, Chelinsford, for the mur- der of William Wass at Colchester. Sadler induced the wife of his victim to leave her husband. During a dis- pute concerning the custody of the children Sadler stabbed Wass behind with a penknife, causing his death. After his condemnation Sadler paid much attention to the ministrations of his spiritual adviser, and asserted that the deed was committed in the heat of passion. Berry was the executioner. Sadler, who attributed his downfall to drink, said when being pinioned that he was quite ready to die. He afterwards took his place in the procession without uttering a word, and walked to the scaffold firmly. He was strapped without any trouble, tut as Berry adjusted the noose a slight trembling was observed. The next moment the bolt was drawn, and and death was instantaneous. The execution was wit- nessed by officials only, reporters not being admitted.

div.head: EXECUTION AT WANDSWORTH.
div.p: EXECUTION AT WANDSWORTH.

Robert Bradshaw, aged fifty-six, labourer, was hanged at nine o'clock on Thursday morning in Wandsworth Gaol, for the murder of his wife, Maria, at Bermondsey, on July 4th. Bradshaw who was addicted to habits of intemperance, requested his wife to withdraw a sum- mons which she had taken out against him for threats, and on her refusing to do so he enticed the woman to his room, and nearly severed her head from her body. Since his conviction Bradshaw devoted his time to the exhortations of the gaolchaplin and in chatting with the prison warders. The convict nassed a fairly quiet night, and dressed at 6 o'clock in the morning, signifying to his prison attendants he was ready to meet his fate. He was engaged in earnest prayer until the end, and on being asked if he had anything to say, said, " I am sorry I did it." He shook hands with the warders, and thanked them for their kindness to him. Bradshaw, walked firmly to the scaffold, and on the bolt being drawn death appeared to be instantaneous. Berry was the executioner. Reporters were not admitted.
A SENSATIONAL SITIO[DE AT WAR,-
RINGTON.

A sensation was caused in the neighbourhood of Warrington Bridge, on Sunday afternoon, by a man who jumped from the bridge into the river and was there drowned. Nothing is known of the man, no- body seeming to know his name, where he came from, or his occupation. He had the appearance of a tramp, and it is said that while on the bridge he spoke a few words to a woman, who remarked, as she was moving away, "I am off now." He replied "I'm off too" and instantly clambered on to the parapet, and threw himself into the waters be- low. He sank for a time beneath the surface of the river, but as the tide was receding strongly at the time, he was carried away towards the railway bridge, end appeared to finally sink near the bridge. This took place about half-past four in the after- noon, and there were of course many people about, and in a very short time there was a crowd of several hundreds on the spot. A vain attempt was made to recover the body by grappling,. but without success, and up to the time of writing nothing had been heard of its recovery lower down the river.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"A. Divided Duty " i tne title of a new nlvol by Ida Lemon, author of" That Little Woman," &c. It is a capitally written story, and shows a practised hand. The scenes are, for the most part, laid in Paris, and there are many bright and picturcsque descriptions of life in the French capital. The principal characters are, however, English, and they are all very clearly defined ;indeed it is due to the novelist te say that every character that she in- troduces is a distinct portrait. The individuality is carefully preserved,and the characters help,in being brought together, to give that deep interest which we see in real life. The plot of the story develops somewhat slowly perhaps, but it goes with some- thing like a rush at the finish and the denouement is cleverly brought about. It is evident that the writer has strong religious feeling, but there is nothing in the way of sectarianism, and certainly nothing ap- proaching cant. The tone is, in this respect, thoroughly healthy. The volume is one of nearly 400 pages. It is well printed and handsomely bound, and published by Mes`ks. Frederick Warne and Co.. at the price of 6s. The same firm have issued Robert Southey's .Life of Nelson." in a shilling volume of 350 pages, with a bright cover reproducing the scene of the death of England's greatest naval hero. Southey's "Life of Nelson "is recognised as a standard work; it is a capital piece of writing, and it is a matter of course to say it is exceedingly readable. "He fell among Thieves" is the title of a power- ful novel by two eminent hands, namely Messrs. Christie Murray and Henry Herman. It is published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., and describes the career of a good-natured clever young fellow,admir- ably brought up, but who getsin a gambling circle and falls into the hands of a number of sharpers, who are the " thieves " referred to in the title. The manner in which the hero is unconsciously led into a breach of the law is skilfully told, and there is a vivid portrayal of the startling adventures which happen to him when he flees his country and joins the Turkish army. His coming back, and the new life he enters upon under a new name, bring about an extraordinary complication, when his identity is discovered by the men who previously plundered him; but in the end he proves his inno- cence and the tricksters are duly punished. "He fell among Thieves," is a love story as well as a record of strange scenes and strange persons, and it all ends very happily as most love stories do. " Good-bye" is a shilling novel by John Strange Winter, author of "Bootle's Baby." It is out of the ordinary run of this writer's works of fiction, but it is none the less interesting on this account. The incidents ot the novel are based upon a divorce decree against an innocent wife, and "good-bye" is the parting from the husband who believes his wife to be guilty on the strength of the evidence that has been presented in the court. He marries again, and then discovers his wife's innocence. This leads, as will be imagined, to extraordinary com- plications, but, as the reader will find, the difficul- ties are ultimately got over in a very satisfactory fashion. If the stAry is not one of the brightest, it is certainly one of the best that has been written by this gifted author. The publishers are Messrs. F. V. White and Co,

.6;The-dentury," for August, opens with an article on the German Emperor, giving a sketch of the first three years of his reign. It is from the pen of Mr. Poultney Bigelow and adorned with two highly-finished full plate portraits of the emperor and empress, besides illustrations of exteriors and interiors of royal palaces. Other strikingly illus- trated papers are "Life on the South Shoal light- ship," "-Play in Provence," "Cape Horn and Co- operative Mining in '49," The Little Renault." The supply of fiction and of verse is, as usual, of the highest class, and the "Bric-a-brac" is, as hereto- fore,.thoughtf ul and clever. " Piccadilly " is the title of the leading paper in " Scribner's Magazine." It is from the pen of Mr. Andrew Lang, with a series of remarkably fine illustrations by W. D. Almond. The present issue is published as the "fiction" number, and, as might be expected, it is strong in this respect. Amongst the series which,are admirably illustrated,are "The anatcmist of the heart." " Uneffectual fires," "At the Ranch of the Holy Cross," " Elsket," &c. It is a matter of interest to note that a new story "The Wrecker" is cosnmenced with Robert Louis Steven- son and Lloyd Osbourne a 3 the joint authors. "The English Illustrated Magazine" commences with an interesting paper by John Todhunter on the late George Wilson. It is illustrated by pictures of the painter, one of them being used as a frontis- piece. "Dickens and Punch" is accompanied with illustrations from the collection of "Mr. Punch," and is of special interest now in connection with the "Punch "jubilee. "Old Landmarks.' by Dewy Bates has some excellent illustrations by the writer, and another illustrated paper is "Tewkesbury Ah,ey" by the Dean of Gloucester. Under the title of "Health—Voyage to South Africa and sojourn there 'S the managers of the Castle Mail Packo- Company have published a , handbook which contains a large amount of valuable ' information. It has been issued in connection with the International Congress of Hygiene and Demo- graphy. and cannot fail to be exceedingly useful to persons who, either for health or business purposes, are thinking of visiting South Africa. The book is adorned with illustrations and maps. "The Art Amateur "is a journal printed in America and devoted to "Art in the household." The Eng- lish edition is published by Messrs. Griffith, Farran, and Company, and the part for August contains three highly finished coloured plates. Amongst the topias treated are" China paintihg," "The House," Treatment of designs," "Art Amateur working designs," Ste. It should be added that every sections is amply and fully illustrated. "The Art Amateur " is in every respect an admirable production, and is published at is. 61 monthly. " Fame " is the title of a new venture which is intended as a journal for advertisers. It is full of bright readable matter, containing a great many valuable hints to advertisers, and if it gets on the right track it ought to command substantial sup- port. We have also to hand "Mrs. Leach's Family Dressmaker," (21.) which is an excellent publica- tion as a guide to home dressmaking, with practical advice to house-wives.

div.head: FURIOUS DRIVING OF STEAM TRAMS.
div.p: THE FURIOUS DRIVING OF STEAM TRAMS.
HEAVY PENALTIES AT ST. HELENS.

On Friday at the St. Helens Town Hall, before Colonel D. Gamble C. 8., and Mr. W. J. Thomson, Ogden Wright. 2, frellington-terrace, was charged with being drunk in charge of one of the steam tram engines belonging to the St. Helens and Dis- trict Tramways Company.— Constable Patterson deposed that on Thursday niteit. he saw the prisoner i driving his engine ata very furious Fate n Warring- ton New-road. The car was being driven at about 20 miles an hour, and witness motioned to the driver to stop, but he took no notice and kept on.—police- constable Griffiths gave corroborative testimony. Inspector Steel said he spoke to the prisoner about his drunkenness when the engine stopped at the terminus. At that moment one of the passengers came up and informed the driver that he had driven at a shameful rate, and had come along the road like an express train; several passengers had jumped from the car through fear.—Chief Constable Wood asked for the maximum punishment in that case. Another charge could be preferred and further proceed- ings would be taken.—ln answer to the Bench, the Clerk (Mr. Davison) said the maximum penalty was a fine of 40s. and costs or imprisonment for one month.—The Chairman: You are committed to prison for a month. We don't think that the offence will be met by the infliction of a fine. Before Alderman J. C. Gamble and Mr. A. Walmesley Cotham, at the Town Hall, on Monday, the St. Helens and District Tramways Co., Limited, were summoned for not having a governor affixed to one of their tram engines. Mr. J. Massey appeared for the Company, and admitted the offence. Constables Patterson and Griffiths gave evidence that in two different thoroughfares on the previous Thursday night they saw the engine in question being driven at a speed of about 20 miles an hour. The engine was in charge of a man named Wright, who was drunk, and on Friday Wright was sent to prison for a month for drunkenness. Mr. Massey said the directors admitted that the offence was a serious one, but they did not consider they were to blame. The man who had been employed to supervise the engines had left them in a detective state, i and the company were working hard to put everything n order. Such a thing could not occur again. 'the Chief Constable pressed for the full penalty. Mr. Massey said that the governors on nearly every engine were broken at one point—the sharp curve at the corner of Shaw and Raven streets. The company had spent something like £7OO through breakages at that particular point, and, do what they could, they could not get them right.—The Chairman: The com- pany will be fined £5 and costs.

EXECUTION OF CONWAY.
CONFESSION OF TIIE CRIME.

John Conway, otherwise Owen Gitlin, aged sixty-two, marine fireman, and latterly paid secretary of the Sea- men's and Firemen's Union in Liverpool,was executed at Kirkdale Gaol. on Thursday morning, for the murder of , Nicholas Martin,aged 10, living in Bridgewater-st.,Tox- teth,on Saturday, 16th May. Berry was the executioner. A small crowd of people assembled near the gaol be- tween seven and eight o'clock, and waited the hoisting of the black flag at the latter hour, which indicated that Conway had paid the penalty for his crime. The mur- der was freely talked about, and it was generally ad- mitted that Conway had deservedly suffered at the hands of the law.

As Berry was putting the white cap on Conway, the criminal, who was staring wildly about said :—" Hold on, hold on, I want to say something." Berry: • You can't say anything now." Conway: "I must. I want to say something.' Father Bonte stepped forward and stopped Berry, whe said—" Then say what you have to say quick." Conway then expressed his thanks to the officials for their kindness to him, and said he forgave his persecutors. After the drop fell Father Bonte read the statement made by Conway on Wednesday morning. In this Conway said he accepted his sentence as a just one, and offered his life in satisfaction to all whom he had offended. He protested that his motive was not outrage, and said that the cause of his ruin was drink, not lust. He was im- pelledby a morbid curiositytn observe the process of dying. During the whole time Father Bonte was speaking, says the representative of the Press Association, the bond from Conway's body was heard streaming on to the floor, and it was then said that the body was hanging merely by the muscles of the neck. As the Press representatives stepped forward to observe what had happened, Berry shouted to the warders to take them out, and they were immediately hurried away. Berry afterwards told the reporters, whom he followed into the warders apart- ments, that the officials would have given Conway another eight inches drop, but for him. If he had had his way he would not have given him above four feet six inches ; but they had given him a six feeb drop, on the advice of Dr. Barr, who at first wanted SiK feet six inches, which would have entirely decapitated the criminal.
At the inquest held at 9.30, a juryman asked why Berry was not present. _ _
The Coroner replied that the Governor had said every- thing had gone off as usual,so that there was no necessity for Berry to be present.
Dr. Barr said the execution was carried out in the usual way, there being no hitch as far as the execution was concerned.
The jury found a formal verdict that judgment of death had been carried into effect.
The reporters expressed a desire to see the body with the jury but were informed that the Governor would not permit it.

div.head: COLLAPSE OF A BRIDGE.
div.p: COLLAPSE OF A BRIDGE.
EIGHTY LIVES LOST.

A New York telegram says the Haytian mails bring advices that a bridge over the River Saint Marc, in Hayti. has collapsed, eighty persons who were crossing at the time losing their lives. The accident occurred on Friday, when the bridge, which was crowded with natives fell into the swollen stream,its foundations having for some time past been gradually undermined. A great many people were thrown into the river. Some escaped, but others were carried out to sea. It is believed, however, that most of the missing wore so injured by falling masonry that they were unable to help themselves.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

A special meeting of this Board was held, on Tuesday evening,for the purpose of considering the Assisted Education Act. Mr. James Pritchard pre- sided,and there were present the Rev. Canon Wood, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. A. Sal- keld, and G. Moss (clerk).

div.head: FREE EDUCATION.
div.p: FREE EDUCATION.

The Chairman moved that consideration of the motion of which he had given notice, in respect to the Elemen- tary Education Act, 1891, be adjourned until the next Board meeting on Tuesday.—Dr. McDougall seconded. —Carried.—The motiln referred to reads as follows "That the fee grant be accepted, and that no fees be charged in Ulla schools belonging to this Board on and after September Ist, 1891.
SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.

Mr. Marshall,secretary to the Board of Commissioners, wrote stating that the Bo•Ird had resolved "That any deficiency incurred by the Runcorn School Board in con- nection with the Science and Art Classes to be held dur- ing the forthcoming winter be made good up to the extent of £75 for this financial year. It was also resolved "That application be made to the Department of Science and Art to sanction the teaching of modern languages, shorthand, bookkeeping and cooking at the Science and Art Classes such form of instruction being required by the circumstances of the district "That Messrs. Grice, Wiscvall and /mison, be appointed to represent the Board under the Technical Instruction Act on the School Board Science and Art Committee.—The Chairman observed that this communication showed the interest the com- missioners took in the classes and their disposition to help all they possibly could by voting £75. The School Board ought to welcome their co-operation by at once accepting the three names suggested, and he moved that the Board constitute themselves a Science and Art Com- mittee for the conducting of these classes with the addi- tion of the names mentioned. Canon Wood seconded.— In reply to Dr. McDougall,the Chairman said the School Board had no fund out of which they could pay a single penny for the purposes of these classes, which were ex- pected to be carried on by fees and Government grant and the £75 from the commissioners if necessary. The motion was carried.—The Chairman said with regard to the evening classes for the teaching of elementary sub- jects he supposed it was the wish of the Board to con- tinue them as last year.—Dr. McDougall: I should say so. They were a highly creditable portion of the Board's work last year.

The concluding meeting of the Hygienic Congress was held on Monday. It was resolved to hold the next year's meeting at Budapesth. _ _

At the London sessions on Monday, James M,Leary was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment for intimida- tion in connection with the carpenters' strike. Sir P. Edlin intimated that it might be necessary to increase sentences for intimidation in order to suppress the practice. A certificate was on Monday granted by the London Court of Bankruptcy removing the adjudication of Mr. G. M. Byrne, M.P..ior West Wicklow, on the ground that the bankruptcy was the result of misfortune and without misconduct. Further captures have been made by brigands on the line of the Salanica railway, and the usual exorbitant ransom is demanded. The Frenchmen who were kid- napped have not been heard from, but the French Am- bassador may be trusted to show the Porte its whoia duty in the matter of brigandage.

Mr. Parnell Mr. PARNELL has an unlimited and capacity in one respeet, and that is Mr. Morley. for quarrelling with his bast friends. He has been bitter in denounling the majority of his former supporters —inveighing against them as " gutter sparrows" and " traitors," because they could no longer follow him as leader of the Irish people. He showed himself anxious in the Boulogne negotiations to keep Messrs. DILLON and O'BRIEN from taking sides against him; no words that ho could utter were too smooth for them; but now that they, too, after spending six months in prison,have taken part with the great bulk of their countrymen, he falls foul of them also. Speaking at Drogheda and Kells on Sunday, he said : "The only thing he regretted about it was that Mr. DILLos- and Mr. O'BRIEN did not give their advice to the country before they went into pri- son, for there was nothing in the world which had happened since to make it more desirable or moire necessary from their own point of view to give their advice to-day than it was six months ago." But a great deal has happened. Mr. PARNELL has placed it beyond doubt that Parnellism is every- thing with him and Patriotism nothing. He has re- fused toseriously entertAin any proposal for releas- ing the Paris funds, and applying them for the sup- port of evicted tenants. Further, he has removed any remnant of doubt as to his innocence in the divorce case by marrying the late Mrs. 0. SHEA. We do not say that he has not made the best of a bad job by marrying the woman he had wronged; but, his guilt being admitted, what does it mean? It means that his life for a number of years has been a living lie, that he is capable of bare- faced treachery to a friend, and that he can no longer be trusted where matters of ,truth and honour are involved. That this is so is demonstr- ated by the breach of confidence as to interviews with Mr. GLADSTONE, and by the way in which he has given the lie to his own utterances as to his satisfaction with the Home Rule propositions which the leader of the Liberal party had laid be- fore him. If Mr. PARNELL spoke the truth when he expressed his approval of the course which Mr. GLADSTONE proposed to take, it is obvioue that he cannot be speaking the truth now; and in either case he is convicted of a lack of probity which unfits him for the position of leader of the Irish people. Mr. JOHN MORLEY has several times had to address the public in contradiction of Mr. PAR - , NELL's reckless misstatements. The operation has become monotonous, and it might almost be re- garded as unnecessary, for whb is there who is not now familiar with the ready way in which Mr. PARNELL resorts to fiction when fact will not serve his purpose? Mr. MORLEY is, however, patient and persevering; and he has taken the trouble to nail down another counterfeit. The ex-leader gave it out, on Sunday, that so far from withdrawing or hiding himself in the interval between the decrees in the Divorce Court and his re-election as chair- man of the Irish party, he remained where Mr. MORLEY saw him nine days before the verdict. Mr. MORLEY'S answer to this is that after the ver- dict he saw Mr. HENRY kjAMPRELL, Mr. PARNELL'S private secretary, as usual in such cases, with a view to an early communication. He adds : Mr. Campbell told me that Mr. Parnell was at Brighton; that he would go down the next day and deliver my request; and finally, that I might rely on hearing from him by eleven o'clock on Tuesday forenoon. At half-past eleven on Tuesday forenoon, I received a telegram purporting to come from Mr. Campbell, saying that he was sorry he could not find "his friend,' but hoped to see him at the House of Commons. I immediately applied to Mr. McCarthy, but, he, too, was entirely in the dark; and so were two other members of the Irish party, I then and now supposed to be much in Mr. Parnell's confidence. Before the hour at which the Irish party were to meet, I went o ver to the House, but the Irish meeting, I rather think, had been accele- rated—at any rate it was over. From the day of the decree down to that time,l had no better means of reaching Mr. Parnell—save those to which I actually resorted—than I have to-day of reaching the " Man in the Moon."

With regard to the other invention, namely that Mr. MORLEY knew nine days before the verdict how it would go,and that he nevertheless expressed the hope that Mr. PARNELL would not in any case retire from public life, it is really too absurd for consideration. What Mr. MORLEY says agrees with what Mr. DAVITT has repeatedly said,namely, that Mr. PARNELL deceived people by assurances as to his innocence. But hero are Mr. MORLE VIS own words :

I did not know that the verdict was going to be against him. I had what I thought the best rea- sons for believing the contrary. Mr. Parneffs.own language on the occasion left me with the clear and untroubled assurance that the verdict would be, not against him, but for him. Finally, to say that I was anxious that Mr. Parnell should not retire, " no matter what happened at the trial," is a not very plausible or probable perversion of my natural hope that nothing would happen at the trial that should render his retirement necessary.

When it is a case of putting' a statesman's dis- interested statements against a trickster's desper- ate inventions, it is soon seen which are valueless. Mr. PARNELL is reaping where he has sown. Ile has acted as if there were no such thing as moral force in the World; but it is a moral force which is crrishing him. His degradation is the penalty of his transgression. "The mills of God grind slowly, but they grind exceedingly small."

SCHOOL Board and School The Education Difficulty Managers are now face to face . with the difficulties of the new Education Act which comes in force at the begin- ning of next month. If it was the intention of the Government to dish the Radicals by forestall- ing them in the matter of Free Education they have missed their way; for it is not "free" educa- cation which is conferred, but a niggardly scheme of assistance which does not appear to please any- body. Indeed, if we are not much mistaken, the peddling in halfpenny and penny fees which the Act will involve will cause so much misconception and so much friction that school manager's will wish the Government had not meddled at all, if they were not prepared to confer complete freedom in the matter of exemption from school fees. Where there are School Boards un4er the control of citizens whose chief thought is the education of the children of the town or district, the sailing will be pretty plain ; for all that the Boards have got to do is to accept the extra ten shillings per head allowed by the Act, make all schools free, and pay the difference out of the rates. But some Boards are not prepared to do that, for they are under the control of denominationalists who have more regard for sectarian than educational interests. The pressing question—" What is to be done ? " was under the consideration on Tuesday of the Widnes School Board; and the whole discussion went to show that the first thought was—how will the course we take affect not the Board Schools, but the Denominational Schools? Mr. T. S. Timm's, the chairman, said "as far as the Church schools were concerned it would be a serious matter for them, if the Board made their schools free." Dean FINEGAN was asked if he and Father CLARKE had settled upon any scheme for the Catholic schools ; and the Dean replied that they were willing to work with the Board, and adopt the fees which the Board adopted. In the end it was resolved on the motion of Dean FINEGAN, and Dr. O'KEEFFE, another Catholic, that a fee of one penny per head be charged in all departments of the Board Schools. The Widnes Board thus throws away for a time a chance of making its schools free—a sacrifice obviously on the altar of sectarianism. When advocating Free Education as a feature of "The Radical Pro- gramme," Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said: "As a matter of fact, the law is administered not in the interests of education, parents, children, or ratepayers, but in those of Denominational Schools." It would seem as if the evil policy is to be continued—so completely have the Tory Government meddled and muddled. And what about the free places which parents are permitted to claim under the Act? Are they to have them without being subjected to an offen- sive and pauperising inquisition, as at present, into the causes and extent of their poverty ? If free places are to be granted as a matter of course , when they are asked for, it is a matter of course to say that the demand will 100 general, and the elaborate arrangements for penny fees will be in vain. If, as we assume, free places are not to be had except as at present,upon proof of povarty,we are left by this pettifogging Act in the ridiculous position of keeping:up and preserving the worst features of the existing system, after presumably setting out to get rid of them. Then as to the fees themselves; it has been generally acknow- ledged that the waste of time in collecting and keeping a record of children's school pence was a great hindrance to the work of teachers and their assistants, to say nothing of the effect which the payment of fees has in lowering the average attendance. It is notorious that in the few cases in which free schools have been tried in poor districts there has been a won- derful improvement in regularity of attendance. With genuine Free Education, this regularity would become general, but with the sham scheme which is about to be tried nothing of the kind is to be expected. And to think of all the machinery of booking and collecting being kept going to secure half-penny and penny fees! It is making not two bites at a cherry, but a bite at a cherry- stone. What is needed to remedy these defects is a system of universal School Boards, where all places in ordinary elementary schools shall be free, the difference between the actual cost and the sum allowed by the Education Department being paid out of the rates. This of course implies re- presentative management of the schools, those who find the money—the taxpayers and rate- payers—being in a position to regulate and control the expenditure. In other words, we want people's schools, paid for by the people, and man- aged by the people.

div.head: "TOTJCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOTJCH AND GO."

The Penketh Park Company, Limited, has a pleasant sound with it; and, as its objects are admirable, it is to be hoped there will be no limit to its success. The experiment is a novel one so far as this part of the country is concerned ; but it is something to know that a similar Company in London has achieved all that was expected of it.

Byron says : "There's nought in storm so much the spirit calms As rum and true religion." It must have been with an eye to this that " a steamer recently took out a couple of missionaries to Africa with a stock of Bibles; 2,100 gallons of Holland gin, and 1,500 gallons of rum." It was certainly a rum cargo.

News comes from Southern Hungary of "nume- rous cases in which peasant women have either poisoned their husbands, or have caused them to be poisoned by a certain class of old women, who follow poisoning as a profession." One of our English essayists wrote upon "Murder as a fine art"; but who over expected to hear of "poison- ing as a profession ?" We must live and learn.

At present the English football team are having it all their own way in South Africa. They are teaching the young Africander how to shoot at the goal, and it may happen, in due time, that he will better the instruction. It is not forgotten that English cricketers played with Australians until the latter were able to despatch a team of cricketers to this country who were equal to all comers.

The young men of Crewe are fortunate. Sir Richard Moon, ex-chairnian of the London and North-Western Railway Company, has decided to expend £2,000 in a Scholarship Fund on behalf of studious engineers of the Crewe Works. One has often heard of money corning secretly and ques- tionably from the Man-in-the-Moon ; but in this case the Moon gifts are above board, and for the best of purposes.

"The Journalist" has a rap at the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes. It s'ays :—" It is not often that the editor's name is kept up' to the extent it was in a recent issue of the Methodist Times.' In this week's issue of that paper the name of Mr. Hugh Price Hughes appeared no less than 52 times. Of the 32 pages of that journal it is found on 26. On one sheet alone it appears 10 times. This is blow- ing the clerical trumpet with a vengeance."

HOLY TRINITY CILURCH, RUNCORN.

The mem-l-o;r; of the choir of this church had their annual trip to New Brighton. The weather was] very favourable and the excursionists were regaled with suit- able refreshments. A very pleasant time was spent. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.
Tbc annual sermons in aid of the trust Fund were rlcavered in Hutchinson-st. Chapel on Sunday by the Rev. E. McLellan. Good congregations assembled at each service and a good sum was realised.

to his knee-cap was caused through the struggle with an officer whom he tried to throw overboard. If Frenchmen will swallow this, they will swallow anything. No official notice can, of course, be taken of such a canard. But it is hard thus to live in "the fierce light that beats upon a throne."

"The rain it raineth every day," and farmers are saying if not singing--" Oh what will the harvest be ?" When the late Edwin Waugh was on one occasion weather-bound for several days at Wastdale, in the Lake District, he asked the landlord," Willie Ritson," if it always rained there. " Nay," said "Willie," it sometimes " snaws." We shall have " snaw " again in this part of the country before long, for -are we not near the end of August?

Bad harvests on the continent are likely to cause an increase in the price of bread in this country, especially if the schemes which are being projected to" corner" wheat should be successful. It is not sufficient to say—" Cursed is he that withholdeth corn from the people." He ought to be punished more summarily and directly. The "corner" man ought to be cornered; and if it can be shown that he is starving the poor in order that he may grow rich, he should be imprisoned for a year or two.

There is a Holy Coat at Treves and there is a •Holy Coat at Argenteuil; and yet there are not two Holy Coats; but one Holy Coat. How is it to be? Which is the genuine article? It is obvious that one of them is "more holy than godly ;" and it is not pleasant to think of growing sentimental over the wrong garment. There was a tender- hearted man, who after long absence, returned to the home of his childhood and shed tears. When he pursued his inquiries, he found that he had sat and wept on the wrong doorstep.

The wretch Turner, found guilty of the diaboli- cal murder of a little girl at Horsforth, was exe- cuted at Leeds, on Tuesday. He asserted his innocence to the last; but if there is anything in evidence, it must be said, as "Festus " has it, that he did— Die with the black lie flapping on his lip, Like the soot-flake upon a burning bar.
Nobody seems to read " Festus " now; and yet it contains more marvellous lines than any other poem written in this generation ; such, for in- stance, as : - - -- --
"Envy's a coal comes hissing hot from hell";
Or— "Men might be better if we better deemed Of them " ;

Or- " Who never doubted, never half believed, Where doubt there truth is—'tis her shadow" ; And— "We live in deeds, not years; in thoughts not breaths; In feelings, not in figures on a dial. We should count time by heart-throbs. He most lives Who thinks most—feels the noblest—acts the best."

The delay of the County Council in settling the claims of the non-county boroughs to a share in the grant they have to distribute, for the sup- port of Technical Instruction, is causing serious inconvenience to Committees like that of Warring- ton which are depending upon that fund in making their arrangements for the coming session. These arrangements cannot be postponed much longer, if they are to have any classes at all this season, on account of the stringent rules of the Science and Art Department. To a Borough entitled from its population to consider itself on a par with County Boroughs, such red tapeism is ex- ceedingly vexations.

If the licensing magistrates of the borough of Warrington have any regard for public opinion, they cannot fail to be impressed with the magni- ficent meeting which was held in the Co-operative Hall, on Thursday evening. As the Rector thoughtfully "remarked, the bulk of the large audience was composed of middle-aged and elderly men, who showed themselv3s in earnest upon the necessity of reducing the present number of licensed houses. The meeting may be described as unanimous, for, as the two who voted against the motion are servants of a brewing firm, they can scarcely be said to count.

As speaker after speaker put it to the audience, the decision in the case of Sharp versus Wakefield throws the responsibility upon the magistrates of renewing,or refusing to renew,existing licenses. It is true that notice requires to be given to license- holders that objection is being taken; but the magistrates can do as they did two years ago; they can instruct their clerk to give notice. They can, if they like, put themselves in a position to re-consider the case of every license in the town ; and may, on Tuesday next, adjourn the court for that purpose. If they neglect to take action, it will be felt that they have failed in their duty,and are therefore unequal to the responsibility which , devolves upon them.

div.head: WIDNES BAKERS' UNION.
div.p: WIDNES BAKERS' UNION.

At a meeting of the members on Saturday night, Mr. T. Delaney presiding, the Secretary was instructed to ,communicate with the secretaries of the various trades' unions in Widnes with a view of forming a Trades Council for Widnes at once. MOSS BANK WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.

Special services were held in this chapel on Sunday and were well attended. In the afternoon a children's service was held, and the Rev. S. Kelsall of the Metho- dist Episcopal Church, America, delivered an address. In the evening he preached a capital sermon to a crowded congregation. Collections were made in aid of repairing the chapel and £5 was realised. Mr. Kelsall had preached in Widnes some fifty years ago.
SAD DEATH OF A BOY AT RUNCORN.

Mr. R. Dobson, deputy coroner for the honour of Hal- ton, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court on Mon- day on the body of George Dooley Owen, aged 4 years, son of John Owen, shipwright, of Bridge-st. On Tues- day at noon, the boy followed his father to the sprinch works and afterwards started for home along the towing path of the canal. He was never seen alive again. The canal was dragged for several days but without result. On Saturday Samnel Inglefield employed on the dredger found the body.—The Coroner remarked that it was a very sad case and the Jury returned a verdict of "Found Dead."

TONIC SOL-CA JUBILEE RUNCORN. A meeting of the Sol-faists of Runcorn has been held to take into consideration the best means of celebrating the jubilee of Tonic Sol-fa. A committee with Mr. J. Halford, G.T.S.C. as chairman. and Messrs. W. Handley and W. Epps as secretaries was formed to carry out the details of the arrangements.

RUNCORN Co-OPERATIVE STORES EXCURSION. The annual excursion arranged by Runcorn Co-opera- tive Society took place on Monday,when a large number of persons travelled to Blackpool. Despite the unsettled nature of the weather a pleasant day was spent at the popular watering place. Owing to delays on the rail- way the return journey was not accomplished until about one a.m. •

SUCCESS OR WIDNES BRASS BAND. In connection with the brass band contest and garden fête given by Messrs. Lever Bros., Port Sunlight, to their employes at Thornton Manor on Saturday, the second and third prizes were won respectively by the Widnes Wesleyan Brass Band (conductor W. Rimmer) and Gossage's Soap Works Brass Band, Widnes (conductor Mr. J. Tomlinson).

PRESSNTATION AT RUNCORN. On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. B. Crosby was the reci- pient of a handsome dinner cruet-stand,presented to him by the teachers and scholars of the Brunswick Wesleyan Boys' School, on the occasion of his marriage. The pre- sentation was appropriately made by Master W. Hamil- ton, one of the senior scholors of the school, who has re- cently gained several successes in connection with the Science and Art Department. DOROTHY AT RUNCORN. Mr. W. B. Redfern's London Company, on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings this week gave a performance of the comedy opera " Dorothy" in the Public Hall, to good audiences. The representations on the whole were very creditable, and the bright and sparkling music and witty dialogue were highly amusing. The stage was far too small for the proper display of the scenery and dresses. The piano used at the performance was from Mr. Timperley's, of Lowland's-road. - -

- - RUNCORN SHIP CANAL MISSION. The anniversary of this mission was celebrated on Saturday, when the scholars and many of their parents marched in procession through the principal thorough- fares, headed by the Mill Brow Brass Band. The Salva- tion Army Band also took part. In the evening a well attended meeting was held ,when the Rev. Hon. R.Grims- ton, and Mr. J. Watson, the former missionary-,delivered appropriate addresses. Special services were held on Sunday, the preacher being the Rev. Hon. R. Grimston, and on Monday evening a tea party was held, the after proceedings being of an interesting character. Prizes were distributed to the scholars who had been regular in their attendance. The celebration was altogether a very successful one.

lIIIN'CORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. At the usual fortnightly meeting of the above order,on Saturday, an essay was read by Mr. Wesley Cooke "A voyage to Australia." The writer gave a most interest- ing account of a voyage to Australia. He graphically described the interior of the ship and the thrilling dents of the passage out, naming the places of call. The essayist showed splendid descriptive powers, and was listened to with mnch pleasure. After the paper there was a conversation, in which the followina officers and members took part :—Messrs. Thomas Cooke, Thomas H. Holt, T. M. Timperley, Daniel Bisbrown, Thos. Heesom, and James Johnson. A cordial vote of thanks was given to Mr. Cooke for his paper. A SIIIP CANAL ROBBERY.

Yesterday at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. J. Handley, Samuel Ward, a Ship Canal labourer, was charged on suspicion with stealing a silk handkerchief worth 6s. 11d., the property of Thomas Holland, also a Ship Canal labourer. On Sunday the prosecutor arid three companions, ,d whom the prisoner wa.s one,went to the hotel at Moore, and after leaving they went down a lane. Them Holland fell asleep and when he awoke he saw the prisoner taking a silk neckerchief from his neck. He also discovered that his earrings and a handkerchief had been taken. His earrings were restored to him but the men would not return anything to him but the neckerchief .—Samuel Miller, assistant to Mr. Imison, pawnbroker, deposed to the prisoner pawning the necker- chief.—On the application of Superintendent Large, the prisoner was remanded to Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, when it was understood the two other men would 6e-apprehended.
