div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT U RDA Y , AUGUST 22, 1891.
RUNCORN BOARD SCIIOOLS.

In accordance with the requirements of the Code the statement of the accounts of Runcorn Board Schools are now exhibited on the notice board at the Town Hall for the information of the ratepayers, and we extract the following particulars. At Mill Brow Infant School the income was £lB4 17s. 6d. including grant from Council on Education £96 is.; school fees £52 183.; cash for books, Sze., £1 11s, ; rent of schoolroom on Sundays £8; balance from rates £26 9s. 6d. The expenditure was as follows :-Salary of teacher £BO 163. Bd. ; assistant £4O; pupil teacher £23; books, &c., £l2 9s. 9d. ; fuel, light- ing,and cleaning £24 13s. 5d.; replacement of furniture, &c., £2 Os. 7d. ; rates, taxes and insurance £1 14s. 9d. At Grreenway-road Schools the total income is £Bl6 3s. Bd. made up as follows: Grant from Council on Edu- cation £394 12s. 6d. ; boys : school fees £154 Os. 4d. ; cash for books, £9 Os. 6d. ; girls: school lees £122 9s. Bd. ; cash for books, Sze. £6 9s. 9d.; balance from rates £129 10s. 11d. The expenditure amounts to the same total and includes :-Boys: Salary of teacher £181; assistants £207 10s. ; pupil teacher £lB • books, apoara- tus,and stationery £4O 4s. : galary of teacher £97 13s. 4d.; assistants £l3l 7s. 4d.; pupil teachers £25 ss. boeks, &e. ; £29 2s. 4d.; general expenses £lO2 16s. id. It may be inentiwled that up to the present no other school in the town has yet placarded its accounts as required. DOMESTIC DIFFERENCES AT WIDNES.

Thomas Pennington, of 14 Farrant-st., was summoned for deserting his wife on the 15th July. Mr. Knowles appeared for the wife and Mr. Mearns (St. Helens) for the defendant. The parties were married on the 3rd February, 1890, and the complainant alleged that her husband had repeatedly thrashed her. On the 14th July she went to visit her sister at St. Helens and she did not return until next day at noon. Her husband knew where she had gone. She found all the doers and win- dows fastened with nails and she could not get in the I house. Defendant earned good wages, but he had not oiven her a penny towards the support of herself and 'children since that date.—The defence was that Mrs. Pe- nnington was very seldom in the house, and neglected to i get her meals ready and t was alleged that when she went away on the 14th July she did not come back for a week. The defendant denied that he had nailed the doors ;he simply locked them while he was at work. The ill-treatment was also denied. Defendant said he gave his wife money to pay bills which he found were not settled.—ln reply to Mr. Gossage, defendant said he would take his wife back if she would look after the house.—Mr. Gossage said it was a woman's duty to look after the house and take care of the man, and if they were willing to live together again the case would be dismissed.—The parties then left the court.
DEATH AND FUNERAL OF AN OLD Rt7NCORNIAN.

On Wednesday afternoon the mortal remains of Air. Thomas Anderton, of Dover-st., Runcorn, were laid in their last resting place,in Runcorn Cemetery. Mr.Ander- ton came to Runcorn from Lancashire about 60 years ago, and assisted his brother, Mr. John Anderton,incon- structing the shipbuilding yard, known for many years past as Speakman's yard, and recently swept away by the Ship Canal operations. A carpenter by trade, Mr. Anderton was the oldest member of the craft in the town, and being of an energetic nature, he worked almost up to the time of his death on Friday last. He had also the distinction of being the eldest Oddfellow in the town, having been a member for no less than 55 years. Be had attained the patriarchal age of 83 years. The fune- ral procession consisted of a hoarse and four mourning coaches, the mourners being Messrs. W. Anderton and Thomas Anderton (sons), George Wilson, Thomas Smith, and Richard Jones (sons-in-law), John Anderton, jun., Wm. Anderton, jun., Thomas Anderton, jun., Thomas Wilson, Robert Wilson, and George Wilson (grandsons) ; Captain LE. Couteur, Walter Anderton, Ralph Atherton, Thomas Weedall,.Charles Abrams, Ralph Abrams, Wm. . . . _ _ _

Rigby, William Shiers, Charles Atherton, T. Deakin, R. Wright, Wm. Hitchmough, and W. Howard. The coffin was borne to the grave on the shoulders of four carpen- ters, viz., Robert Roberts, Richard Edwards, W. Rhodes, and D. D. Pickstock, and the last sad rites were per- formed in the presence of many who attended out of respect to the memory of the departed.

NEW ALTAR AT ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH,WIDNES. There has just been erected in St. Mary's Catholic Church, Widnes,a handsome new altar,and the ceremony of consecrating and opening took place on Sunday morn- ing, the Right Rev. Dr. Reilly, Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool, officiating. Solemn high mass was sung, the celebrant being the Rev. Father Rimmer, assisted by the deacon, Rev. J. Holdham ; sub-deacon, Rev. J. Clarke ; deacons at the throne, Revs. Der Kelly and Dean Began; assistant priest, Rev. Dean Finegan ; and in the sanctuary, the Rev. Father Shea, of Waterford College. The preacher was the Rev. Father Kelly, B.A. (Lond). Service was also held in the evening and the sacred edifice was crowded. The new altar is thus de- scribed by the builders. The base is of dark marble moulded, above which is a dado of alabastor, there being a dark marble moulded string between. Above on the Gospel side is the Ambry, the piscena being in a similar position on the Epistle side. Over this is a carved mould- ing with carved foliage. In the two side bays there are three panels with cusped heads, and O.G. canopies, carved and crocheted. A richly carved cornice runs round the top, beneath which are carved verses from the Magnificat. The altar is supported in four dark marble columns, behind which are 'carved panels, and in the centre one are shown the Chalice and Vine, The centre canopy rises to a height of 30 feet and is supported on two marble columns. This canopy is richly gabled, moulded and crocheted and is of unique design. On each side are two panels filled with paintings of the Annunciation. The panels on the Gospel side are filled with angels adoring, and on the Epistle side paintings of the Assumptici. All the paintings are from the atelier of Messrs. J. Hardman and Co., Birmingham, and the altar has been erected by Messrs. Norbury and Paterson, sculptors, Myrtle-st., Liverpool, from the designs of Messrs. Pup.;in and Pugin, Westminster. The tabernacle and Altar Cross have been made by Messrs. Hardman.
IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE, WIDNES. • At the weekly meeting of this League on Sunday a number of new members were enrolled and the routine business transacted. Dr. O'Keeffe presided.

RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meething was held on Wednesday after- noon, under the presidency of-Mr. T. Riley. There were also present Messrs. Grice' Hankinson, W. Handley, and J. D. Jones (secretary and librarian). The report for the month showed that 1,686 vols. had been issued, a de- crease of 279 on the corresponding month last year. The Secretary presented the ninth annual report, which stated that there were now in the library 5,859 vols. compared with 5,424 last year, increase 435 vols., of which 66 had been presented, and 369 purchased. The number of borrowers' tickets issued during the year was 769, being 69 less than last year. The library had been open for the issue of books 149 days, and 22,390 works I were issued, being an average daily issue of 150, as coin- I pared with 164 last year. The reading room, which had been open 311 days, was a source of attraction to in- creasing numbers of both sexes. The Committee had to again express their thanks for the valuable gifts of money, books, periodicals, and newspapers. The names of the donors are Messrs. J. T. Brunner, M.P. (£5 and books), W. F. Blake (London), Lord Brassey, British Museum. Cassell and Co., Miss Cobb, Clarendon Press, Robert Foulkes, Dr. Gastaldi, Thomas Greenwood, W. Handley, Henry De Borte, Thomas Riley, John Simpson, Geo. Orme, Geo. Steward, the Swedenborg Society, G. C. Thompson, C. H. Warne (Brighton), and Rev. Canon Wood. The financial statement showed that the receipts amounted to £219 ss. Bd., which with a balance in hand of £6 13s. 6d. brought the total up to £226 4s. 2d. The ' penny rate realised Ll9l 35. 6d., the expenditure amounted to £215 Bs. id. the principal items being new books £66 6s. 2d., magazines and newspapers £23 7s. 6d., fittings £l7 19s. id., bookbinding £l3 us. The report was adopted, orders being given for printing 100 copies. The Librarian was instructed to purchase the following local Acts of Parliament :—Mersey and Irwell Act, 1721; Runcorn Commissioners Acts, 1852; Runcorn Water- works Act, 1865; Runcorn Gas Company Act, 1847; London and North-Western Railway Act, 1861; and the general acts for the years 1887 to 1890 inclusive. WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD AGRICULTURAL SHOW. The entries for this exhibition close this (Satur- day) night's post. As the entries are so far below last year's, the Committee will be glad if intending . exhibitors will send in without further delay.

div.head: Two MEN KILLED AT GARSWOOM
div.p: Two MEN KILLED AT GARSWOOM

On Tuesday morning, Hugh Flannigan (45),Long- lane, Ashton, and Patrick Regan (21)7Reservoir-st., Ashton, were killed at Garswood Hall colleries. They were engaged roofing, when a great quantity of debris fell upon them. They were dead when unearthed about half an hour afterwards. J. & W. BUTTON'S BUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street. Warrington.—Advt. SHIP CANAL MISSION AT CADISHEAD.

The Ck)cd Templars connected with this mission had a special day on Saturday. The services of the Congregational Brass Band had been secured, and, headed by them,the Templars,iu their regalia,formed a proceesion and paraded the village. An adjourn- ment was afterwards made to the Mission Hall, where tea was provided. 13.issuurrrE5.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-Bt., Warrington.—Advt. A TECHNICAL SCHOOL FOR SALFORD.

_ The Salford Town Council,on Wednesday,adopted plans for a technical school to be erected on a site close to Peel Park. A rough estimate of the cost of the building and fittings is £40,000. The school will include departments for dyeing, chemistry, en- gineering, weaving and spinning,building construc- tion, physics,and electric lighting. There will also be a school of art and a school of cookery. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—GARLAND, IW/flint= --Advt. • THE MISSING CHESHIRE GENTLEMAN. There is no news of the missing Altrincham visitor up to this. A friend of Mr. Mason's visited Peel on Saturday,searching for Alfred, but it is said without success. Mr. Mason's family are still stay- ing in Ramsey, but have not made any communica- tions to the police or outsiders as to the where- abouts of Alfred. It is generally believed in Ram- sey that they are satisfied he is not drowned. J. &W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt. THE I OLICE AND THE TELEPHONE. During this week the circuit by which the police stations at Earlestown, Newton . Leigh, Atherton, and Padgate, are brought into telephonic communi- cytion with each other has been completed. This will be a very great convenience to those in charge at the various police offices, and much delay will be avoided in obtaining information from head- quarters, which otherwise would entail a special journey. RMIORATISN.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Guion, American. Aus- tralian, Oriental. and other lines.—John Walker, agent. "Examiner ' Office. Bewsev-st.. Warrington.—Advt. PILL-MAKERS' HOLIDAY,

The employes of Messrs. Thomas Beecham and Son, the well-known pill manufacturers, of St. Helens, were entertained to their annual holiday on Saturday, when Morecambe was visited. The party, numbered about 70, were conveyed in saloon carri- ages, and left St. Helens by the 6.43 a.m. train. Favoured with line weather, the outing was very much enjoyed. As on all former occasions, the entire expenses were defrayed by Mr. Beecham. LAWN Mowmis.—Garland, 51, Bridge-Bt., Warrington. and at Earlestown.—Advt.
CROSFIELD'S " PERFECTION " SOAP WRAPPER
COMPETITION.

The result of this competition, in which 500 silver watches are given to those who send in the largest numbers of "perfection" soap wrappers. has just been declared. Winning competitors seem to hail from every part of England and Wales. We notice that nearly thirty of the watches have been won by residents in Warrington ; and neighbouring places such as St. llelens, Runcorn. and Lymm are repre- sented in the list of prize-takers. J. W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street. Warriugton. -Advt. DROWNED AT nOLLINS_GREEN.

On Tuesday forenoon Charles Naylor, employed on a dredger on the Ship Canal at Hollins Green, was drowned in the Mersey. He was on a barge getting coal off a stage, when he stepped backwards too far and slipped into the water. His body was not recovered until three o'clock, when it was removed to the Boathouse Inn, Hollins Green, to await an inquest. Naylor has resided in Hollins Green for some time, and is supposed to have been about seventeen years of age, but nothing is known of his parentage. FATAL FALL AT WIDNES.

_ of Mary Walker, aged 77 years, 15, Wright-st., Widnes, died on Tuesday fromthe effects of injuries received on the 10th July. Owing to her extreme age the woman was subject to giddiness,and on the day named, while walking across the kitchen, she became giddy and fell. Her thigh was broken, and Dr. Hutchinson was unable to set the bone because of her age and feebleness, and she never recovered from the shock of the accident. A Iverdict of "Accidental death" was returned at the inquest held by Mr. Husband on Wednesday. A SERIOUS FALL.

Andrew Kelly, 13 years of age, of Victoria-street, St. Helens, met with a serious accident, on Monday. Kelly was in the employ of a sub-contractor engaged in widening the Carr Mill Viaduct, near Garswood, belonging to the London & North-Western Railway Co., and while at work on the girders, he slipped and fell a distance of nearly 60 feet to the ground beneath. He was at once removed to the Free Provi- dence Hospital at St. Helens, where, on examination by Drs. M'Nicoll and Challenor, it was found that his most serious injury as a fractured aim, coupled with a severe shock to the system. J. &. W. Durroies BUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt. THE COUNTESS OF CARLISLE AND SUNDAY CLOSING. The temperance party of Brampton, in Cumber- land, headed by the Countess of Carlisle, have been endeaving to secure Sunday closing in the town. At the licensing sessions, on Wednesday, it was stated that the bonsent of twenty-five publicans out of thirty had been obtained to a six-day license, and a memorial bearing 800 signatures in favour of Sunday closing was prepared for presentation to the justices. The magistrates refused to receive the memorial, and renewed the licenses, the temper- ance party having omitted to prove service of their notices of objection. SAD DEATH OF A CROFT SCHOOLMASTER. It is with regret we record the death of Mr. William Charles Savage, the respected head master of the Board School, Croft, and the organist, choir- master, and superintendent, of the Sunday school of Christ Church, Croft, which took place at Birming- ham, on Saturday. The deceased, who was appointed head master about a year ago, on the resignation of Mr. Ball, had a severe attack of influenza and bronchitis during the winter, when he was attended by Dr. Sefton, of Culcheth. A fortnight ago, during the usual midsummer holidays, he went to Blackpool, where he remained until Friday, when he returned to his native town, Birmingham. On Saturday evening he went into the city for a walk, and according to a letter received by the Clerk to the Croft School Board, it appears that he was taken into a druggist's shop, where he suddenly died. Much sympathy is felt in the village for his bereaved widow and relatives.
BAND CONTEST AT THORNTON, CHESHIRE.

In connection with the garden fete given by Messrs. Lever Bros., Port Sunlight, to the employes at Thornton Manor, on Saturday, there was a band contest. Seven bands competed, and Mr. J. 0. Shepherd, musical director of the Court Theatre, Liverpool, was the judge. His award was:—First prize, Skelmersdale (conductor, W. Rimmer) ; second prize, Widnes Wesleyan (conductor, W. Rimmer) ; third prize, Gossage's Soap Works, Widnes (conductor, J. Tomlinson) • fourth prize, Tranmere Gleam of Sunshine (conductor W. Sed- don) ; fifth prize, Warrington Catholic United. The unsuccessful bands were Birkenhead Borough Band and Birkenhead Mission Band. J. .t W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Adrt. EXCURSION FROM COLLINS GREEN.

On Saturday the employes of the Collins Green Colliery Co., had their annual excursicn to Black- pool. About 1,000, colliers and their families accompanied the trip to the favourite watering place, trains calling at Earlestown to pick up a very large number of those who resided in and about Earlestown. The day was most favourable for the outing and in consequence the miners had an enjoyable time. The various places of resort were in turn visited special facilities being pro- vided to enable the excursionists to do so. The return journey was made rather late in the evening, and it was nearly one o'clock on Sunday morning, before the last train reached home. THE HOME IRON TRADE.

The English iron market continues depressed. and it is difficult to determine in what quarter to expect the first signs of improvement. The threatened strike of blast-furnace engine-men, &c., has been obviated, the men acceding to the proposed reduc- tion for a time. No 3 Middlesbro' pig is 9d. lower on the week. From nearly all the pig•iron centresa dearth of orders is reported. Manufactured iron is in moderate request generally. Tinplates remain quiet. Steel continues in very slack request. The demand for old materials is rather more active. Shipbuilding shows a further slight improvement, and it is expected that the rivetters' strike on the Clyde will speedily collapse. Engineers generally are slacker. The coal trade is fairly steady.—lron. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE CONFERENCE ON RAILWAY RATES.

A meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Con- ference on Railway Rates and Charges was held on Thursday. Sir J. Harwood, who presided, presented the Report of the Executive Committee setting forth the work that has been done. The Committee expressed the opinion that a substantial gain had resulted from the efforts of the Conference. The principal result of the legislation, it was said, had been the codification of a great number of Acts, so that traders " will for the first time be enabled to measure the statutory powers of the various com- panies affected, without the same danger as hereto- fore of being drawn into expensive litigation." An appeal is to be made for a further contribution on the part of the bodies constituting the Conference and Consultative Committee. NEW MAGISTRATES FOR THE BOROUGH OF WIGAN.

The following gentlemen have been placed on the commission of the peace for the borough of Wigan: —Messrs. Alfred Barlow, Lower Whitley, Wigan- lane, gentleman; John Bolton, 12. Dicconson-st., gentleman; George Lamb Campbell, of The Popu- lars, Wigan-lane, secretary of the Central Associa- tion for Dealing with Distress Caused by Mining Accidents; William Chalk, Millgate, iron merchant; John Gee, Scholes, provision merchant; James Hil- ton, Scholes, brassfounder ; Charles Butler Holmes, Home Leigh. Wigan, builder; Robert Leyland, Powell-at., estate agent; Samuel Allenby Oliver, Bellingham House, general merchant; John Bar- low Stuart, Standishgate, house surgeon. Eight of these gentlemen appointed for Wigan are Conserva- tives, and two of them are Unionists. PRIMITIVE METHODIST PICNIC TO FRODSHAM. The teachers and friends of the Warrington and Widnes circuit joined in a united picnic to Prod- sham, on Thursday afternoon. They all met at Warrington Bank Quay station and proceeded by train to Frodsham, and thence made their way to Mersey View. Some went off on various rambles and others indulged in different out-door games. Afterwards over a hundred sat down to tea, and then the Rev. Wm. Thornley called upon Massrs. Titchett, Seddon, D. Wright, and Done, superinten- dents of the various schools, to offer some remarks in respect to Sunday school work, A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. A. E. Calvert, the circuit Sun- day school secretary, to whose energy and enter- prise this outing owes its success. The gathering wound up by giving a very hearty welcome to the Rev. W. Thornley, who has recently come into this circuit. WitisToN FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.

The third annual sports in connection with the Wht,ton Football Club were held on the football ground, near the Prescot Union Workhouse, n his- ton, on Saturday. The judges were Mr. J. J. Tickle and Mr. W. Cheetham ; handicapper, Mr. W. Platt; starter, Mr. Thomas Smith ; and the energetic secre- tary, Mr. S. Price. The results of the various events were as follows :-220 Yards Boys' Race: 1, K. C. Gould, Widnes, 45 yards; 2, Albert Thompson, Widnes, 6; 3, J. Morris, Widnes, 69. 120 Yards Members' Race: 1, W. Lawrenson, 4 yards; 2, R. Pritchard, 3; 3, Luke Chorley, 6. 100 Yards Open Race: 1, J. H. Winstanley, Ashton-in-Makerfield, 8 yards; 2, J. Banks, St. Helens, 10; 3, C. H. Painter, Ashton-in-Makerfield, 8. Mile Local Bicycle Race: 1, H. C. Reichardt, Huyton, scratch; 2, W. Edmu.nd- son, Thatto Heath, scratch; 3, J. Platt, Whiston, scratch. Two Miles Open Bicycle Race: 1, M. Bailey, St. Helens, 240 yards; 2, Thomas Black- ledge, Rainford, 310; 3, W. Ward, Tuebrook, 310. 220 Yards Open Flat Race: 1, J. Critchley, Thatto Heath, 10 yards; 2, J. Johnson, Sutton, 12; 3, W. Birchall, Thatto Heath, 10. Half-mile Open Race: 1, P. J. Kenyon, St. Helens, 56 yards; 2, Thomas Davies, Roby, 55; 3, W. Torkington, Ashton, 48. 440 Yards Open Flat Race: 1, R. Bickerstaffe, War- rington, 27 yards; 2, J. Barr, Roby, 22. 3, W. Wlslelly, Liverpool Harriers, 20. One Mile Open Flat Race: 1, G. Eastwobd, Warrington' 135 yards; 2, W. Torkington, Ashton, 100; 3, P. J. Kenyon, St. Helens, 120. A potato picking race for the mem- bers of the club, the prize being a silver cup pre- sented by Mrs. Willis, of Halsnead Hall, was won by R. Pritchard. J. Sc. W. DUTTON S SUMMER SALE ROW OR. Sankey Street, Warringtou.—Advt.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
Tutrasray.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage, Mr. T. S. Timmis

and Mr. H. W. Deacon. DRUNKENNESS.—James O'Brien and Sarah Jervis, were each fined ss. and costs for this offence.—Jane Jones was fined 10s. and costs for a similar offence. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—A number of parents were summoned by the School Board for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and a fine of ss. was imposed in each case. Doe CASs.—S. Eyes, Lugsdale-road, was charged with having his dog improperly muzzled.—James Gilden said he was passing the defendant's house when the dogran at him and bit his leg. The dog was not properly muzzled. As the defendant had been previously fined, he was now crdered to pay 10s. and costs. THEFT OF A TURNlP.—William Griffiths of Widnes-road, I was charged with stealing a turnip from a field belong- ing to Mr. Longton, farmer. On premising not to offend again the defendant was ordered to pay costs. ROBBING A FARM YARD .—William Jones, no fixed abode, was charged with stealing a macintosh, the pro- perty of Mr. Bennett, farmer, Speke. The macintosh had been left in the farm yard, and when it was missed, the prisoner was found wearing it. The prisoner pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. ROBBED WHILE ASLEEP.—Maria Makin, no fixed abode, was brought up on remand, charged with stealing a watch and knife worth £1 18s. 6d., from the person of Edward Williams, of Ellesmere Port, on the 17th inst. The couple were drinking together, and Williams fell asleep on a doorstep in Ann-st. When he awoke he found that the woman had left him and his watch and knife were missing.—The prisoner pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 14 days' hard abour. HARD SWEARING.—Martin Nugent and Wm. Nugent brothers, of Wright-st., were charged with assaulting Michael McNamara of Sankey-st., on the night of the 15th inst. It was alleged that the prisoners, because the prosecutor would not send for some beer,got hold of him and kicked him on the head and other parts of the body. He had a severe wound on the head, his eyes were blackened, and he was generally bruised.—The evidence was very conflicting and the Bench said although there was some hard swearing they believed the prisoners were guilty and fined them 10s. and costs each.

Early this morning a fire broke out at a private house in Duncan Square, Hackney, London. Stephen West, aged four and a half years, and George West, aged 15 months, ware burned to death, and another child, named Ann West is so badly injured that she is not expected to recover.

A strike affecting several thousand hands engaged in the Clyde shipbuilding yards, and which has been going on since the beginning of June, terminated on Wednes- day, the men having by a vote decided to accept a re- duction of 5 per cent. in wages as proposed by the em- ployers.

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. I a fortnight beyond the original time. Whilst the I scholars have been away, the trustees have embraced the opportunity of making some long-needed alter- ations in various parts of the school. Some years ago, owing to the increased number of scholars, the class-rooms were enlarged, and this somewhat en- croached upon the kitchen accommodation. During the present vacation it was decided to re-model the kitchens and adjoining rooms. The old kitchen has been re-modelled, and is now used as a " servary," where the meals are passed through into the dining room for the scholars. A servants' sitting roam and library has also been provided, where the servants may retire when their duties are over. Adjoining the kitchen, a room has been formed, with hot and cold water taps, Ate., for washing purposes,and out- side this room new larders have been made. The bailding has been done by Messrs. Gibson, the plumbing by Mr. Hedgcock, the tank by Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, and the hot water arrange- ments by Messrs. J. R. Cooper and Sons, of Liver- pool. The whole of the work has been carried out under the superintendence of Ur. W, Owen. BILLIARD HANDICAP.

A special meeting of the Board of Commissioners was held at the Town Hall, yesterday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. H. J. Grice, to consider plans for the setting back of Waterloo Hotel, and the widening of High street. After a lengthy dis- cussion it was resolved:--!‘ That the surveyo and law clerk be authorised to produce to the juStices, at the annual licensing sessions, the plans showing the line of frontage of High-street and Waterloo-road desired to be obtained by the Commissioners for street improvement." ,
THINGS NEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Mr. Charles E. Linaker, estate agent and sur- veyor, Frodsham, has been appointed agent to the Marquis of Cholmondeley of Cholmondeley Castle, for Runcorn, Frodsham, and Helsby properties, in place of Mr. H. Beswiek, resigned,

The enterprise of the Liverpool evening news- papers is phenomenal. Conway was launched into eternity at 8 o'clock on Thursday morning,and nine minutes later an edition of the" Echo" containing an announcement of the execution passed through Runcorn by train en route for Chester. That train had left Liverpool at 7.40 a.m., twenty minutes before Conway was hanged, so that the newspaper must have been printed over half-an-hour ahead of the event. Fortunately Conway "shuffled off the mortal coil" according to order—or at least had it roughly " shuffled " for him.

A special meeting of Runcorn School Board was called for Tuesday evening for the purpose of decid- ing what action should be taken on the Assisted Education Act. The Chairman had given notice of his intention to move a resolution accepting the fee grant of 10s. per head and declaring the Board Schools free. Previous to the meeting the members present held a private consultation in the clerk's office,with the result that the chairman postponed his motion until Tuesday. I afterwards learned that the Board intended to have a conference with the managers of Denominational Schools this afternoon. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. S. Taylor, and Mr. J. J. Howitt, were absent from the meeting, but it is to be hoped that in the interests of the ratepayers they will endeavour to be in their places next Tuesday evening, when a decision will have to be arrived at. •

On Saturday afternoon the return billiard match between the Runcorn and Penketh Liberal Clubs took place, at the Liberal Club, Penketh. The match commenced at 4.30 p.m.' and after half an hour's play, everyone adjourned for tea, which was on the tables at five o'clock. The expense of the tea was kindly borne- by the president of the club (Mr. Broadhurst), who entrusted the catering to Mr. and Mrs. John Mainley. In the prepiration of the tea, Mrs. Mainley was assisted by Mrs, Wilkin- son, Mrs. J. Routledge, Mrs. F. Wilkinson, and Miss Mainley. The players, numbering 24, did justice to the good tea provided, and afterwards a short meeting was held. A hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Broardhurst, for his liberality in providing tea, was I proposed by Mr. Cross, seconded by Mr. White, and unanimously carried. Mr. Mainley responded on the President's behalf. Mr. Cross also spoke in flatter- ing terms of the kindness of Mr. Broadhurst at all times in relation to the club, and his willingness to do anything to further its interests. Mr. White expressed the pleasure he felt at meeting the Runcorn friends at Penketh. A vote of thanks to Mrs. Mainley and others for preparing tea was proposed by Mr. W. Wright, seconded by Mr. Richard Moores (both of Runcorn), and adopted. At the conclusion of the meeting,play was resumed, and after an exciting but pleasantly contested game, the Runcorn friends eventually proved victorious. VESTRY MEETING AT GREAT SANKEY.

To declare the Runcorn Board School free would entail a deficiency of about £3O which is equal to about an eighth of a penny on the rates. it is diffi- cult to see what fee could be charged to make up this small amount were the Board disposed to act in such a manner. And it should be borne in mind that should the 10s. grant and the fee charged amount to more than the average fee at the present time the grant would be reduced by the amount of the excess. Practically the parents will be taxed to ease the imperial exchequer. The best and most straightforward plan is to declare the schools free at once.

In Widnes Board Schools the amount of the de- ficiency is £416, and the Board, on Tuesday last, decided to charge a fee of a penny a head. The Chairman did not disguise his feelings ix favour of free education, and it was only a wish to work harmoniously with the Denominational Schools,and in order, as he termed it, that they should not be "starved out," that he agreed to the penny fee. That fee will bring in about £5OO a year, so that the ratepayers will lose the difference between that sum and the amount of the deficiency, or about £BO. To free the schools would mean a penny in the £ on the rates. At the same time it should not be for- gotten that some free places have to be provided, and, as Mr. Deacon pointed out, unless the Denom- inational Schools co-operate with the School Board in providing these free places, a hitch will most likely occur. However, twelve months' experience will show how the arrangement works.

On Monday evening a vestry meeting of the par- ishioners of Penketh and Great Sankey was held in the School, Sankey. The meeting first assembled in the church vestry, and after the notice conven- ing the meeting had been read by the Vicar, every- one adjourned to the school. The chair was taken. by the Rev. E. S. Jackson. Amongst those present we noticed the Rev. T. E. Winder. Messrs. Skelton, Ifillington, Owen, Woodward, Newcombe, Taylor, , England, R. Boardman, Travers, and BrOOMEL in opening the meeting, the Vicar said this was the saddest vestry meeting which had been held since his arrival in the parish. As they would have heard from the notice which had been read, their business that evening was to elect a people's war- den in the place of their late friend, Mr. T.H.Wilson. Mr.W.P.Skelton then proposed a vote of condolence with Mrs. Wilson and the members of his family,on the sad loss they have sustained by the sudden death of Mr. T. 11. Wilson, whose worth all highly appreciated. Mr. Skelton said he felt in proposing this resolution that he could echo all that bad been said about Mr. Wilson. He had known him since he was a boy. He knew of the terrible agony Mr. Wilson endured whilst with the trip at Windermere, and of his struggles to put aside his pain to make the ex- cursion a success. He died doing his duty. It was only his great strength of will and high spirit that *trebled him to reach Warrington alive.—Mr. Prayers seconded the resolution, which was supported by Mr. England and unanimously carried.—ln the course of some further remarks, Mr. Jackz,on said he had known Mr. Wilson for twelve years, and during that time he had been intimately arquainted with him. He wanted them to bear in mind that they had not only lost a parochial officer, but a personal friend. It would be a great consolation to the sor- rowing relatives to know how much Mr. Wilson was respected and honoured.—The next business before the meeting was the election of people's warden.— Mr. Owen had great pleasure in proposing Mr. W. P. Skelton to fill the vacant uffice.—Mr. Millington seconded, Ur. England supported, and the resolu- tion was unanimously carried. The next business was the election of sidesman. Mr. Skelton proposed Mr. John Warburton, Mr. Boardman seconded, and the resolution was unanimously carried.—This con- cluded the business of the meeting.

For many years one of Runcorn's most pressing wants has been science and art classes, and the School Board have this week taken the initial step towards their establishment, and the disgrace of a town that nearly wholly exists by scientific opera- tions being void of all science teaching will be swept away. The School Board and the Commis- sioners are working hand in hand, and no doubt a tempting syllabus will be issued shortly. Of course when we get the Technical School these classes will cease, but until then they will fill up a great gap, and Mr. Pritchard deserves the best thanks of the community for the part he has taken in their formation.

The annual Licensing Sessions for Runcorn Petty Sessional Division will be held at Runcorn on Monday next., and the publicans and general public are waiting with anxious interest to see what atti- tude the magistrates will take in the altered cir- cumstances brought about by Sharp v. Wakefield. There will be two memorials presented to the Bench by the temperance section of the community and there is no doubt that now a grave responsi- bility rests on the shoulders of the magistrates.

I understand that the Rev. C. Norman, of Run- corn, who has this summer finished his theologi- cal education at the Lancashire College, has had a call to Peckham. All Runcornians will wish him suc- cess in the path he has chosen for himself.

The election of Commissioners approaches day by day, and the excitement increases as the time approaches. There will be at least eleven candi- dates for the six sects that are vacant. The whole of the retiring six will come to the poll, but whether they will give an account of their steward- ship remains to he seen. It was said that Mr. John Wilson would seek the suffrages of the rate- payers but there is a mistake; he had no iLtention of doing so.

On the present occasion Mr. Once will be the returning officer, and he has effected one improve- ment. One booth will be set apart for the voters who wish to be quiet and unmolested,and the thanks of the ratepayers are due to Mr. Once for this con- cession.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
RETURN OF MR. WINDER.

The Rev. 'I. E. Winder, curate of St. Mary's, Great Sankey, has just returned from a visit to America. He will officiate in the stead of the Rev. E. S. Jackson, who, as already announced, leaves early next month for Montreal. CRICKET.—PENKETH V. RIXTON. The above cricket match was played al, Nixton, on Satil..,lsy. The team left Penketh in a 'bus at 2.30 p.m., and Rixton was reached at 3.45. A well contested game was played, Duill playing well for the visiting team, making a score of 22. The total scores were—Rixton, 37 ; Penketh, 67. After the match the players adjourned to the Eagle and Child Inn, where an excellent tea was served by Mr. Shaw. After tea the members of the team inspected the Ship Canal, and visited Cadishead. The return journey was commenced at 930, Penketh being I reached at 11.30, after spending a very enjoyable lafternoon.

div.head: TRIP TO FRODSHAM.
div.p: TRIP TO FRODSHAM.

On Saturday, in connection with the second annual demonstration of fiatmen of Liverpool and Birkenhead and district, a number of flatmen, resi- dent at Penketh, journeyed to Frodsham, where a demonstration was to be held. A 'bus containing about 30 men, with their families and friends, left Penketh about 12.15 p.m., and Frodsham was reached about 2.30 p.m. The afternoon was pleasantly spent in visiting the various places of interest round this popular holiday resort, and at 7.40 p.m. the return journey was commenced, and Penketh reached about 10.40. The day was most enjoyably spent throughout. The weather was good, and during the afternoon various games were engaged in. THE WESLEYA.N CHAPEL EXTENSION.

During the past fortnight, the work in connec- tion with the Wesleyan Chapel extension has been rapidly proceeded with. Since the foundation stone was laid on August Bank Holiday, good pro- gress has been made with the building, both at the front and back. Behind, where the new vestries are to be, the walls are practically built to their full height, and the rafters and roofing beams are being laid preparatory to slating. At the front the work has not been proceeding quite so rapidly. The walls are built to about half their required height, the stonework for some of the windows is fixed and built in, and the entrance door is erected. If good weather is experienced, the work ought soon to be completed. PENKETH FRIENDS' SCHOOL. The summer vacation of the teachers and scholars of he above school is now at an end. Owing to extensive alterations, the holidays were prolonged

div.head: PENKETH PARK COMPANY, LIMITED._
div.p: PENKETH PARK COMPANY, LIMITED._

The first annual general meeting of the share- holders of the Penketh Park Company, Limited, was held on Tuesday evening at the offices of the Penketh Tanning Company, Limited. The meeting, which was largely attended, and a thoroughly representative one, was presided over by Mr. C. E. Parker. Amongst those present were Messrs. S. Dodds, R. E. Garnett, T. Gandy. R. IL Posnett, J. C Routledge, Picton, Mainley, W. S. Walker, H. S. Jones, R. Boardman, Snoddy, Randall, Tetlow, White, Atherton, Watson, and several ladies. After the notice convening the mceting had been mad by the Secretary, Mr. C. E. Parker proceeded to give a brief account of the history of the company up to present time. In the course of his remarks he said they would welcome all who were desirous of carrying out the objects of the company in accordance with those set forth in the articles. They were not dependent upon the help of anyone, but they welcomed everyone who would work with them. After the 31st of August it would, unless otherwise ordered, be impossible for any- one to join. They looked to building and building land as a permanent source of revenue. They were in negotiation with Mr. R. Garnett about the land, and he had met them in a very liberal and open spirit. He had practically agreed to let them have what land they re- quired; and it now remained with the directors to deter- mine how much was required. Next year they might let land and hold houses or let them. An idea had been entertained that the company was financially rotten. He could not say what foundation there was for that idea, and did not see why with proper management it should not pay and be successful. A number of cottage gardens had already been let, and more would be let next year. He trusted everyone would determine to put put away All private feelings and work for the common- wealth and common weal.

div.head: ELECTION OF DIRECTORS.
div.p: THE ELECTION OF DIRECTORS.

This was the next business brought before the meeting. The following were elected directors on the, proposition of Mr. J. Dodds, seconded by Mr. J. Jackson :—Messrs. C. E. Parker, R. E. Garnett, T. Gandy, J. C. Routledge, T. B. Tetlow,.G. Randall, and A. J. White. Subordinate to the directors it is proposed to form a number of Com- mittees to preside over the various departments, viz., baths, allotments, bowling green, and recreation. These Committees will be formed at the first meeting of direc- tors.

div.head: ELECTION OF AUDITORS.
div.p: ELECTION OF AUDITORS.
On the proposition of Mr. IL S. Jones, seconded by Mr. Watson, the following were unanimously elected auditors: Mr. W. J. Wigfield and Mr. J. S. Snoddy.

div.head: OTHER BUSINESS.
div.p: OTHER BUSINESS.

This concluded the business, and the meeting was thrown open for anyone to ask question.. Mrs. Parker asked if a day would be set aoart for ladies at the baths. It was thought that such would be the case. Some dis- cussion arose as to the advisability of laying down a bowling green, but upon the feeling of the meeting be- ing tested, it was agreed that such a project would be a , likely development of the company. Mr. Parker said the first thing to be proceeded with would be the bowl- ing green, recreation ground, and cottage gardens. In reply to a question, Mr. Parker said it had not yet been settled when the first call would be made on the shareholders or what amount it would be. They had thought of calling in ss. per share at a time but some of the promoters thought it would be like making too many bites at the pie. Opportunity would be given for those who wished to pay up their shares at once and interest would be allowed them at a rate to be agreed upon. Mr. Parker said one of the things it was thought of starting was a deposit department, but this would not be doneimmediately, as it was thought all the share- holders' money would be required to pay up the shares. He had received from Mr J. H. Raper, of London, an account of a similar department which had been started there and proved very successful. The meetinc, concluded after passing a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Parker for his services in the chair.

A correspondent states that the depression in the steel and iron trades of Cumberland is becoming more pro- nounced and that many of the workmen are in great straits. At Workington alone 5,000 men and boys are out of employment, and have had r.o work for some time.

div.head: BEFORE THE MA.GISTRA.TES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MA.GISTRA.TES.
GA rim RN PILLAGING. -CIA RG RS AGAINGT WARRINGTON LADS.

Two batches of youths were charged before the magis- trates on Monday with stealing fruit and vegetables from gardens in Warrington. The first lot of lads were named Wm. Potts, Wm. Owen, Win. Seddon, Wm. Mather, John Sid3all, and John Foden, and charged with stealing apples and hears from the garden of .Wm. Robinson. in. Manchester-road. A policeman stated that he had been watching the garden of Mr. Robinson early ep the previous Thursday morning and saw four of the lads named amongst the fruit trees, the other two keep- ing "nix," or watching from the wall. A fine of ss. was imposed in each case.—Four other lads named Gleave. Bennett, Roughley, and Appleton, were charged with stealing beans from the garden of Mr. George Perry, on the 19th August, but the evidence not being sufficient to convict they were discharged.

div.head: AN UNCLEAN LODOIN6IHOUST3.-EfRAVY PBNALTY.
div.p: AN UNCLEAN LODOIN6IHOUST3.-EfRAVY PBNALTY.

William Preston, who keeps a lodging-house in Upper ,Bank-st., was charged at the Borough Court, on Mon- day. witn not washiMg the floors before ten o'clock in tke morning, and also with not ' clearing away liquid and other refuse before nine o'clock in the 'morning of the 11th August. Inspector Spinks proved the charges, and pointed out Use bye-laws under which lodging-house keepers are re- quired to do what the defendant had omitted doing. The Chairman (Alderman Burgess) said that lodgings were provided in Warrington of a different character to those of the defendant, and those who kept superior lodgings must not be put at a disadvantage ; -therefore, if defendant came up again, he might depend upon it his license would be cancelled.—A fine of 20s. and costs in each case was imposed.

div.head: THR'FT BY A WORKMAN.
div.p: THR'FT BY A WORKMAN.

At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, Wm. Hodgkinsor, wire worker, Percival's Fold, was charged with stealing from the workshop of Joseph Rudd,Turner- st., the previous afternoon, a pair of pincers, a pair of pliers, and a wire guard, value Bs. in all. Mr. Rudd Identified the articles, and a lad in his employ stated that the prisoner Came into the workshop about five minutes to one and waited till the men went out, then took the articles away, and stated that a boy had sold them to him. A constable deposed to finding the pliers and guard in the kitchen of a common lodging-house in Percival's Fold, where the prisoner lodged, and the pincers in his pocket.--ihe prisoner who pleaded that the articles had been sold to him and that he had in- tended to pay for them, and Mr. Rudd not pressing the case, waq fined ss. JUVENILE RAIDERS ON A TURNIP FIELD. _

At the noac,ristrates' court, yesterday, Elward Savage, 14, David W3rsley, 14, Frederick Roden, 14, and John Hood, 10, were charged with doing wilful damage, to the amount of 20s. on the Ist inst., to turnips in enclosed ground occupied by Wm. Thomson, off Winwick-road, Mr. Thomson said he drove up in a cab and caught the defendants on the ground. They had rooted up a quar- ter of an acre of turnips, and done damage to the extent 4of £s.—lnspector Spinks said he was in the company of Mr. Thomson when the lads were caught. He captured three of them on their coming over the fence. Stones were thrown at him by the neighbours, and he, had Mr.Thonison not been tnere, would have been mobbed. It was no use one or two officers going into the nrighbour- hood, as the people there seemed thoroughly adverse to the polce. The boys were fined ss. each including costs, except Hood, who being interceded for by the complain- ant, was only fined 2s. 61. and costs. A HOPELESS INEBRIATE.

A deplorable case of domestic infelicity came before the Police Ccurt on Thursday. Sophia &Tinton, who lives in Liverpool-road, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on the pre- vious day, and Inspector Spinks proved the charge. Mr. A. Browne appeared on behalf of the defendant's hus- band, who, he said, was a most respectable man and earning good money at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.'s works. He had given her as much as £3 a week for household expenses, but he (Mr. Browne) believed that out of that she had spent £2 ss. in drink, and besides that she had pawned everything she could lay her hands on. Her husband had gone to some of the pawnbrokers telling them not to take anything from her but she now got other people to pawn articles for her. He had tried every method he could think of to break her off this habit, and he (Mr. Browne) had written to her threaten- ing certain proceedings. But it had been all of no avail. Mr. Browne now suggested to the Bench that defendant should be bound over to appear when called upon, and in the meanwhile undertake to keep away from her hus- band who would pay all the costs and 12s. 6d. a week to her. To pay her more would just be giving her money to drink. The Chief Constable said they had had many complaints about defendant whose husband was, much to be pitied. For some months past she had been in the habit of drinking in private houses and sending people out for the drink. After some hesitation defendant con- sented to the course suggested by Mr. Browne, saying that she would go to live with a sister at Sheffield. She was accordingly bound over to appear when called upon.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

MAGISTERIAL CENSURE.—J3hn Bums, jun., fireman, 2, Dolan's-court, was charged on warrant with assaulting and beating his father. The prosecutor said his son struck him, and the son in return said that his father tried to strangle hina.—The daughter stated that a few days ago the father came into the house drunk, with other men. On saying to her father that she thought it "was shameful for married men to carry on so," he threw her out of the house. When she came back, shortly afterwards, her father was asleep, and in attempting to waken him by knocking the prop against the door, she accidenta,ly broke the window.—Alderman Burgess advised the young man to leave his father's house at cnce, and to make a new home. For the assault he would be fined 53. In addressing the father, Alderman Burgess said he thought his conduct was most shameful, and he was sorry that they could not deal with him that morning,but if he came into the court again he would remember the present case, and deal with him accordingly. DRUNKENNESS. Tom Taylor, labourer, Orford-lane, was charged with toeing drunk and disorderly in Horse- market-st, on the prerious night.—He was fined 53.

He was fined 10.3. and costs or 14 days.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.
TUESDAY.—Before Mr. J. White and Mr. J. C.
Parr.

MISCELLANEOUS.—A collier named Thomas Handley was charged, on a warrant,he having failed to appear to a summons, with having been drunk at Golborne, on the sth April. The case was proved by P.C. Crossley, and the prisoner was fined ss. and costs.—The same day, be- fore Mr. Parr, two Ship Canal labourers, named Edward Kirk and Albert Marchman, were charged with having, on the 16th inst., at Moore, stolen two half-sovereigns, a jubilee shilling, one and sixpence in silver, four coppers, and two silk handkerchiefs, the property of Thomas Holland. The prosecutor, who is a young man also employed on the Ship Canal, stated that on the day in question he took the prisoners to a public-house at Moore, and paid for some beer for them. Before leaving the house he paid for some more beer, which was put in a bottle,after which all three went in the direction of the Ship Canal works. On the way, they rested in a lane, and prosecutor went to sleep. He was awoke, however, by one of the prisoners attempting to take the rings out of his ears and a silk handkerchief off his neck. He then discovered that his nurse had been stolen. Looking round he found it lying on the ground, but the money tiad been taken out of it. The prisoners, who denied having committed the robbery, and alleged that the prosecutor was drunk,were remanded to the next Dares- bury Petty Sessions.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PErrY SESSIONS
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. W. J. Bleckley, Major Pick-
mere, and Mr. G. Comber.

THE PENHETH ASSISTANT OVERSEERSHIP.—Jas. Forster, who had resigned the overseership of Penketh, and had been appointed assistant overseer at a salary of £3O a year, now applied to have his appointment confirmed. The application was acceded to. CRUELTY TO HORSES.—Peter Shaw and Edward Collard were charged with cruelly using a horse by working it while in an unfit state at Southworth-with-Croft, on Sunday, the 19th ult.—lnspector Dowty said the animal was one of two horses which were drawing a waggonette with 19 passengers, and had been driven seven miles. It was suffering from contracted tendons and covered with weals on the off side, from the whip. The defendants were in the waggonette. Shaw said he was bound to use the whip to keep the horse up.—Shaw now said the horse was sound but "stood awkward' on its knees.— Collard had nothing to say.—Shaw was fined 40s. and costs, and Collard ss. and costs.—Jas. Green, whose case had stood adjourned for him to produce a veter- inary surgeon, but who did not do so, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit-state at Sonthworth- with-Croft, on Sunday, the 26th ult. A constable said the animal was attached to a one-horse waggonette loaded with passengers, and had under the collar a new wound, the size of a penny, and an old one of the same size.—William Collett, Peter Unsworth, wad Harry Tay- lor corroborated, all stating as the constable had done, that the collar was pressing against the wounds.—Thos. Critchley and Thomas Kerwood said the collar was hol- lowed out to prevent such pressure. He had worked the horse on the 25th, and on the 28th and 30th ult., and it was perfectly fit to work. It belonged to Mr. Connor of Sankey-st., Warrington,—The defendant said he had mentioned about the horse to Mr. Connor, who said there was nothing the matter with it.—The magistrates' clerk said the reason Mr. Connor was not summoned was that the police officer did not know Mr. Conner was the owner of the horse, or whether he was responsible. WARRINGTON Y. Set-Torr.-1f evidence was wanting as to the high estimation Warrington cricket enthusiasts place on the capabilities of Lee, the clever professional attached to the Warzington club, ampler proof was forth- coming on Saturday, when he took his Arst annual bene- fit. A match with the Sefton Club is always a guariantee, for a good "gate." and such was the case at Arpley on Saturday, for, despite the unsettM state of the weather an unusually large crowd favoured the match. The Warringtonians won ths toss, but general regret was expressed at the absence of Mr. N. Hornby, who we understandtwas indisposed. Warrington elected to bat, on what was apparently a true wicket. J. S. Crosfield, and R. Smith opened to Oakley and Rees. The first- named bowler opened with a maiden? but Rees wades- patched for three. However with 13 on the board,. Rees got past Crosfielc.Ps defence,the retiring batsman having only made one. Lee met with a good reception, and after almost being bowled by a yorker first ball, hit Rees past square-leg to the boundary. Another boundary hit was credited to the now-corner, but eventually Smith, opened his shoulders, and Oaklsy came in for some pun- ishment. With 42 runs on, Champion took the ball from Oakley, and Lee drove him for a single. The next ball proved fatal to Smith, for, putting his- leg where his bat should have been, he had to retire for a well-played 29. Lee continued to bat very steadily, and some of his drives were tremendous hits,. but so well was the field placed for the big hitter that no never reached the boundary. Rees was bowling very well at this portion of the game, and after Clarke had+ added five, Rees beat him, whilst Bell was caught at short slip after registering four. Taisey was run out first ball, and Yonge being tempted to hit out, missed a slow one from Champion, the bails being promptly re- moved. The question at issue now was, who was to. remain with Lee to enable the Warringtonians to make. a respectable score, and the unexpected was forthcoming. when Captain Adam joined the professional. Lee was playing admirable cricket, and Adam hitting vigorously,. the century was hoisted amid cheers. Oakley relieved Champion, and the total had reached 103 • when the amateur was bowled, the last wicket having added 17: Lee carried out his bat for a fine 37, made without the semblance of a chance. Sefton had an Ixarr and a half in which to get the runs, and during that time lost four wickets for 75 runs. Roper played well for his 35 (not out), but was considerably helped by rather loose field- legs. J. J. Crosfield bowled an excellent length, and some idea may be formed by the large number of maidens he sent down. Podmore was very smart, and the catch which brought about the dismissal of Cham- pion was well worth the applause which greeted it. Score'

SEFTON v. WARRINGTON (2Nn ELRVENS.)—At Sefton. Sefton won the toss, and commenced on a very slow %icket. Three wickets were quickly down for 12 runs; but T. Stubbs and F. Dickenson put on a lot of runs,the latter being particularly lucky in just putting the ball over the fielders, and,73 runs were notched on the fall of the sixth wicket ; three more were down for another 13 runs, but the tenth wicket added 16 runs in spite of a double change of bowling. Dutton and Isherwood were far away the best of the visitors' bowlers. Unfortunately for Wax rington, a bright sun burst out at the close of the Sefton innings, and, by the time the visitors went in to bat, the wicket, began to help the bowlers, and several wickets were quickly down. While Jolley and Smith were together things looked more hopeful; and again, when Bibby and the captain were together there seemed a chance for the visitors, the last two taking the score to n: The last wicket added 16 runs, and certainly looked like pulling the match off; but Isherwood was too anxious to win, and in trying an impossible run threw the match away. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
MISCELLA NEOUS.

The annual sports of the Warrington Cycling Club came off very successfully on Saturday. The attendance was good and the racing rather exciting at times. The three mile club championship was the most exciting event, and, although W. H. Bellian, the winner, was never very severely pressed, the second and third men rode pluckily to the finish.

The English football team in South Africa played at Johannesburg, on Saturday, against the Country Clubs, and added another victory to their record of successes. The desire to see the Englishmen play was great, and 51000, to 6,000 spectators assembled to witness the game. The weather was delightful, though rather hot for foot- ball. The Englishmen were greeted with enthusiasm, and in response to the cordial welcome of the colonists played up well, though their task was an easy one. The local club did their best, but could make no headway against their opponents. Score :—England, seven goals and two tries; Country Clubs, nil.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Farewell seasons are as common to footballers as they are to people in higher walks of life, and Eagles, after all his talk of discarding the jersey, is again to be a certain player amongst the Salford forwards. The club is under- stood to have a rod in pickle in the shape of a new three- quarter, who, however, is not Sudiow, but may possibly be Smith, of Radcliffe.

Everton have not lost much time in securing a succes- sor to the abeent Doyle, and last Wednesday signed on Collins, of Cambuslang, at a salary of £2 103. per week,. a present of £5O, and 103. for each match wen. These are, I believe,the same terms Donald Gow received from, Sunderland. They are big enouag.,,h, but Everton were in, a bad way, and last week J. Marsden's leg gave way. Collins is a very fair man, and as he is young, he should, de well at Everton.

Preston North End have engaged two new men in Sharpe, of the Vale of Leven,. and Towie,,of Dumbarton, Union. The latter is a centre forward.. A man named Sharpe had his collar bone broken whilst playing for the Vale of Leven against Clyde, on Saturday. Jam not certain if it is the same man who has signed for the North End.

There will be 140 competitors for the Yorkshire Foot- ball Cup next season. The warmest ties in the first round proper are Pontefract (the Cup-holders) v. Brad- ford (at Bradf )rd) and LiveAedge v. Castkgord (at Liversedge), whilst Huddersfield v. Efalifax at Fartown) seems to the plum of round two.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

"The Athletic News" says S. M_Crosfield,Lancasliire's vice-captain, never bats better than when he is in com- mand of the eleven, and everyona.is pleased to find such an able and popular cricketer doing sa well. By the way, the deputy has not yet lost a single- county match in which he has been boss of thashow. it is to be hoped that he will keep it up.

In spite of the weather not being of a favourable kind, there was a capital gathering of spectators to witness the benefit of Fred Lee, the Warrington professional, on Saturday. Lee is a very popular player, and it will be welcome news that he has been re-engaged again for next season,
EX.PLOS/ON AT BELLE VUE GARDENS.

An explosion occurxed on Saturday afternoon in Belle Vue Gardens on tho steamer which runs on one of the lakes. A number of holiday-makers were injured, three of them so seriously that they had to be detained as In-patients at the Royal Infirmary. The boiler was reported favourably upon by the Government inspector in the spriugoL the year.

div.head: AN FARLESTOWN MIN AND HIS WIFE AND DAUGHTIR.
div.p: AN FARLESTOWN MIN AND HIS WIFE AND DAUGHTIR.

HE IMPERILS THEIR LIVES DY ASSAULT. AN EXTRAORDINARY LETTER FROM THE DEFENDANT. At the Warrington County Sessions on- Wednes- day before Mr. W. 11. Bleckley (chairmen), Major Pickmere, and Mr. G. Comber, Joseph Birchall, formerly a grocer and provision dealer, of 1.3, Hay- dock-st., Earlestown, was charged with assaulting on the 11th inst, Mary Birchall, his wife, and Mary Tamar Birchall, his daughter. Mr. A. Browneo olici- tar, appeared for the prosecution. Ile said the facts of the case were rsost lamentable, and the Bench would consider it was a mercy that the defendant was not there to answer a charge of manslaughter for his violence and brutality. The defendant was formerly a grocer and provision dealer, but failed, and a meting of cre,iitors was held, Mr. Alderman Sutton, of Warrington; was appointed trustee, and it was decided that the defendant's' wile should have , the furniture- and that she should:continue the busi-1 ness in her awn name and on her own account. She did so, but unfortunately far her the defendant I was given to-drink and when he- got same he was like a madman,and if he smoked a. cigarmerely the effect of it cc-him was sufficient to maks- him turn everybody out of the house. He was zasarried to the elder complainant at Liverpool, in 1867, and they had three children liAng, one of whom, the eldest, a young man aged 24; did not live at home. On the morning of the 10th inst., Mr. Birchall left home for the purpose of going to Liverpool, and at 12 p.m.. came home. Mrs. Birchall and her daughterTatnar went to bed about 11, and' they had unfortunately forgotten to leave his slippers in the usual place. When he came home she heard him, making a fearful noise,, and her daughter rushed dovmstairs with her skirt about her shoulders, and found him exclaiming about his slippers, and apologised to him for their beingmisplaced and gave thern to him. He immediately began cursing in the most fearful manner, and got hold of her, and was going to strangle her. Her screams were so loud,, that her brother, who was sleeping in the house, was awakened, and came down and had bodily to throw himself against kis father to knock him off his daughter. She escaped upstairs, and rushed int) her mother's bedroom, and though she came out and, apologised to him about the slippers, she had to fly from his violence. As the son was going upstairs, the defendant caught held of his legs and was pulling him downstairs, when he very pro- perly "landed him one." The complainants shut them- selves up in their bedroom, and barricaded the door, and the-defendant came up and burst it hr. When the-door was giving way, and Mrs. Birchall screaming, her daughter and she in their fright jumped out of the win- dow; both. of them in their night-dresses, and had to walk- along a very narrow cornice, and were dragged' by some neighbours into an adjoining bedroom through-the window. The son had bolted himself in his bedroompad knowing that his life was in darwer, let himself down-by means of the sheets and blankets tied together. A policeman came and demanded that their clothes should be-thrown out of the window, and after some- demur the defendant threw these out. On the constable asking him-what he was doing at the windevr on seeing him there the defendant replied that he was studying the White Bear and began looking up at the ;Ides. The Bench would have no doubt he (Mt. Browne) thought that this man was not only eccentric but something- worse. His. wife did not wish to punish him; but she dare not go home and she, her daughter, and-her son had not been since. He (Mr. Browne) suggested that Mr. Birchall should be bound over in his own recognisances. to come up for judgment when called upon, and his wife, if he would only keep away from her, would allow him 124. a week. Mrs. Birchall owned the furniture and the business and was perfectly willing to go• back and carry it on, and her daughter and son were willing to.. help her, but they dare not go back if this man was be permitted to be there.—The defendant was asked by the Chairman if he would accede to Mr. Browne's suggestion, but said he would not.—Mr. Browne then read the following extraordinary letter addressed by the defendant to his wife

13, flaydock-st., Earlestown, Aug. 18th, 1891. My dear wife,r---No letter has been received from r. Browne. I hereby acquaint you that lam summoned by somebody unstated to the Warrington Sessions room at ham, in Warrington on the 19th August for unlaw- fully assaulting Mary Birchall,and Mary Tamar Blrchall, which I utterly contradict, and which if pressed' will oblige me to cross-examine you on all the incidents of our married life. Let me advise you to be wise in time, to come home and receive the blowing up. (" pitching into" is Mrs. Cbrlett's expression) you richly deserve for not having my slippers where they should be, whichyou are to get fromme when I get you by yourself, before I give you, the pardon you have begged through Mrs. Weir. Never mind Tamar and Josey ; they can provide for themselves. This is one way the money goes, and two masters in the house, one a husband of authority,.and thaother a wita of -- • - - -

are not in any ways injured by your couragecins jump, and that von arcquite well. lam your affectionate•hus- band. Signed, Joseph Birchall.—P.S.—l won't with- draw my complete forgiveness which I gave to you when you owned to Jesus in the presence of Tamar and myself that our downfall was your fault. I did'nt and won't upbraid you about it. Don't be such a-hypecrite and. commit another fault. You say you won't come to live with me. Well, if you won't where will you go to ? And if by any chance I can't get on in the world laymy- self I'can claim shelter under your roof when you arethe master of one,and you can claim shelter here in my house which. is in your name. The furniture is mine and the business is mine only in your name. Don't expose your- self any more: You wicked stupid fool. I'm not drunk-- 4 a,m—but I am very sleepy. I have hardly slept since the last bother. Come home. Be happy ; he as happy as you can. Don't receive visitors if they are the cause of such an upset. Who was she? Pardon me writing to you,but I have had no word from your solicitor, And don't know his address, lam acquainting your George and Ellen, and your Charles and Jane with your intended prosecution. I'neither assaulted you nor Tamar, nor yet did I intend, so helpine God. I didn't see you at all. I have had an application from a woman whose husband threatens to turn her out for the purpose if have her for a housekeeper, a very likely woman too, one whom you will know besides other young ones who come in full of smiles. I have plenty of suitable bedrooms. I can do without you, you prodigal woman, but come home, do, and receive your just deserts and have done with it. I am‘ drinking nothing much but pop mostly, whisky,. ale, stout, and smoking tobacco and cigars, besides eating, hut very little sleeping worst of all. Shall I send this letter through Mr. Browne? If so, please send it back with address. Go on with your pro- secution if you like. I am ready for you with an un- noted barrister. Come and wash if you like. I will give you half-a-sovereign a day. nave plenty of money now. I arn allowing myself as your manager during your insanity twenty shillings per day, and charging it to your debit. I cannot think who that gentleman pos- sibly was who here in my absence, and whose comfort you looked after, by removingany slippers, and forgot your husband's comfort by raplacing them, Nobody about here seems to know ; it was done so quietly. Was Tamar out of the room while he was here ? Do tell me, and ease my mind upen the subject. I cannot bring my- self to believe auything serious. No, Mary ; a thousand times, no. / have just been having a god cry,, and feel &little shaky, and perhaps would burn this, only it is written at last. Believe me your hopingand yet affec- tionate husband.—P.P.S.—li am very sleepy, and it is now six o'clock. A humming, whirling noise passes through my head,but I'll do, my duty as far as I can.and keep things together. MP back and feet keep right. Mr. 13rowne in the reading of the letter was closely followed by the defendant,, who several times corrected him as to punctuation.—On the reading being finished the Magistrates' Clerk appealed to the defendant as to whether he would accept Mr. Browne' a offer, but he emphatically retused.—Mr. Browne A. very good plan would be just to apply for a remand until be has been examined as to his mental state.—ln, the course of con- versation with the magistrates, Mr. Browne admitted that the defendant, apart from his violence in drink, was a most respectable man.—The defendant: Right you are, sir.—ln reply to the Bench,, the defendant still declined to accept the offer.—Mrs. Birchall was then sworn, and corroborated Mr. Broatnths statement. She had put her husband's slippers on a shelf for tidiness, because her sister-in-law had come, to see her. They were not in the usual place. Her daughter went down- stairs to apologise to him, on hiaanaking the disturbance, about the slippers, and witness heard her screaming terrifically, and she ran upstairs in a terrible state. Ho followed them upstairs and they barricaded themselves in, upon which he said he would, go for a hammer. She knew if he came with a hammer in the state he was, in there would be no mercy for any ef them. It was a sort of fit of insanity with him, and she did not think he knew what he was going. to do when he vras in it. After &tailing the circumstances of the aasault and the escape already described, she stated that she would allow her husband 12s. a, week and bedding to provide him a comfortable bed if he would keep away from her and let her have the house. He wanted her to desert her children, but she could not do that. There was no truth in the charge made in the letter about a visitor. He knew it was her aister-in-law. The defendant closely and lengthily but frequently most irrelevantly ozoss-examined his wife. On her admitting that he did not see her on the night in question, he declared that he could not have assaulted her if he did not see her. He claimed a dis- missal on this ground.—The Chairman said the Bench could not dismiss the case on this ground.—ln reply to the defendant Mrs. Birchall admitted that he had pro- mised some years ago never to strike her again and had not done so.—He denied using a hammer to break the door in but said it was a brush handle.—P.C. Cameron having deposed to his part in the affair, admitted that he had never seen the defendant drunk.—Mr. Browne applied for a remand, but the Bench decided to proceed with the case.—Mr. Birchall cross-examining Caniergn somewhat irrelevaatly the Ranch checked the

1 defendant, who saidhe only wanted to prove that he was not out of his mind.—Mise Birchen then deposed to the assault upon her. She stated that on coming in the defendant came to the foot of the stairs and shouted "Where' is my slippers " She went down and gave him them, and apologised, and he raised them to strike her. She ran into the cellar, and he followed her. She held the door and ran out on his goino•aaway. When she get to the bottom of the stairs he seized her by the throat and raised his fist to strike her, and then her brother came, and she got away. The witness described the after circumstances already de- tailed, and how she and her mother escaped along the narrow cornice and were dragged into the next house.— The defendant, after cross-examiaing kiedaughter, char- acterised her as a very disobedient girl, but her mother rejoined that she wasthe best girl that ever lived.—Miss Birchen state] that her father was under the influence of drink at the time, though not drunk, but he was ten times worse than he would have been if drunk.—Joseph Alfred Birchall, the son, having given evidence, Joseph, W4sley deposed to dragging Miss Birchall through his' bedroom window, and also;. with the help of histrother, Mrs. Birchall; and said it was marvellous how they managed to get along the.narrow ledge.—The eefendant 'was' again asked whether he would accept his wife's offer, -but still declined, and said he would sooner 'go to prison. Phsently he handed the house key to her, ask- ing," Why net let me come ?":—Mrs. Birchall: Well go away for six months, then you will be better then. —The de!endant lam well now.—Mrs. Birchall : And give up • drinking, and be another man.—The defendant: Mind put my slippers under the sofa. (Laughter.)—Major ickmere : We were just thinking about giving him six' months.—The defendant: Well; sir, I will go. lam , Birchall (to theßench): You will punieh us if you do. We shall suffer more than he will. (TO the defendant) Now take the money and go away, and have a nine-time of it. Give ap • drink. Now do take advice, JOseph.—The defendant: ;But I shall remember you waking me with your talk in bed- (To the Chair- man) : It is a fact, sir. I have teen put upon.—On the magistrates again appealing to him, he replied "Let them do vitiat'l telt them, put my slippers under the sofa. (Lanehter).—rhe Chairman, told him that he had endangered 'the lives of his wife and 4aughter and if they had fallen and been killed he would have been indicted for manslaughter.—The defendant :.Well, I should have got off because it was not my fault. Itave not assaulted them yet. I annaerfectly willing to go home and work like a slave, tart rwill not be trodden on. (Here the de- fendant leant down with his head on his arm and wept bitterly. His daughter also commenced weeping.) He promised that he would go home anti `never contradict them in anything;:and they could have whatever they had a mind, and they could put his slippers where they liked. He would Are governed by thetni and if they chose to deprive him, of his glass of beer he would not touch another glass: It was no use sending- him to prison, because when he came out he might be worse than ever. —The Bench fined the, defendansllo3. and costs, and granted his wife a i3dicial separation.—Ml; Browne said Mrs. Birchall asked/for no alimony. He explained as to denying the assault upon her that though < the defendant did not strike her- his conduct amounted to assault under the Act of Parliament.—The defendant did not pay the fine but was allowed some days to pay. A most affecting scene took place in court between, him and his wife and daughter, at ,the close of the case, Mrs. Birchall assuring him of her assistance, if he would keep away from her.
A BERLIN TRAGEDY. A BARON COMMITS MURDER AND SUICIDE.

LEIPZIG, THURSDAY. horrible tragedy was perpe- trated here in the early hours of this morning, when Baron Zedlitz Neucherch, a student at the University, paid a visit to the lodgings of Madame Lizzie Neissner, a woman with whom he had for some time been intimate. He appears to have teen jealous, and had a qizarrel with her, in the course of which he shot her head, and then committed suicide. The Baron is the son of a well- known Berlin politician.

THEIR MEANS OF COMMUNICATION

Mr. Gladstone writesas follows to the Central News: The letter of Mr. Parnell in the "Pall Mall GAzette " of yesteraay states that I have possessed means of com- rsunicatim with him which I have frequently employed on behalf of Mr, 'Morley. On very rare occasions I have ben so fortunate as to see• Mr. Parnell in the House of Commons, otherwise his address and residence have been totally unknown to me. He told me his best address was at the House of Commons, buta could not count upon any period within which a letter so directed would reach him, hence / addressed my letter of last November to Mr. M'Carthy, for I had no other means of getting anything into the hands of Mr. Patnell before the meeting of the Irish members. div.p: TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIEENT IN SWITZERLAND. FOURTEEN LIVES LOST.'
34114.-01r-Ttlth‘4"..rti..isa,

-,014 at 7.15 a most serious railway accident occurred at the villa7.o of zollilsofen, close to Berne. The special train No. 2246 of the Jura-Simplon Line,filled with people coming from neighbouring towns to attend Monday's fête at Berne, arrived:at the station of Zollikofen and was about to be shunted + off the main line so is to allow the passing of the Paris. express train, when the latter came, up before the special had been shunted and dashed into its rear. Happily there was an empty luggage van at the end of the train, and this staved off the shock to some extent. Eta the long pas- senger carriage next to it was overthrown and wrecked, with appalling results.- The number of killed and in- jured is reported to be large. According to the latest information, 14. persons, mostly women, were killed on the spot, while at least 24 were seriously injured. The spectacle presented by the dead and wounded, most of whom were in holiday attire, was a most gruesome one, and afforded a revolting contrast to the festivities in which the ill-fateit passengers had hoped to participate. The injured were conveyed with all possible speed to the hospital at Berne, and steps were at once taken by the authorities to bring the popular rek-ins, in which the whole tq.wn was engaged, to a close at the earliest possible moment.
