THE LATE MR, JAMES MITSPRATT : AN EXTRAORDINARY CAREER.

The late Mr. James Muspratt (father of Mr. E. H. Muspratt, of Widnes and Liverpool), was born in Dahlia in the eventful year 1793—the year in which the French brought their King and Queen to execution: declared War against England, Spain, and Holland ; invaded the Netherlands ; conquered Savdy, and broke into Germany. We read that in 1812, when he was 19 years of age, young Mae- pratz: joined Wellington's army, and, as a soldier in the Spanish struggle—fought, no doubt, like a Hotspur, and took part in the use of "vile guns, drums, and villainous saltpetre." Bat James, after a time, was led to indulge the thought that the. sea rather than the land was the domiin for which his energies were destined. To him the campaign had bsen a most unprofttable piece of service. Thus, en reaching Lisbon, he decided that he would relinquish the army for the navy. He had been anything but fortunate. under Wellington, save as. to " honour and glory?' Whether he was more fortunate at sea is a question; but it was only after' several years in the naval service that he resolved to make another change. It was to return to DUb- link where, when we nemt meet with him, !leis. married, and is in partnership with a Mr. Abbott, their business the preparation of certain chemical products for which. they feel they could increase• the demand by making the supply less difficult of attainment. It was while here, in 1821,.that Mr& Muspratt gave birth to James Sheridan Muspratt,. afterwards so distinguished iirchemical science.

We-next find James Muspratt in England, and in? the year 1822, it is seen that helms commenced his. Liverpool career as a manufacturer; his earliest task being to enable the world, to dispense with kelp and barilla. Raw soda WA* first made, and then (after chambers for sulphuric acid had been erected and many stages of development succe.s- oively attained) large quantities- of the new pro- dticts—carbonate and sulphate off soda—began to tell upon commerce and manufactures. For six years- (1880-36) this business was productive of immense profits ; it was virtually a monopoly, and was not only the making of the Vauxhall works as. an established success, but was also the commence- ment of the' making of Widnes, and U) some extent of St: Helens- and Newton as well. Of course the Liverpool success had its disadvantages; a onoe beautiftil suburb of the town was brought under mephitic fumes antagonistic to vegetation, paint, and breathing.

When James Muspratt had first succeeded with his new, substitute and had arrangei for a large production; he was obliged to give away tons of materialto the soap manufacturers in order to in- duce them to make a trial. After a time the demand became so great that he had to discharge the crude soda red-hot into iron carts, to be hurried off to these same. manufacturers. And truly,- it offered many advantages. In its form for glass-making one was bothered no longer with what—as those who have read Hugh Miller's delightful autobiography, "My Schools and Schoolmasters," will ramember— is a seaweed most difficult of collection. Mixed up with the other ingredients used in making glass, it secured an effectual fusion of the mass; but there were several troublesome operations with it before it could be used, and its preparation was eostly as well as cumbersome.

James Muspratt was the leader in the rsvolution which brought the new possibilities into play. :It is noteworthy, too, that he was revolutionary in something eli3e. In the summer of 1836 there was held a public meeting under the auspices of the Liverpool Rtform Association. The patriotic party "wish to show their respect and grat!tude:"" to the "great agitator," Daniel O'Connell, for the eminent services be has rendered to the cause of civil and religious liberty. They also propose to raise a fund towards defraying the political expenses to which Mr. 0/Connell has been subjected in the defence of his seat for Dublin. Mr. James Brine- - ker occupies, the chair, and among the gentlemen who addressithe meeting are Mr. Egerton Sniith, . Mr. William,nathbone, and our Irish friend (who settled here because we were near the coal, beds) Mr. James.M'uspratt. Everything goes off :admir- ably, and,a subscription, amounting to a consider- able sum,,is raised for the champion of Ireland's "reasonable demands," so-called in those days. Politics, however, could not be allowed to check Mr. Muspratt'S chemical ingenuity. In 1839;1 in conjunction with Mr. Tennant, of the, -Glasgow Alkali Werlts,he had the satisfaction of introducing pyrites into use. This was another important indus- trial achievement; and now we have to hurry for- ward to another scientific battle and victory, result- - ing from ,a connection with the eminent German chemist. Jiistus von Liebig. Mr. Muspratt had resolved, that his sons should have the best scientifiC - education possible, and three of them., studied chemistry at Giessen and Munich under this great German. It was from a desire to carry oat some of t Liebig's suggestions that Mr. Muspratt obtained a. patent, in- 1845, for the manufacture of mineral, manures. These were intended to supply to the - land exactly what was wanting for the growth of any particular article of field produce, and so render- fallowing and the rotation of crops unnecessary. In this -matter too strict a regard for .Liebig's ideas ledi to a partial failure at first; but James Mnspratt also had ideas, and he pulled down, rebuilt, and ex- perimented with a result that, opened out, an astounding field of good fortune, in the waynf -pro- ducing artificial manures; indeed, everything ultimately prospered that this man had his own free play with; thus, in the course of years "41us- pratt's Chemical Works" in Liverpool,. in Widnes, and in, Flint. became noted, not only. as- among the largest in the world but, also as models, from,. which the greater portion of the. British and., German chemical industry has profited. Liverpool has directly and indirectly, derived immense gains:from these : for consider what an amount of benefit there has been, merely; in the . dock, harbour, and town dues,-upon th e innumerable .articles of export owing their form„ to the earlier thought of James Muspratt, Think,... for instance, .of what St. Helens sends daily that but for this ms,n.'spraetical genius and spirit of enterprise,.would never, perhaps, have been produced! : Then, as to Widnes, should not Liverpool look nponler-as her own.prai_gi ? _

In, a ripe old age Mr. Musprett, retired from business, and, no doubt, at his Seaforth MIL often recalled old times, when, "without shouldering a crutch," he could "show .how fields were won." One of his delights must have been to coatrast the e.Q.called "good old times "of the • press-gang, pro- hibitive fiscal duties, and dark.bread,.writh, our own times of free trade, national education,. and cheap literature. He would look back and speak with pardonable pride c the part he had played in ad--- vancing scientific Mssprovements ; not the least no-- table facts in his-purview being these: that the. discovery he had worked upon was. first made by.- De. Brian Higgins in 1781, but (s.e.Dr..James Sheri-- dun Muspratt tolls us in his Dictionary of Chemiat.- try) was too expensive a process that the National., Convention of the French Republic; being unable to, r. obtain barilla from Spain, owing to The war, made :an appeal to the chemists. of Vtance for a cheap, process, and that of mamy, suggestions, the one -of M. Le Blanc was the best. A manufactory was. erected at St.. Denis so early as the year 18041; :yet England was unable to profit by the discovery. °w-. ing to a virtually prohibitive duty of 15s. a bushell lon salt (which had to-be decomposed with sulpburi*. lacid or sotzra other clietnical to-produce the requiredi sulphate of soda). This impost was not reduced: until'about the year.lB22, -when, as we have seem, James Dinspratt took, up the idea and added. im- provement to improvement till quite a successlou of discoveries were made,

A CHRISTIAN MARRIAGE IN TURKEY.

The population of Aleppo (seys Puller, in his interesting Tour through the Turkish empire) is considerable, and almost exclusively Mahometan ; for the Ensyrian idolaters reside chiefly ,in the 'villages, and not more than a hundred Christian families are now to be found at this primitive seat of their religion, all of them Greek schismatics. To one of the principal of these—a young man named Yussuff Saba—l had letters of introduction from Moosy Elias. He received me very kindly, but excused himself from lodging me in his house, wlich he said was in a state of great confusion. An old steward who had lived for many years in his family was going to be married; and, acoording to the customs of theeeconntries, where the distinction between master and servant is not so strongly marked as among nations which-have made a greater progress in refinement, the marriage was to take place at his master's house; and Yuseuff, in order to show his respect for his old domestic, had determined that It should be celebrated with due magnificence. The ceremony was not to take place till two days after- wards, but the visitings and feasting-s had already commenced, and the bustle of preparation was at its height. Yeseuff, therefore, provided me with an apartment at the house of his brother-in-law, another wealthy Christian, where he thought I should be more quiet than in his own. Durieg the ,greater part of the next day, the rain kept me 'in-doors, and when evening came I was glad to seek for amusement in a visit to the wedding party. I found a large assembly, chiefly composed of the -Christian inna.bitants of the town, but mixed with a few of the neighbouring Ensyrian peasants. fn the middle of the room was an emaciated old man, with grey hair and beard, whom I soon discovered to be the family buffoon. The company seemed much amused by his odd sayings and grotesque attitudes; but the most effective part of his wit ap- peared to consist in the enormous quantity of aquavitre which he drank, and at every draught there was a general peal of laughter. Nor did the other guests appear less disposed to imitate than to applaud old Simone, as a small glass was handed round every quarter of an hour, and I observed very few who ever allowed it to pass. The Christians In the north of Syria are extremely addicted to -aqua-vitre, partly from taste, and partly because their Mahometan neighbours are confined to water only. Drinking they therefore esteem a distinctive 'mark Of their religion, and their zeal and orthodoxy are gauged by the quantity of strong liquors which they are able to swallow. The other amusements of the nevening were singing and dancing, in which several of the company took a part. About an hour after midnight, the party broke up, having passed the evening with the greatest harmony, and 'without riot or excess.

div.head: PRESENCE OF MIND
div.p: PRESENCE OF MIND

Daring 'Lord Exmouth's attack on the batteries of Algiers, in 1816, the Algerines used a great llUM- ber of red-hot shot, particularly in the early part of • the action. On board his majesty's bomb Infernal, one of these comfortable articles came in, throogh Wallis the purser's cabin, in the after cockpit; and having bundled a shelf full of books on the top of • the assistant surgeon, Jones, who was lying in the purser's cot, given over with the Gibraltar fever, it • rolled across into the opposite cabin, and was there • got into a bucket of water, by the gunner and some others stationed near the spot. This interesting • amusement was but just concluded, when the men in the magazine, the door to which was close by, heard a desperate smash among the powder barrels, and were almost covered with a cloud •of loose dust and powder, which was thrown all over them. Knowing the business which 'employed the gunner in the cockpit, but just the moment before, they naturally enough, in the con- fusion of the moment, called out to him, "A red- hot shot in the magazine I" and were rushing out of it to circulate wider the same cry, should their new red-hot acquaintance permit them. The ill consequences of this may be easily conceived; the only chance for any one on such an occasion being to jump at once overboard. The gunner in an Instant saw that if the cry was false, it was folly to spread it, and, if true, it was useless. He flew to the magazine, shoved the fellows back into it, and turned the key on them, and stood there, with his hand on the lock, till he knew all danger must be past ; rather a queerish situation, gentle reader! The chaps were afterwards a little laughed at; for, strange to say, we could not find this intruder on their equa- nimity of temper any where; and many doubted at last if any shot had come into it at all. To be sure there were the broken barrels and the spilled pow- der in favour of the narrators of the story' but tills . seemed still not fully to convince; for even the worst of dangers generally get laughed at when they are over, by our happy-go-lucky sons of Neptune. When, however, she came to return her powder into store, after arriving in the Thames, the mystery was solved; it was then found that the said shot had gone through four barrels of powder, and lodged itself very comfortably in the middle of a fifth. The gunner's name was Coombs; and the last time I saw this man, who had shown such .an unexampled presence of mind, was In 1824; he was then mending shoes in a .solitary room in the .back lanes of Deptford, to help out a precarious *existeace.— United Service. Journal.

div.head: GARRICK AND 818 STEAK.
div.p: GARRICK AND 818 STEAK.

On one occasion, Garrick dinedin the beef-steak :room at Covent Garden, ready dressed in character for the part of Ranger, which he was to perform the same night at the other theatre. Manger appears in .the opening of the comedy.; and as the curtain was •not drawn up at the usual time, the audience began to manifest considerable impatience, for Garrick had not yet arrived. A call-boy was instantly dispatched for him, but he was unfortunately retarded by a line of carriages that blocked up the whole of Russel- street, which it was necessary for him to cross. This protracted still farther the commencement of the piece; and the house evinced considerable dissatis- faction, with cries of " Manager,manager 1" When Garrick at length reached the green-room, be found Dr. Ford, one of the patentees, pacing backwards and forwards in great agitation. The moment the doctor saw him, he addressed him in a strong tone of rebuke. "I think, David, considering the stake you and I have in this theatre, you might pay more :attention‘to its business." "True, rn.y.good friena," returned 'Garrick, "I should have been in good Lime; but I was thinking of my .steak in the other." The appearance of their favourite soon pained the ,audience, and Garrick went through the character 'with more vivacity than ever.

div.head: TWO BLOWS.
div.p: THE TWO BLOWS.

Cardinal Mazarin was dictating one day a letter .io his secretary. The latter, overcome with laces- aant work, fell asleep, and the cardinal continued dictating, while pacing up and down his study. When he had come to the conclusion, he turned towards his secretary, saying: "End as usual." 'He then perceived that the first lines of the letter anly were written. The cardinal was very partial ;o that secretary, and treated him as a father. To make him, he gave him a box on the ear; the iecretary, in a fury, returned the blow. The utrdinal, without showing the least emotion, said, "Now, sir, as we are both wide awake, let us ?mooed with our letter."—The Parrot.

div.head: WIDOW OF BURNS.
div.p: WIDOW OF BURNS.

An 'English gentleman visiting the widow et Robert Burns, the Scottish poet, at Dumfries, was ticeedingly anxious to obtain some relic of the pard, as lie called it; that is, some scrap of his landwriting, or any other little object which could ae considered a memorial of the deceased. Mrs. Burns replied to all his entreaties, that she had already given away every thing of that kind that was remarkable, or that she c.ould think of parting with; that, indeed, she had no relic to give him. still the visitant insisted, and still Mrs. Burns aeclared her inability to satisfy him; at length, pushed by his ,good-humoured entreaties to very, txtremity, she as good-humouredly said, Wolf, sir, unless you take myself, I really can think of no Atter relic (relict) of him that it is in my power to rive, or yours to receive." Of Course this closed he argument.

WARRINGTON WATERWORKS COMPANY..
HALF-YEARLY MEETING.

The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders ef this Company was held on Wednesday afternoon at the offices of the Company in Cairo-st. In the absence of the chairman, Lord Winmarleigh, the deputy-chairman, Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., pre- sided. There were also present Messrs. .T. C. Parr, P. Stubbs, J.Geddes, T. B. Foster (Manchester), T. W. Mellor (Ashton-under-Lyne), R. Davies, •H. Nield, J. Shaw-Green, James Jolley (South port),W Fairhurst, W. Mawdsley (Garston), Jno. Sankey, (Appleton), E. J. Nicholson (law clerk), and J. Ross (secretary). The Directors submitted their report and state- ment of accounts for the half-year ending 30th June, 1891, as follows : "The revenue account shows a balance including £1,167 9s. 3.0 d. brought from the previous half-year, of £5,366185. Bd. The dividend on the £40,000 preference stock amounts to £9OO, leaving a balance of £4,466 183. Bd., out of which the directors recommend that there be paid for the half-year the maximum statutory dividends of £7, £7 10s., and £lO per cent. upon the Company's ordinary seven per cent., seven-and-a-half per cent., and ten per cent. shares respectively. The balance remaining unappropriated is £1,354 Bs. Bd. As stated in the last half-yearly report, by virtue of the provisions of the Warrington Extension and Water Act, 1890, the undertaking of the company has been acquired by the Corporation of Warrington, as on and from the Ist July instant, and has become the property of the corporation, subject to the adjustment of current accounts , and to the execution ot the deed of conveyance and other necessary documents. The accounts are now in process of settlement, and the company's undertaking will shortly be legally transferred to the Corporation. At the present time the directors, under the provisions of the Act, are carrying on the undertaking for and at the ' cost of the Corporation, as from let of July instant until the actual transfer. This report and statement of accounts therefore constitute the last ordinary half-yearly report and statement which will be laid before the share- holders Ly the ditectors. Each shareholder and stock- holder in the company will receive from the Corporation of Warrington, in exchange for his share or stock-certifi- cate, an annuity certificate as provided by the act, and will be entitled therefrom to an annuity, redeemable as stated in the act, of equal amount (in the case of shares) to the maximum statutory dividend upon such shares respectively, and (in the case of preference stock) to the present preferential dividend of £4 10s. per cent. upon such stock. The annuities are payable half-yearly, on the 30th June and 31st December, without deduction (except for income- tax), the first payment falling due on 31st December next. Holders of preference stock who have given notice of their intention to exercise the option conferred upon them by section 37 of the Act will receive, in lieu of an annuity certificate, an Annuity Bond, redeemable by the Corporation within one year from 30th June last, at 30 gears' purchase (i.e. at £.135 per £lOO stock), together with a proportionate amount of the annuity for the current year. Notice will be given to all share- holders and stockholders as soon as the annuity certificates and bonds are prepared, and the Corporation are ready to 'exchange them for share and stock certificates respectively. In the meantime any further information required on this ot other matters relating to the transfer can be cbtained on application to the company's secretary. A final report and statement of accounts will be.submitted to the shareholders previous to the dissolution of the company." On themotion of the Chairmau, seconded by Mr. J. C. Parr, the report was unanimouslyadopted,and dividends according to the recommendations of the directors were declared. A cordial vote of thanks having been accorded the Chairman for presiding the meeting terminated,
THE FOOD TEMPLAR VAN MISSION.

The mission van, which is at present touring in England, honoured Earlestown with a three days' visit, commencing on Saturday. To many the in- stitution and object of the van may be a mystery, and perhaps it would be as well to state that it is purely and simply a porLable meeting place, for the dissemination of temperance principles throughout the kingdom under the auspices of the Good Temp- lar order. Its institution emanated from the mind of Bro. J. B. Collings, of Birmingham, grand secre- tary of the order, and the interior of the van was designed by Bro. Jos. Malins, G.U.T., a large portion of the fittings being his own handiivork.Outwardly, it has the appearance of a better class gipsy's van, but the interior is arranged in such a manner as to render it a most comiortable and 'unique living apartment. Everything is of the collapsible order, and the domestic equipments are of the unbreak- able description. There is a well-lined bookcase, stored with hundreds of temperance books, and sleeping accommodation reduced to the very smallest space possible. On the Bth of July, last year, the van and its work was inaugurated, and on the 21st of the same month, it started on its work of carrying tem- perance principles into almost unapproachable villages and hamlets. Penshurst was its first halting place, and after working Kent, Surrey, and the country parts of Middlesex, it found its way into Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. On the last day of November it completed its outdoor campaign for that year. In a little over four months by the aidof the van, and its energetic occupants Mr. and Mrs. Fisk, nearly 4,000 pledges were taken up, and 20 Good Templar Lodges were established, besides Temperance Societies and Bands of Hope. After a win- ter spent in organising, Ar,c., the van again started on its tour on the 9th March this year. Its course was through Southampton to Winchester, but it was overtaken in the great blizzard, and was snowed up for over a week. Re- turning to London, it worked through Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, to Yarmouth. After five weeks in Norfolk, Lin- colnshire was next visited entering from Lynn, and finishing at Butterwick. They crossed the Trent, and got into South East Yorkshire, taking Doncaster and Barnsley and over the Pennine range into Lancashire. In three weeks, ending at eadishead In South Lancashire, they took 334 pledges, and not a meeting passed but they were successful in taking some pledges. Wherever the van goes. those in charge avail themselves of local talent, principally temperance helpers and nobody is allowed to speak from the plat- form of van who is not a practical total abstainer. Sometimes Mr. and Mrs. Fisk have to work alone, and they have been speaking every night, with one or two exceptions for over four months. Before taking charge of the van, they both had a large experience as temper- ance advocates, Mrs. Fisk for the British Womens' Temperance Association and the Band of Hope Union, and Mr. Fisk for the National Temperance League Grand. Lodge lecturer., and general advocate for the good tem- piars and Band of Hope; and they gave up all their spare time to the work, but when the van was inaugu- rated they felt it their duty to break up their home and take to the work in which they have done so much good. The van came to Earlestown from Pesusley Cross on' Saturday, and at night an open air meeting was I, held ,on the Market Ground, at which there was a large crowd present.—Mr. Dring, town missionary, presided, and addresses were given by Bro. R. W. Kirkins, D.T. of Liverpool, and Mr. and Mrs. Fisk. Concertina solos were given by Bro. J. Molyneux,of Liverpool,and several melodies were sung by Bros. J. Taylor and A. Haynes, of Earlestown. On Sunday open-air services were held in the afternoon and evening, conducted by Mr. Dring. At six o'clock a service was also held in the Mission-room Stanley-st., at which Mrs. Fisk delivered an inspiriting address. On Monday evening there was another open- air meeting on the Market Ground, which was well at- tended, despite the unfavourable state of the weather.— Mr. George Clarke presided,and addresses were delivered by Mr. and Mrs. Fisk. During the stay of the van 24 pledges have been taken.—The van left Earlestown on Tuesday for Golborne.

SUDDEN DEATH IN THE PULPIT.

While preaching at the afternoon service at St. Canice's Cathedral, Kilkenny, on Sunday, the Rev. Canon Carle- ton suddenly expired. The suddenness of the event caused a profound sensation amongst the congregation, and the service was at once suspended. It was at first thought that the rev. gentleman had only fainted. The deceased had not been in very good health for some time past. The immediate cause of death is said to have been heart disease.

div.head: CONGRESS OF HYGIENE.
div.p: THE CONGRESS OF HYGIENE.

The final meeting was held on Monday morning in the theatre of the London University. Sir Douglas Galton, who in the absence of the Prince of Wales, pre- sided, described the proceedings of the Congress as a high value, and said that hereafter it would be necessary to increase or sub-divide the sections. It was hoped the formation of the Tropical Sec- tion would lead to beneficial results. After the read- ing of the resolutions passed by the section during last week's sittings, the usual votes of thanks were passed. Invitations had been received from the authorities of Budapest to hold the next Congress in that city, and Minnesota had also been suggested as the place of meet- ing. It was now unanimously resolved that the invita- tions of the authorities of Budapest be accepted.

div.head: SHOCKING DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.
div.p: SHOCKING DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.
MURDER AND SUICIDE BY A MOTHER.

On Sunday, about noon, a shocking domestic tragedy was enacted at Twickenham, near London resulting in the death of one child, the attempted murder of another, and the suicide of the mother under peculiarly painful circumstances. Mrs. Beresford, wife of the steward of a local club, whilst her husband had gone to a neighbour- ing doctor's to fetch some medicine, suddenly attacked her younger son, aged about ten, and cut his throat from ear to ear. She then attacked her other son about two years older, but he succeeded in escaping from her and rushed downstairs, pursued by his mother. Meanwhile, the injured boy, despite his serious wound, managed to leave the house and run across the road to a sweetstuff shop opposite. His path was marked by a trail of blood, and arriving at the doorstep he fell exhausted and died immediately. The alarm was at once given, and the hus- band, returning with the police and a doctor, was horri- fied to find his wife lying dead upon the stairs from a gash which she had inflicted in her throat. No cause can be assigned for the sad occurrence beyond the statement that her husband was under notice to leave his situation, and this is said to have preyed on her mind.

div.head: MORE BALLOON FATALITIES.
div.p: MORE BALLOON FATALITIES.
A MANCHESTER PROFFsISOR KILLED.

NEW YORK, MONDAY MORNING.—In the presence of a large number of spectators Professor Dieve said to be a native ot Manchester, and an accomplished aeronaut, Made an ascent with his balloon at Pleasant Beach, New York, intending to reach the earth again by means of a parachute. The wind at the start was not exactly favourable for the enterprise, blowing steadily along tha shore. Directly after ascending the balloon was caught by another current of air, and wafted out to sea. The parachutist must evidently have misjudged his position, or else considered an immediate descent as his only chance of safety. He detached the parachute, and descended quickly. He fell with some force into the water, where he was drowned, being doubtless entangled in the wreckage of his parachute. The spectators were horrified at the result. FRIGHTFUL FALL OF 500 FEET.

NEW Yoßx, SIINDAY.—Miss Annie Harkes, a rung aeronaut, in descending with a parachute at Cincinnati yesterday, met with a frightful death. The parachute would not open, and the performer fell 500 feet with an awful crash.

ANOTHER ACCIDENT. ROME, MONDAY MORNING.—An aeronaut named Louis Pilroni yesterday afternoon made an ascent from the city of Macerata, on the borders of the Adriatic. The balloon was blown out to sea and -fell into the water. The aeronaut is supposed to have sunk with his car and been drowned. The balloon, free from entanglement, was seen by those on shore to soar away.

letter to tbe Obitor.
A LITTLE FACT.

Sir,--kfter an absence of over two months from War- rington,l returned late one Saturday night,and in walk- ing from the station to my home, I saw more drunkenness and distress in the short space of half an hour than I had done whilst away. And this, notwithstanding that I had been amongst millions of people !—Yours &c.
AN OBSERVER.
THE BREWSTER SESSIONS MEETING.

Sir,—l attended the meeting at the Co-operative Hall, last evening; a meeting of which the inhabitants of our good old town have cause to be proud, not only with respect to the members who put in an appearance, but Slso for the spirit in which it was conducted. The plat- form, I feel bound to say, was such a one as I have never before seen during my residence in Warrington, which is now close on 40 years. I was proud to see our esteemed Rector, in conjunction with the various other ministers of nearly every denomination, acknowledging by his presence the importance of this great question of the reduction of the facilities of the drink traffic. True there was a little opposition, but it emanated from persons interested in the trade—in fact managers for one of the great brewing firms. I sat in close proximity to them, and could name them if necessary,and feel confident that upon mature reflection, they will come to the conclusion that their conduct was not such as to make any right-thinking man feel desirous of emulating it. I am sure it dii not in any way add lustre to the firm of which they were the representatives.— Yours very truly, August 21st, 1891.
WIDE AWAKE.

THE SHUNTING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON. Sir, —Being one of the jury on the inquest of William Buckley, who lost his life in the goods warehouse of the Clitshire Lines Central Station, Warrington, I can- not but think about the Coroner's statement in the sum- ming up of the evidence that had been Fplaced before us where he remarked that the jury had exhausted the question three times over. He also said it was a very stupid act on the part of the deceased to get between the buffers, but he thought it might be taken for granted that the engine did whistle. Tnere seemed to have been a certain amount of carelessness on the part of the de- ceased. He also admitted that there was a little bit of carelessness on the part of the persons who had charge of the train, as well as on the part of the deceased. Now, Sir, as to the first part. I think we (the jury) did nothing but our duty in trying to fully investigate how that death occurred, as I consider it a responsible public duty to perform, and I consider that there was a great deal more neglect on the part of the persons who had charge of the shunting and the train than there was on the part of the deceased, wh3 was taken away from his wife and three small children. My belief is that had he been with us and able to speak for himself he would have told us that he did not hear the foreman shunter shout to warn him, nor yet the engine whistle, the same as Samuel Storey told and John Burgess. George Wilson, working at the same waggon, said he heard the whistle but not before he heard the waggons bump. There was another man also working at the same time that said he was hurt, but he was not called to say whether he heard the foreman or the whistle from the engine. The two that said the usual warning was given were the foreman shunter, Peter Knight, and his fathsr-in-law, Inspecter Woods. Had the engine driver and stoker been called before us, we the jury might have found a little more out. Sir, I should not have troubled you with this letter, only for the coroner's remarks.—l remain, yours, &c., EQUAL JUSTICE. Warrington, August 19, 1891.
MORAL COURAGE AND OUR LICENSING JUSTICES.

Sir,—Our Licensing Justices have a grave and impor- tant responsibility resting upon them, clearly defined by the highest court in the Realm in the appeal case of Sharp v. Wakefield, and proving their absolute power to grant or refuse licenses in the interest of all concerned. They may bless or curse the people by granting or refus- ing licenses. They need no convincing that the facilities for intemperance are too numerous in our midst. They know full well that to increase the number, such.places, would be a curse to the people. To reduce them would help to bless the people. Which must it be Ye jus- tices of the people from your hand must come our bless- ing or curse. 0 let not your moral courage fail you, on this occasion; but carry to a successful issue, your noble and humane cohvictions and intentions made known two years since; which then failed through no fault -of:your own, and reduce the number of drink shops in our town. The people who now suffer through them, will in their heart of hearts bless you for removing those traps hitherto laid to the right and to the left in the way of the people. VVe know that brewers, public*, and their allies will •cunningly and heartlessly do all they can for the welfare of their friends interested in the sale of strong drink, and plead that they do not force their victims to waste their money in drink, which entails such destitution, crime, and suffering amongst the victims themselves, and upon helpless children. But they entice their victims to spend their money in drink. Think of the children who suffer through drink and violation of the laws of nature. These laves of our licensing authorities and drink sellers piti- ully call for the help of all true lovers of humanity.

" Do you hear the children weeping 0 my brothers, Ere their sorrows come with years ? They are leaning their young heads against their mothers, And that cannot stop their tears. The young lambs are bleating in the meadows ; The young birds are chtrping in their nests ; The young fawns are playing with their shadows; The young flowers are blooming towards the west. But the Children 0, my brothers, They are weeping bitterly I They are weeping in the play-time of the others In the country of the free." And all this largely through the injudicious granting of licenses, and the temptations to drunkenness. May our Licensing Magistrates.on this occasion lay the matter deeply to heart, and display their lawful and moral p.)wer by reducing the excessive number of drinking licenses in our town, as they proposed to do two years since, and thereby take up the stumbling block out of "the way of the people."—Yours sincerely, A RILL AMONG THE ROCKS. August 20th, 1891.
FOUL SMELLS.

Sir,—As regards healthfulness Warrington should be above suspicion. Not only are the inhabitants blessed gratuitously with the great scientific knowledge of Mr. John Burgess and his faithful henchmen of the Sanitary Committee; but they have also a staff of paid officials to look after the health of the Borough. These officials are,—

£ s. d. A Medical Officer, salary 150 0 0 An Inspector of Nuisance do 166 0 0 An Assistant do do 91 0 0 And an Office Clerk do 38 10 8 Does it not seem strange then that there should be so much wrangling and speech-making in the Town Council about Sanitary matters ; and, stranger still that there should be so many and so frequent complaints about the bad smells that are continually emitted from the sewers and intercepting depots ! Can it possibly be, after all, that the boasted wisdom of the Sanitary Committee and its remarkable head is only a thing that exists in the imagination of some heated partisans? Or can it be that the paid officials are either incompetent or neglect- ful of their duties? I cannot pretend to solve these pro- positions, but I can and do assert most positively, from personal experience, that the stench in the streets is at times disgraceful, and most prejudicial to health and comfort.

Passing along Manchester-road, on Sunday evening, I encountered, for the whole of the way, most disgusting and sickening odours from the open grids in the streets ; and yesterday the smells sent out from the Lythgoes-lane depot were simply horrible. The day was hot, and many of the poor people living in the neighbourhood had opened their windows toadmit a little cooling air;,but they were soon compelled to close them in order to keep out as much as possible of the stench so very liberally provided for them by their municipal rulers! And it seems that there is no use in complaining. "The Jacks in office," who talk so loudly and promise so many reforms when they are seeking votes, are not to be depended upon. Like their exalted patterns in the House of Com- mons, they promise anything and perform nothing. S.) long as the government of our town is used for the propagation and upholding of Greenallism, or any other "ism," so long will the rople suffer in sanitary as well as in other matters. They have the making of their members in their own hands, and in selecting candidates to represent them let them act wisely and not politically; and above all things eschew the party wire-pullers. Surely in a town of 52,000 inhabitants there should be no great difficulty in finding competent and honest men to form a Town Council without invoking the shibboleth of Gilbert Greenall or any other political partisan.—Yours truly, BETA.

div.head: NEW COUNTY MAGISTRATES.
div.p: NEW COUNTY MAGISTRATES.

On Tuesday morning, at the office of the County Sealkeeper, Preston, the gentlemen named below were placed on the Commission of the Peace for the county of Lancaster :—Messrs. William Mortime-, Warrington; John Phethean, Bolton; Samuel Rigby Armitage, Warrington; James Hodgson, Ulverston ; Henry Taylor Deakin, Bolton; and the Hon. William Cavendish, M.P., Ilolker Hall, Cark-in-Cartmel Ulverston.

It will be noticed that two of these gentlemen belong to Warrington. Mr. Armitage is a member of a family which is well-known and highly- respected in this locality, and, along with Mr. Ziba Armitage, takes a leading part in the managerner., of the large Cockhedge Cotton Mills. Mr. Mortimer lives at Orford where he has a large tannery, and he is also in other ways interested in the trade of Warrington. He has not hitherto figured as a pub- lic man, except at occasional local political gather- ings on the Conservative side.

div.head: COLLISION ON THE MERSEY.
div.p: COLLISION ON THE MERSEY.
CROSFIELD'S STEAMER SUNK.
CAPTAIN MONKS BADLY INJURED,

On Thursday evening, about nine o'clock, a disas- trous collision occurred in the Mersey, opposite New Brighton, resulting in the sinking of the coasting steamer, Ada. The Ada, which belongs to Messrs. Crosfield and Sons,soap manufacturers, Warrington, was inward bound from Carnarvon, with a cargo of slates, and was proceeding up the Rock Channel. There was a slight breeze at the time, and when a little to the north of the Perch Rock Lighthouse a large three-masted steamer, which had evidently ' just come up the Crosby Channel, was ob- served by the crew of the Ada, close inshore and apparently heading round. Somehow the vessels failed to clear each other, and the large steamer—the name of which could not be ascer- tained—struck the Ada on her quarter, cutting her clean in two. The force of the impact was so ter- rific that the captain of the Ada, David Monks, and the engineer, Richard Sudlow, were knocked over- board. The Ada immediately began to settle down, and William Roberts, the mate, and another hand, named James Ward, launched the small boat, which was on deck. On casting it from the sinking vessel they noticed the captain in the water hanging on to a life buoy. They got him into the boat, and then pulled towards Sudlow, who is a good swimmer, and was supporting himself. Having got him on board, Roberts and Ward headed the boat towards the north end of the New Brighton stage, which they reached safely. On getting Capt. Monks on to the stage it was seen that he was very seriously injured. He was conveyed on the ambu- lance stretcher to the top of the pier, and a mes- senger was despatched for a medical man. Police Constable Schofield, certified member of the St. J3lin's Ambulance Association, in the meantime set to work to render first aid to the injured man. Dr. Ross arrived shortly afterwards, and by his direction Monks was removed to the S,-.acombe Cottage Hospital, where it was found that he had been dreadfully injured, both legs being broken and a thigh fractured. Sudlow was more fortunate,escap- ing with only a severe shaking, but he suffered severely from the shock of the immersion. Monks resides in Priestly-st., Warrington ; Sudlow, the engineer, at Selby-st., Warrington; Roberts, the mate, at Runcorn ; and Ward at Liverpool-road, Warrington. Ward and Roberts subsequently pro- ceeded to Warrington to acquaint the relatives of the injured men of the disaster. The steamer which sank the Ada afterwards proceeded into one of the Liverpool docks.

Lieutenant P.O. Simpson, R.N., the water bailiff, left the Landing-stage at 10 minutes past six yesterday morning on board the Dock Board's steamer Vigilant to inspect the position of the sunken vessel and to ascertain if it is an obstruction to safe navigation. The steamer which was in collision with the Ada is stated to be the West Indian, belonging to the West India and Pacific Steam Navigation Company. The West Indian is a new vessel, and was just returning from her trial trip when the accident occurred. She subsequently docked in the Sandon Dock. The news of the disaster was received in Warring- ton early yesterday morning, and was heard with the deepest regret,especially in the Bank Quay dis- trict where the injured men are well known. Cap- tain Monks is a prominent officer of the Working- men's Mission, and is very highly respected by all who know him. It is gratifying, however, to know that his injuries do not seem to be quite so serious as it was first reported, as, we are informed, he has not been bruised about the head. Mr. Ward one of the men on the flat at the time of the collision, came to Warrington yesterday morning, but shortly afterwards he again proceeded to Liverpool with Mr. John Crosfield. Mr. Ward, however, again returned to Warrington last night, as did also Mr. Sudlow, the engineer, who had to a considerable extent recovered from the shock and the evil effects of his immersion. The cargo of slates which was in the flat at the time of her sinking belonged, we understand, to the Warrington Slate Company and was insured, though the flat itself was, we believe, not insured.

div.head: EXA NUNER, SATURDAY; AUGUST Is9l.
div.p: THE EXA NUNER, SATURDAY; AUGUST Is9l.
THE LICENSING QUESTION IN
WARRINGTON.
ENTHUSIASTIC MEETING IN THE CO-

magletrates and, with ehameless greed of gold 'ask that they nekeht be allowed to plant another temptation in the way of the people. (Loud applause.) The magistrates had told these parties to go elsewhere in the past, and he trusted they would tell them this year and in years to come to do The sarnee (Applause.) Warrington had already sufficient temptation, and the burden had year by year become more and more intolereble. (Applause.) The resolution not only asked the magistrates to grant no additional license, but it asked them also—and this with great hopefuNess owing to the recent legal decision —to go still further' and give effect to the universally expressed opinion that there were too many houses, by shutting up some that were now doing a harmful traffic. (Applause.) The magistrates had had dculties in their way in the past, and the fact must be frankly recognised, as it had been diffkult for them- to know, while anxious to do their duty, precisely how far the law would allow them to go. They had not to administer the laws they would wish to have on the statute book but those that were nere. As the rector had pointed out, there had been a general feelihg that a license once given was a sort of property ;:and that being so, magis- trates as a rule had been in the habit of granting a renewal of licenses at a matter of course. lint the recent deci- sion in the High Court of Appeal had eirown the failicy of that position. It was now declared that the magis- trates had an unfettered discretion, in this matter. He ventured to assert that the magistrates of Warringtcn would not be doing the duty which the -law had imposed upon them,unless they considered judicially at the forties coming Brewster Sessions not only the applications for new licenses, but the applications for renewal. Each of the licenses in the town demanded the most careful , scrutiny, and it was clearly laid down by Lord Bram- well in the case of Sharpe v. Wakefield that the renewal , of the license meant no more than the renewal of a lease. The magistrates were now bound to give as-careful and judicial consideration to the wants of the neighbourhood, to the questions of police supervision and of character in the matter of renewals as in that of new Erenses. He trusted the resolution would be supported in a unani- mous manner, and that on this and every occasion the people of Warrington would do all they could to strengthen the handsof the magistrates. They did not come there that night to dictate to or lecture the magis- trates as though they were not prepared to do their duty. They had a duty to perform that might be to some of them a very unpleasant duty, and they wanted them to feel that they had at their backs all the right feeling of this town—(applause)—that they were not alone and if they suffered in conseqnence of what they did they would have the consciousness that a grateful town was behind them. (Loud applause.) Mr. Anna WaratEre seconded the resolution. Ile said he thought they were very deeply indebted to the Rector for the historical sketch he had just given them of the rise of the licensing system. It struck him while the Chairman was speaking, that in one or two ,respects, instead of going forward as civilised people were supposed to do, we had gone backward, for, in the first place, some two or three hundred years ago, as the .Rector told- them, when the authorities took upon them- selves to do such a good work as lessening the number of drinking houses, they were rewarded. Now-a-days, so far as he could observe,itwasthe very reverse. (Hear, hear.) In the second place,he thought it seemed a little odd that,while those who at one time made people drunk gave them clean straw to lie upon—(laughter)—the pub- licans,now instead of. havinga man to-take their drunken customers to clean straw, employed what was called a " chucker-out," and tumbled them intse the street. (Re- newed laughter.) As to the suggestion, about the distri- bution of licenses, he should like to say—and he dared say the Rector agreed with him—that it should not be commenced until, the licenses had first been reduced to something like one for every 1,000. inhabitants. (Ap- plause.) It struck him when reference was made to the 130 millions per annum spent in drink in this country,that the amount per head for every man,woman, or child in Warrington, was something like £3 per year, and that meaut that there was spent in Warrington in drink at least £150,000 a year. (A voice:, and what is tha paying?) That means a sum of £3,000 per week; and if the licenses could possibly be reduced one half only what an immense advantage would accrue to every tradesman in Warrington,and to every institution in the town,moral, intellectual, and social. (Applause.) Touch- ing the question of facilities, he was-speaking to one of the men who would have to deal with the licensing of public-houses, and he said he did not think it made much difference whether there were more licenses or fewer. (" A lie.") This maeistratehad to pass frequently down Buttermarket-st., an'd he (the, speaker) could not help thinking that that street above-all others yeas that in which there were enormous and appalling facilities for taking drink ; -and from his observation as a press- man that street had been the most frequently publicly referred to by the magistrates and the Chief Con- stable in connection with drinking and the results of drinking. (Applause.). A friend of his, visited the town two or three-years agoeand the very first thing he said on coming to his house was that he had seen more drunken people in Warrington that day than in his own town in 12 months. (Some interruption.) Touching this question of-facilities for drinking he might say that in Gothenburg they had a system of their own which had been advocated for this country, control of the public-houses being placed in the-hands ot the- authori- ties and of the people, and as the result of this system the number of licenses had been so curtailed that the convictions for drunkenness had been reduced 70 per cent. (Applause.) He took it that that, as well as a thousand facts that could be adduced,went to show that if you increased the facilities for drinking you necessarily increased drunkenness. Knowing these facts-they should strain every nerve to try to make such art impression upon the magistrates as would cause them to- do their duty by reducing the number of licenses. (Applause.) The difficulties were, great,. but all great problems had to be settled by grappling with difficulties. They wanted the right sort of men to deal with the question, and he might say thatsome of their magis- trates were like the man he had heard of who was said to be three handed, and have a right hand, a left hand, and" a little behind hand." Their magistrates on this question seemed to be a little behind hand, and public opinion as expressed in Warrington, had beert a little behind hand. They were thereto-night to say they were advancing, and coming up to to the level of the opinion of the rest of the country, and meant to take-a step for- ward from that time. The magistrates now knew to a certainty that the matter was in their hands. (" Pity you had'nt been one."—" Turn him-out.")- The speaker appealed, amidst loud applause, that the interrupter might not be ejected. The responsibility clearly devolved upon the magistrates, aud they could- not pos- sibly escape it, and they must be made to understand that if they did not take the path that was clear before them the time was not far distant when the matter would be placed in the hands of the people. (Loud and continued applause). Reference had been made that week by a magistrate to what was called the lax ad- ministration of justice in Warrington. He did not know whether that was intended to apply to the- magistrates, the police, or the Watch Committee—he should think it was applied to all three—but that it was true was be- yond all dispute. So far as his observation went there had not been thisyear a single conviction of a publican or a beerseller. ("Shame.") The administration was lax , compared to what was done 20'to 30 years ago. In 1866 ' 38 publicans and beersellers were fined for breach of the Licensing Act. (Applause.) The speaker after com- ment-hag on the discouragement the police met with in their prosecutions of licensed victuallers, and to the Chief Constable having to be directed by brewers and others interested in the tradeeexclaimed amidst enthus- iastic applause that this state of things ought to come to an end, and that if they were earnest in the matter it must come to an end. He concluded with a stirring ex- pression of conviction of the ultimate triumph of tem- perance principles. (Loud applause.)

The Rev-. A. FREEMAN, in supporting the resolution, said the earliest and certainly the saddest impressions he had received in that town were given him on a Saturday 'night in last September. He had just come to live here, and, after he had walked through the principal streets he got the impressions, first, that he had met an extra- ordinary number of people who were palpably under the influence of strong drink;' and, second, that there was a large number of public-houses in close proximity to each other. (Hear, hear.). Those impressions had been confirmed as the months went on. He thought they were all agreed that the number of public-houses was far too large, and, indeed: he could not understand how a man could walk through certain of the streets of the town without coming to the conclusion that the number of public-houses was far in excess of the public needs and the interests of the neighbourhood. If a man did not reach such a conclusion he must either think that the people of the neighbourhood were afflicted with an unrommon and unquenchable thirst, or that they differed altogether from the people of other neighbour- hoods. (Hear, hear.) It was sometimes said that magistrates could not act purely on their own initia- tive in a matter of that kind, but he referred to in- stances in which magistrates had so acted, and, if he was not misinformed, it was not many years ago. that the magistrates of Warrington asked their- officers for certain returns connected with that ques-. tion, presumably with a view to action like that whinh they were now desired to take. He was told that they had received those returns.and but for some technicality action might have been taken on them. What was now asked was that the magistrates might again have these matters under their observation, and this time see that no technicality barred the way. (Loud applause.) They might be told that property had its rights, which cannot and ought not to be ignored. Very well, let all due consideration be given to that, but he should like to remark that the property argument cut both ways. (Hear, hear.) What about the depreciation of property in the neighbourhood of the houses which were neither more nor less than simple drink shops? What about the memorials from certain parts of the town that no licenses be granted to those parts because of the inevitable de- preciation that must ensue if a public-house was placed there. (Loud applause.) The magistrates might say that there was no strong opinion in the town to support them if they took the action that was urged upon them, and that there was no strong sentiment or opinion in Warrington on the licensing question, but they were there that night to give an emphatic denial to that. There was a sentiment and an opinion and it was, gain- ing strength and force every ita,y, (Hear, hear.), There
was no doubt abouMs—that the flowing tide was with them. (Loud applau.) The resolution was thim put to the meeting, arid was carried enthusiastically, there being only two disacn- tients.

The Rev. F. K. FREESTONMOVed 'That a copy of the foregoing resolution,which has been passed by this meet- ing be forwarded to each of the borough magistrates." (Applause.) It seemed to him that they should not only convey tattle magistrates, in so many words, the resolu- tion that had been passed ,but that when it was conveyed it should be accompanied by a statement fairly put of the important charecterof that meeting,of the large numbers that had attended it, and, further, of the spirit in which the resolution was passed. (Hear, hear.) He refused to relieve that, if the magistrates coned only know of the spirit which had promoted that meeting throughout, they wculd not ueanimonsier accord to the resolution thet de- gree of attention which it deserved. Pf it was said, for example, that that was only a meeting of teetotaller), he thought not OrAy the assertion of their respected Chair- man hut also the unanimity of the vote we a denial to any such mis-statement. (Applause.) If it be said, and he had heard this said in anticipation, that it was nre- thing more than a parsons/ affair, then, he-said, the pr'. ' sence of that audience in those numbers gave the lie' also to that mis-statement. At the same time, if it ; be said that that was but a parsene' affair he for oncedid not mind e he rejoiced on that, occasion that they Bad there ministers of practically every de- nomination. who had come forward to combine- in a bit , of practicanhristianity under the leadership of the rector of the town e (Loud applause'.) They would hear' it said that that meeting was an, attempt to prejudiee the 'magistrates and dictate to bench, but again they had to say that was simply not true. (Hear, hear.) When ibunsel for the plaintiff brought forward his plea and his ease was he dictating to the judge, or was he prejudicing the jury? No, he was simply giving his side of the eyes- t:on and they took that occasion ef making public the other side of that question. It was an old saying teat Enelishmen liked'fair-play, and he believed the magis- trates would welcome the expression of public opirubn and give it due effect. (Appleuse.), If they did not, they were forced into this position; that the only other means open to us to guage public opinion and to give expression to it was by appealing to every person individually,and he believed that if they had in Warring- ton toanorrow,as there had already been la other towns, a personal poll upon the question of reducing the licenses they should have an overwhelming majority in favour of it. (Loud applause.) Referring to a recent report cf a committee of Cheshire county, magistrates on the licensing question Mt. Freeston . said, he just wished to quote from it one short telling sentence. It was this : " We think it our duty to point out that Mr. Congreve, a member of our committee,has saidto,us from 21 years' experience as a chief constable, that no improvement in the character and conduct of licensed houses can be ex- pected, and it is useless to strive for it', until their num- ber is reduced. We endorse that statement and adopt it as our own." (Loud applause.) That was the deliber- ate opinion of a committee of magistrates ;And what that meeting asked the magistrates in this locality to do was to not only endorse those opinions but toact upon them. (Loud applause.) Councillor 1113NRY Roseites - seconded the proposal made by Mr. Freeston. He remarked , that if some of the men who had passed away from , theranles of tem- perance work in the town had been there that night they would have rejoiced to -see that the temperance sentiment in the town had grown to the pitch it had done. (Hear, hear,) It had been statedthat a number of licensed houses in Warrington was eqoalto every 243 inhabitants, but they took that sum and calculated a little further they would find that it meant one' for every 97 adults, which practically meant,' one licensed house for every two decent streets in the borough. Na.one could contend that that was not far in excess of the re- quirements of the town. (Hear, hear.) , They had been told that they had no right to intimidate the -magistrates, but they did not wish to do so,and he found it a remark- able fact that the people who wished to lay the charge against them were themselves attempting to bring in- fluence to bear upon the magistrates of Werring k ton r fearthey should do what was undoubtedly their detty to do at the forthcoming btewster sessions. He had in his hand a remarkable leaflet which had heen issued, he pie- sumed by the Licensed Victuallers' Association of the borough,and sent as he knew to every magistrate in con- nection with the borough. It made some curious state- ments,and one of these was to the effect that the districts• which had the least convictions for drunkenness had the most licensed houses.; that is that there was. most drunkenness where there were least facilities for making people drunk. (Laughter.> He had heard Some very remarkable things said, but he ventured to say that was the most remarkable assertion he had ever heard. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) But he found sufficient from the leaflet itself to e)istify them in demanding that the • magistrates should do their duty, for out of 181 districts Warrington stood, to her disgrace and discredit, eleventh on the whole list for the number of convictions for drunkenness per 1,000 of the popula- tion. They needed no other statement than that to justify their position in holding that meeting. (Applause.) There was a good deal to be said with regard to the equitable. distribution of licenses. He believed in local option, and if a district undoubtedly by a proper declaration,obtained in a duty authorised way. required a license, let it have it ; but they must first ascertain what the opinion, or the district was, and not allow an irresponsible magistracy to take a public-house from one district where it was clearly no use but, a curse and a nuisance, and put itin a district where the inhabitants did not reqyire it. (Loud applause.) What they-had to do was first to reduce the number of licenses to one in I,oooe and then ascertain whether the people required them or not before spreading them about. (Applause.) The question had been asked how it was there were so few con- victions of publicans for permitting drunkenness, but everybody who knew anything at all about it knew what the explanation was—they had first got to purift their Corporation. (Loud and continued applause.) -Grapes did not grow upon thistles,and when they had a Corpora- tion combining within itself the elements of' mischief that the Corporation of this borough did, they must expect to have from it a Watch Committee embracing, a brewer and a publican and a distiller and two or three other members who are directly or indirectly interested in the trade. (Hear, hear.) They must alter -the con- stitution of the TOwn Council, and through, that the constitution of the Watch Committee,and then the police would do their duty as he believed many of them were willing and anxious to do. (Applause.) The magis- trates of this town could not. evade or shirk their , They had not otiir responsibility by saving tlipey-sdhlidp not r nwotahngnitto Some move. ' of them preferred to look upon it as a mere ornamentation,. but it ought not to be so, and it was never intended to be so. Their town cried more loudly than ever that these men should rise to their respensibilities and play the man "for the people and the cities of, their God?' (Loud applause.). The Rev. J. YONoe, said he believed they had made out their case, andlif the justices of Warrington didnot listen to them they would incur very serious responsibility in- deed. None of them could say with any accuracy that there had been no expression of the public 'mind on. the question, for when a meeting of that size could. be got together in the middle of that hot weather he thought it an unistakeable token that the feeling of thecommnnity had been reached and roused. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.)—mr. TONGS then referred to a letter he had re- ceived from Mt. Lawrence Flood, of the •Crosby Hotel, Withy Grove, Manchester, setting forth some objections Ito the action of that meeting in passing resolutions to influence the magistrates. Having referred to the neces- sity of purging the Watch Committee, Mr. Yengeadded that another thing they had a right to ask was that no magistrate should sit on the licensing bench who was even indirectly interested in the business of a brewing firm in any capacity whatever. (Loud applause.) The resoltition was then put to themeeting and carried with acclamation.
On the motion of the Rev. T. Ross seconded by Isift. J. WArtunr; a very hearty vote of thanks was passed to the Rector for presiding, and the meeting thenterminated..

div.head: OPERATIVE HALL.
div.p: OPERATIVE HALL.

On Thursday evening a crowded and enthusiastic meeting was held under the auspices of the War- rington Temperance Federation, for the purpose of making recommendations to the magistrates in view of the approaching Brewster S6S- sions. The Rev. F. W. Willis, Rector of Warring- ton, presided, and was supported on the platform by the Revs. J. J. Langham, C. E. Jackson, John Tonge, F.K. Freeston,E.Moore, A.Freem an, J.Davies, Thomas Ross, Dr. J. H. Gornall, J.P., Councillor H. Roberts, Councillor F. W. Monks, Messrs. W. Roberts, John Walker, C. E. Parker, J. Gandy, R. Storey, J. B. Isaac, G. Bayley, Thomas Birchall, Wm. Twiss, W. H. Butler, C. H. Pigott, C. Wylie, S. B. Stringer, J. Pemberton, J. Warlow, J. Price, J. Owen, W. Diggle, J. Drury, J. Mounfield, jun., W. Johnson, Sec.

The proceedings having been opened with prayer by the Chairman, Mr. W. Roberts read a letter from the Rev. H. V. Pigot, Vicar of St. Paul's,. apologising for absence on account of a service at that church. Mr. Roberts then read a letter from the Rev. J. A. llennelly, of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, Latchford, expressing his regret that an engagement prevented his presence, but his full sympathy with the object of the meeting and hope for its success. Several Catholic clergymen, Mr. Roberts explained, would have been present that night but Thursday night was one on which most of the Catholic clergy were engaged until a late hour. The Rev. H. Gunnell, superintendent minis- ter of the Warrington Wesleyan circuit, also apolo- gised for his inability to be present,but sympathised entirely with the object of the meeting. A letter was also received from the Rev. W. Thornley who said he was impressed with the need of urgent and united action to reduce the evils of drunkenness. The CHAIRMAN, who was received amidst much applause, then addressed the meeting. He explained that on Thursday, while away on an excursion, he received an invitation from the secretary to take the chair, and after his return home late on Satur- day, decided to accept it, but in the meantime MT. Tongs had been advertised to preside, and he now had to thank him for his kindness in at once giving way to him to allow him to take the chair. It was perhaps fitting for various reasons that he should do so. It was right that the rector of Warrington ' should be foremost in every good work. (Applause.) He conceived the present work to be a very great and very good one indeed. He was not, as they knew, a total abstainer, and therefore his words might perhaps come with a greater force to some outside than if he were an abstainer. For these two reasons, therefore, it was perhaps right that he should take the chair. He had the matter under consideration very deeply at heart. He wanted first of all to touch upon licensing legislation for over two centuries, that was, in the 16th and 17th centuries and the first half of the 18th, as detailed in a pamphlet by the head master of the Merchant Tailors' school, at Crosby. He (the Chairman) wanted, them to notice the tendency of that legislation—that it was- throughout, with one single exception, always for the benefit of the community, and not to favour the interests of the drink seller. The first Act was in 1504, at the end of Henry 7th's reign. That Act made it lawful for justices to put away ale-selling wherever they found it convenient to do so. The next Act was in 1552 in Edward eth's reign, and by that Act a license was required from the justices before any person could keep an ale-house. That was, he believed, the first licensing Let. in 1602, at the end of Queen Elizabeth's reign, instructions were given to make enquiry as to what public-houses had been pulled down as not well kept, or unnecessary, and that those justices who had adopted such measures should be rewarded. The next Act, a very terrible Act, was passed in 1689, in the year of the revolution when William and Mary came to the throne. It was said that that Act was the result of a very great commercial impulse; but it was thought necessary to prohibit by this Act the importation of wine and spirits, I and to encourage as much as possible the production of home spirits iu order to increase the funds of the ex- chequer. It was a fatal mistake. The result of that Act was, it was said, that the English people then began to drink spirits,and the practice became so common that people used to put up at certain houses painted boards with notice that there a man might get drunk for a penny, and dead drunk for twopence, and straw would be provided for nothing. There followed three more Acts, in the reign of George 2nd. The first of these laid a very heavy penalty upon spirit-drinking, but it was impossible then to carry this out, and the next Act was a repeal of this ; and then there came one more Act, which was for the regulation of public-houses ; and re- duction if necessary of their number. From that time forward all the Acts had been in favour of the repression of drinking, and they tended every one of them towards the benefit of the community, not to the interest of the drink seller. And yet, not- withstanding that, there had been a failure, and he wanted them to notice what had been the chief causes of that failure. First of all,in the last century and the first half of this, he was afraid public opinion had been very lax in the matter. In high social quarters it had been very little thought of if a man got drunk ; and conse- quently large fortunes were acquired in the trade, and great rewards followed. Thirdly, the idea became very prevalent that a license was permanent property, in- stead of, in fact, terminating at the end of the year, and renewable at the Brewster Sessions. The fourth and last cause was, he believed, this, that the people got an idea that it would be a good thing to have free trade in licenses, and let everybody have a license if he liked. The fatal mistake was this, that though in trade gene- rally the demand created the supply, in this case the supply created the demand. (Applause.) He thought they ought to bear that very carefully in mind—that the more facilities you gave the people for drinking, the greater would be the amount of drinking. He wanted to touch next upon the number of houses. He would compare Warrington, first of all, with Liverpool. The population of Liver- pool was said to be 600,000. In Liverpool last year there were 2,089 drinking places, and dividing 60,000 by 2089., that gave one drinking place for every 285 persons. He thought that was a very awful thing. (Cries of "hear, hear"). The population of Warrington was 50,000 and its number of drinking places 205, one for every 243, That was a very awful thing indeed. (Applause.) But even that was not so bad as the state of things in the country generally, there being one drinking place for every 175 of the population of Great Britain. The proper proportion should be according to competent authori- ties, one to every thousand. He believed 130 millions were absorbed every year in the drink trade, an enor- mous amount when you came to think upon it. Liver- -000l had tried to reform and had succeeded. In 1870 there were about 2,300 drinking places there;. in 1880 ' there were 2,200, last year 2,089. If there had been this steady improvement there why should there not be the same in Warrington? (Applause.) He only wished to touch upon two more points. First he would say that the magistrates should be most particular in their consideration of each application, not take them, as he hoped they did not, wholesale, but consider each case on its own merits—(cries of "hear, hear,")— and where the applicant did not bear the character that he should, refuse to grant his license. (Applause.) And he thought that some encouragement should be given to the police in this matter. (Applause.) They had a most difficult and unpleasant office to perform, and ought to be supported in the performance of it. Another point he had to touch upon was as to the transfer of licenses. He knew that some held very strongly that where a neighbourhood had been free :from a license it would be a great mistake to grant one, and a good deal might be said for that view, but in this town they had places where there were a great number of honses together the inhabitants of which had to go a mile or two to get their glass of beer, and he hoped the magistrates would not refuse to transfer a license from neighbourhoods over- crowded with public-houses to those which were not. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman concluded by saying that he felt very deeply on the matter, none the less deeply because he was not a total abstainer, and lie was most intensely anxious to have the number of public-houses reduced in Warrington, and that it should no longer have the name that he was afraid it had now. (Applause.) The Rev. J. J. LANGFIAM proposed the first resolution. —"That this meeting is of opinion that there are far too many licensed houses in Warrington, and respectfully urges upon the borough magistrates, in the interests of the inhabitants,to refuse all applications for new licenses, and to largely reduce the number of existing licenses,by I exercising, at the forthcoming krewster Sessions, the unfettered powers which the law has conferred upon them in dealing with renewals.". (Applause.) The rev. gent tem a n said he had never since he came into this neighbourhood met with a single person who had dis- puted the proposition .that there were far too many licensed houses in Warrington. (Applause.) The drink sellers themselves tacitly admitted it ; witness their attempts to bargain with the licensing justices in Brewster Sessions. As the chairman had remarked,there was in Warrington one drinking-place to every 24.3 inhabitants. That was a fact of a most appalling des- cription, and it behoved everyone who was interested in the welfare of this town to do all he possibly could to bring to bear upon the magistrates and those in authority influ- ence to induce them to diminish the number of temptations to drink that beset people on every hand. (Applause.) He took that opportunity of recognising in public what he was sure was felt by every member of the Warrington Temperance Federation, the debt of gratitude owed to the magistrates for having in. past years opposed the attempt that had been so speciously made to add to the number of drink shops in this town. (Applause.) In spite of the appalling fact that every 24.3 people in this town were expected to keep a drink shop going, izt spite of the dissipation and vice caused through the tempta- tions laid at the doors of the people, there were not want- ing men of wealth who actually dared to Geme to the

Considenable sensation was.caused in Strabane, County Tyrone, en Monday, by the police arresting nine men— named James Jackson, William Harte, John Cooke, James Kincaid,, John Fletcher., A. Wilson, John Kidd, j'un., and Thamas Kidd—on a charge of causing the death of Hugh M‘Laughlin, a member of the Liverpool police force.. M‘Laug4ilin, it appears, as on furlough in the vicinity, ot Strabane,. and on the fisrt inst., and when walking from Strabane to Arhgarven, was, as alleged, beaten seriously. He was afterwards con- fined to bed, and. died on Monday morning. The accused were brought before Mr. Smith, LP., and Head Constableßobinson asked for their remand without bail, . on the ground that the case might result seriously to one. or all of them.--Mr. Smith declined to accede to the defendants application for bail, and the prisoners were conveyed to Derry Gaol. An inquest will be held. A tenth man, Zhomas Dodd, was afterwards arrested at Derry Quay, on board one of the Strabane banes, ma a similar charge, and was also remanded.

div.head: VIM' OF THE FRENCII,FLEET.
div.p: THE VIM' OF THE FRENCII,FLEET.
Yesterday, just at the time fixed for-the Queen's do— parture for Otborne, the rain began to fall in torrents sadly disappointing the thousands a Aspectators whok had assembled on the beach.

A later telegram oays the Queen has just left Cowes in the Alberta, and is making her way for Osborne Bay, where her Majesty will go on board theirfctoria. All the ships in the Spithead roadstead are decked with bunt- ing, and the gunners are standing by the guns ready for the salute. The-procession of yachts is a magnificent spectacle. The shore islined by thousands-of spectators. The Queen embarked on the Victoria and Albert yacht and steamed through the lines of the French and English warships, anchored in Osborne Bay. Theyacht stopped beside French flagship Marengo, and admiral Gervais went off and visited Her Majesty on her yacht. The weather was very rainy and disagreeable. .
